Given that FIB-4 is derived from routinely available tests at no additional cost, its potential as a practical risk marker within the KDIGO framework deserves further investigation. The concept of risk-enhancing factors, which identify residual risk among individuals classified as low or intermediate risk by conventional prediction algorithms, has been successfully implemented in cardiovascular disease prevention, most notably in the 2019 American College of Cardiology/American Heart Association (ACC/AHA) guideline for the primary prevention of atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (ASCVD). The potential for FIB-4 to serve as a risk enhancer within the KDIGO framework, however, remains incompletely defined, particularly in patients with T2DM and hypertension. In this context, FIB-4 is viewed as a conceptual analog for risk stratification, rather than a marker of causality or temporal prediction. We hypothesize that elevated FIB-4, as a marker of subclinical hepatic fibrosis, identifies individuals with increased kidney disease risk beyond what is captured by standard KDIGO stratification. Accordingly, this study aimed to examine the association between FIB-4 and KDIGO-defined kidney risk (primary outcome) and CKD defined by conventional criteria (secondary outcome), and to evaluate the potential utility of FIB-4 as a risk marker within the KDIGO framework among patients with T2DM and hypertension. Methods Study design and population We conducted a single-center, retrospective cross-sectional analysis of adults with T2DM and hypertension undergoing routine clinical evaluation. Inclusion criteria were: (1) age≥18 years; (2) T2DM diagnosed according to the 2025 American Diabetes Association Standards of Care and (3) hypertension defined by documented diagnosis or current use of antihypertensive medications. Exclusion criteria were: active malignancy, acute coronary or cerebrovascular events within 3 months, acute infection, autoimmune diseases, maintenance dialysis, history of kidney or liver transplantation, decompensated liver cirrhosis, hematological disorders affecting platelet count (eg, idiopathic thrombocytopenic purpura), and excessive alcohol intake (≥140 g/week for men or ≥70 g/week for women); however, in this study, patients with alcohol consumption below these thresholds were retained, and alcohol use in the baseline characteristics refers to social or habitual drinking below the exclusion criteria, viral hepatitis (hepatitis B surface antigen or hepatitis C antibody positive), or known hepatotoxic medication use. This study was approved by the Ethics Committee of Pu’er People’s Hospital. Informed consent was waived due to the retrospective design. Data collection Clinical assessment Demographic characteristics (age, sex), anthropometrics (height, weight), blood pressure (systolic and diastolic), lifestyle factors (smoking, alcohol), diabetes duration, and current medications were extracted from electronic medical records. Blood pressure was measured using standardized protocols (seated position, arm at heart level, average of two readings≥5 min apart). Body mass index (BMI) was calculated as weight (kg) divided by height squared (m²). Laboratory assays Venous blood samples were collected after overnight fasting (≥8 hours). Glycated hemoglobin (HbA1c) was measured by high-performance liquid chromatography using the Tosoh Automated Glycohemoglobin Analyzer (HLC-723G11, Tosoh Corporation, Tokyo, Japan). Serum ALT (alanine substrate method), AST (aspartate substrate method), serum creatinine (Cr; enzymatic method) were measured using a cobas c 702 module (Roche Diagnostics, Mannheim, Germany). Lipid profiles, including total cholesterol (TC), triglycerides (TG), high-density lipoprotein cholesterol (HDL-C), and low-density lipoprotein cholesterol (LDL-C), were also measured on the same Roche automated analyzers. Platelet counts were determined by electrical impedance method using the XN-10 Automated Hematology Analyzer (Sysmex Corporation, Kobe, Japan). Spot urine samples were collected, preferably first morning void. Urine albumin was measured by immunoturbidimetric method using the cobas c 702 module (Roche Diagnostics, Mannheim, Germany), and albumin-to-creatinine ratio (ACR) was calculated and expressed as mg/g. Hepatitis B surface antigen and hepatitis C antibody were assessed by magnetic microparticle chemiluminescence immunoassay (Xiamen Wantai Kerry Biotechnology, Xiamen, China). Ultrasonography Abdominal ultrasonography Abdominal ultrasonography was performed using a high-resolution ultrasound system (Aplio i700, Canon Medical Systems, Tokyo, Japan). Hepatic steatosis was diagnosed by experienced radiologists based on established ultrasonographic criteria, defined as diffusely increased echogenicity of the liver parenchyma relative to the renal cortex or spleen. Carotid ultrasonography Carotid ultrasonography was performed using a Doppler ultrasound system (EPIQ 7C, Philips Healthcare, Netherlands) equipped with a 3–12 MHz linear transducer. Carotid plaque was defined as a focal structure encroaching into the arterial lumen by at least 0.5 mm or 50% of the surrounding intima-media thickness value, or demonstrating a thickness >1.5 mm as measured from the media-adventitia interface to the intima-lumen interface, according to the Mannheim Carotid Intima-Media Thickness Consensus. Lower extremity arterial ultrasonography Lower extremity arterial ultrasonography was performed using the same ultrasound system with a 3–12 MHz linear transducer. Atherosclerotic plaque of the lower extremity arteries was identified using B-mode and color Doppler imaging of the femoral and popliteal arteries, defined as focal echogenic structures protruding into the arterial lumen. Lower extremity arterial ultrasonography Lower extremity arterial ultrasonography was performed using the same ultrasound system with a 3–12 MHz linear transducer. Atherosclerotic plaque of the lower extremity arteries was identified using B-mode and color Doppler imaging of the femoral and popliteal arteries, defined as focal echogenic structures protruding into the arterial lumen. The presence of atherosclerotic plaque at any examined carotid or lower extremity arterial site was recorded. Definitions and classifications Renal assessment and KDIGO risk classification eGFR was calculated using the Chronic Kidney Disease Epidemiology Collaboration 2009 creatinine equation. KDIGO risk categories were derived from the eGFR×albuminuria grid according to the KDIGO 2024 Clinical Practice Guideline ; risk categories were defined as follows: low risk (category 1) = G1 G2 with A1; moderate risk (category 2) = G3a with A1 or G1-G2 with A2; high risk (category 3) = G3 b with A1, G3a with A2, or G1-G2 with A3; very high risk (category 4) = G4 G5 with A1-A3, G3b with A2-A3, or G3a with A3. FIB-4 index and BARD score The FIB-4 index was calculated using the following formula: FIB-4 = [age (years)×AST (U/L)] / [platelet count (×10⁹/L) × √ALT (U/L)] Participants were categorized as FIB-4 >1.3 versus ≤1.3, consistent with previous studies investigating FIB-4 and kidney outcomes in patients with T2DM. The BARD (uses BMI, AST/ALT ration and diabetes) score was calculated as: BMI ≥28 kg/m² (1 point) + AST/ALT ratio ≥0.8 (2 points) + diabetes mellitus (1 point), with participants categorized as BARD ≥2 versus <2. Clinical target definitions Clinical targets were defined following current practice guidelines: blood pressure <130/80 mm Hg; HbA1c <7.0% ; BMI <24 kg/m², and LDL-C <2.6 mmol/L. Clinical history definitions History of cardiovascular disease and stroke was ascertained through comprehensive review of electronic medical records, including documented physician diagnoses in hospitalization and outpatient records. Outcomes The primary outcome was KDIGO high/very high risk (categories 3–4). The secondary outcome was CKD, defined as eGFR <60 mL/min/1.73 m² and/or ACR ≥30 mg/g. Statistical analysis Continuous variables were assessed for normality using the Shapiro-Wilk test and summarized as mean±SD or median (IQR), as appropriate. Categorical variables were presented as counts (percentages). Between-group comparisons were performed using Student’s t-test or Mann-Whitney U test for continuous variables, and χ² test for categorical variables. Associations between FIB-4 (> 1.3 vs ≤ 1.3) and renal outcomes (KDIGO 3–4 and CKD) were estimated using multivariable logistic regression, with results reported as ORs and 95% CIs. Three models were constructed: model 1, unadjusted; model 2, adjusted for age, sex, BMI, systolic blood pressure (BP), diastolic BP, HbA1c, TG, LDL-C, HDL-C, and diabetes duration; model 3, further adjusted for smoking, alcohol consumption, oral antidiabetic drugs, insulin, antihypertensives, statins, and fibrates. Restricted cubic spline (RCS) regression with four knots (placed at the fifth, 35th, 65th, and 95th percentiles) was used to explore the dose-response relationship between FIB-4 and renal outcomes, with FIB-4=1.3 as the reference. Non-linearity was assessed using the likelihood ratio test. Subgroup analyses stratified by clinical target achievement (BP, HbA1c, LDL-C, BMI) were performed, with interaction effects evaluated using multiplicative interaction. Key variables for FIB-4 calculation and renal outcome assessment were complete. Missing data were minimal for lipid parameters (TG, LDL-C, and HDL-C; < 1% each). No imputation was performed; analyses were conducted using available cases. All analyses were performed using SPSS V.31.0 (IBM Corp, Armonk, New York, USA) and R V.4.5.2 (rms package). Two-sided p<0.05 was considered statistically significant. Results Baseline characteristics A total of 1208 patients with T2DM and hypertension were included in this analysis. The mean age was 58.28±10.64 years, and 726 (60.1%) were men. Among all participants, 514 (42.5%) had FIB-4>1.3, 286 (23.7%) were classified as KDIGO high/very high risk (categories 3–4), and 588 (48.7%) met the criteria for CKD ( ). Compared with patients with FIB-4≤1.3, those with FIB-4>1.3 were older (63.85±7.91 vs 54.14±10.52 years, p<0.001), had a longer diabetes duration (10.62±7.55 vs 8.05±7.05 years, p<0.001). They also had lower BMI and diastolic BP. In terms of metabolic parameters, patients with elevated FIB-4 had lower HbA1c, TG, TC, and LDL-C, but higher HDL-C levels. AST levels were significantly higher in the FIB-4 >1.3 group, whereas ALT levels were comparable between groups (p=0.324). For renal parameters, patients with FIB-4 >1.3 had lower eGFR, higher ACR, and Cr. The distribution of combined eGFR and ACR categories differed significantly between groups (p<0.001). A smaller proportion of patients with FIB-4>1.3 had preserved renal function (eGFR ≥60 mL/min/1.73 m² and ACR <30 mg/g; 45.3% vs 55.8%), while a larger proportion had reduced eGFR (<60 mL/min/1.73 m²; 27.0% vs 14.7%). Discussion In this cross-sectional study of 1208 patients with T2DM and hypertension, FIB-4 was independently associated with both KDIGO 3–4 (OR 1.57, 95% CI 1.12 to 2.19) and CKD (OR 1.51, 95% CI 1.14 to 2.01). These associations remained even among patients achieving BMI/LDL-C targets, suggesting that FIB-4 reflects residual renal risk beyond conventional metabolic control. Moreover, elevated FIB-4 was associated with greater vascular comorbidity burden even within KDIGO 1–2. Collectively, these findings demonstrate that FIB-4 may function as a complementary marker for risk stratification within the KDIGO framework. Our results extend previous evidence linking hepatic fibrosis markers to renal impairment. Saito et al reported that FIB-4>1.3 independently predicted incident diabetic kidney disease in a Japanese cohort (HR 1.54, 95% CI 1.15 to 2.08). Takahashi et al observed a significant inverse correlation between FIB-4 and eGFR in middle-aged and older adults , while Mima et al confirmed this relationship across diverse renal pathologies, including nephrosclerosis and IgA nephropathy. Similarly, Oikawa et al demonstrated that high FIB-4 predicted 5-year CKD incidence even in metabolically healthy individuals. However, these studies primarily relied on binary CKD definitions (eGFR<60 mL/min/1.73m² or albuminuria≥30 mg/g), without integrating both parameters into a comprehensive KDIGO risk classification model. In the present study, we evaluated FIB-4 across both KDIGO-defined risk categories and conventional CKD definitions, thereby extending the analysis within the contemporary KDIGO framework. In sensitivity analyses, FIB-4 demonstrated more robust and consistent associations with renal outcomes than the BARD score ( ), and the dichotomized threshold (FIB-4>1.3) outperformed the continuous measure ( ), validating the clinical relevance of the 1.3 cut-off in patients with T2DM and hypertension. To our knowledge, this is the first study to position FIB-4 as a potential risk marker within the KDIGO 2024 framework for CKD management. This concept parallels the 2019 ACC/AHA cardiovascular prevention guidelines, which introduced risk-enhancing factors to refine risk estimation among individuals at borderline or intermediate risk of ASCVD. Similarly, FIB-4 may serve an analogous role in nephrology by identifying patients whose renal risk is not fully captured by KDIGO categories based solely on eGFR and albuminuria. This framework is supported by growing evidence that liver-kidney crosstalk contributes to cardiorenal-metabolic disease. MASLD, particularly in the presence of advanced fibrosis, has been shown to independently increase the risk of both cardiovascular disease and CKD. However, accumulating data also point to marked heterogeneity in the relationship between MASLD and CKD. Accordingly, a recent Lancet review emphasized that MASLD represents a spectrum of heterogeneous disease phenotypes, with varying contributions from metabolic dysfunction, hepatic insulin resistance, and systemic inflammation across individuals, which may translate into differential downstream renal risk. Moreover, the reported strength of the association between MASLD and CKD varies substantially across studies, reflecting differences in disease definitions, diagnostic criteria, adjustment for shared cardiometabolic confounders, and the evolving nomenclature from NAFLD to metabolic dysfunction-associated fatty liver disease (MAFLD) to MASLD. In this context, our stratified analyses by MASLD status ( ) demonstrated consistent associations between FIB-4 and renal outcomes irrespective of the presence of MASLD presence, with no significant interaction (p=0.176). These findings suggest that fibrosis-based markers such as FIB-4 may capture clinically relevant renal risk beyond that explained by steatosis status alone, supporting their integration into multidimensional frameworks for cardiorenal-metabolic risk stratification. The analysis of vascular comorbidities across KDIGO 1–4 ( ) demonstrated that elevated FIB-4 was associated with a significantly higher prevalence of carotid plaque, lower extremity arterial plaque, and cardiovascular disease history, even within KDIGO 1–2 (all p values for trend<0.01). Within KDIGO 3–4, similar patterns were observed but did not reach statistical significance within individual categories, likely due to smaller sample sizes (KDIGO 3: n=137; KDIGO 4: n=149) and limited statistical power. Nevertheless, the overall trend across KDIGO 1–4 remained significant, supporting a consistent gradient of vascular comorbidity burden associated with elevated FIB-4. Subgroup analyses ( ) demonstrated consistent associations across age, sex, diabetes duration, MASLD status, medication use, and alcohol consumption (all p values for interaction>0.05). The interaction between smoking status and FIB-4 reached nominal statistical significance (p=0.022), with a stronger association among smokers (OR 2.66, p=0.002) than non-smokers (OR 1.26, p=0.269). However, this observation should be interpreted cautiously, as interaction tests in cross-sectional analyses are often underpowered and may produce statistically unstable results. Nevertheless, smoking and hepatic fibrosis share biological pathways characterized by oxidative stress and systemic inflammation, which may underlie the observed effect modification. Confirmation in prospective studies is warranted. Notably, despite exhibiting more favorable metabolic profiles, including lower HbA1c, LDL-C, TG levels, and higher rates of achieving clinical targets, patients with elevated FIB-4 displayed worse renal parameters and greater vascular comorbidity burden ( ). This apparent paradox likely reflects disease-related metabolic alterations rather than a genuinely protective metabolic phenotype. Lower lipid levels in the high FIB-4 group may result from disrupted lipid metabolism and impaired hepatic synthetic function associated with advanced liver disease, rather than improved cardiometabolic health. Similarly, lower HbA1c may reflect intensive glucose-lowering treatment (eg, higher insulin use), rather than intrinsically better glycemic control. Reduced BMI in this group may further indicate sarcopenia or chronic catabolic states commonly observed in advanced hepatic fibrosis, rather than metabolic resilience. Collectively, these findings suggest that seemingly favorable metabolic markers may paradoxically signal greater systemic disease severity. Beyond these clinical observations, several interrelated biological pathways may underlie the association between hepatic fibrosis and adverse renal and vascular outcomes. Subclinical hepatic fibrosis is increasingly recognized as a driver of chronic low-grade inflammation, characterized by increased release of proinflammatory cytokines (eg, Interleukin (IL)-6, Tumour necrosis factor (TNF)-α) and dysregulated hepatokine secretion, including fetuin-A and fibroblast growth factor 21. These liver-derived factors act as endocrine mediators influencing systemic inflammation and insulin sensitivity, thereby contributing to multiorgan injury, including renal dysfunction. Emerging experimental evidence further supports a direct role of hepatokin-mediate liver-kidney crosstalk in promoting renal fibrogenesis. Concurrently, hepatic insulin resistance may amplify systemic metabolic dysfunction and lipotoxicity, while activation of the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system, endothelial dysfunction, and oxidative stress represent shared pathogenic pathways linking hepatic fibrosis with renal and vascular injury. Taken together, these mechanisms provide biological plausibility for the observation that FIB-4 captures residual cardiorenal risk beyond traditional metabolic risk factors, even in patients who appear metabolically well controlled by conventional measures. RCS analysis confirmed a nonlinear association between FIB-4 and renal outcomes, with a threshold effect around 1.3 (p value for non-linearity<0.001 for KDIGO 3–4; p=0.010 for CKD; ). This pattern supports the use of FIB-4>1.3 as a clinically meaningful cut-off for identifying patients at increased risk of adverse renal outcomes. This threshold aligns with the current AASLD guideline recommending 1.3 for identifying individuals at elevated risk of clinically significant hepatic fibrosis. Sensitivity analyses testing alternative cutoffs (1.0, 1.5, 2.0) demonstrated that 1.3 provided optimal statistical discrimination for both outcomes ( ). Moreover, dichotomized FIB-4 showed stronger associations with renal outcomes than continuous FIB-4 ( ), underscoring the clinical utility of threshold-based interpretation. Bootstrap validation (1000 resamples) confirmed the stability of the effect estimates. Because ALT is a component of FIB-4, additional analyses were conducted to evaluate potential confounding ( ); the association persisted after adjusting for low ALT levels, indicating minimal confounding. Our findings have important clinical implications. FIB-4 is calculated from routinely available laboratory parameters and requires no additional cost or specialized testing, making it particularly practical in resource-limited settings. Current guidelines already recommend FIB-4 screening for hepatic fibrosis in patients with T2DM ; extending its use to kidney risk assessment would require no additional testing. Among patients classified as KDIGO low risk but presenting with elevated FIB-4, clinicians might consider closer monitoring of kidney function, intensified management of cardiovascular risk factors, or earlier initiation of nephroprotective therapies such as sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 (SGLT2) inhibitors. These agents have demonstrated dual hepatic and renal benefits. Emerging evidence further suggests that SGLT2 inhibitors may lower FIB-4 and improve hepatic outcomes while simultaneously conferring cardiovascular and renal protection. These findings collectively support the integration of FIB-4 into comprehensive cardiorenal-metabolic risk assessment strategies. Several limitations should be acknowledged. Emerging evidence further suggests that SGLT2 inhibitors may lower FIB-4 and improve hepatic outcomes while simultaneously conferring cardiovascular and renal protection. These findings collectively support the integration of FIB-4 into comprehensive cardiorenal-metabolic risk assessment strategies. Several limitations should be acknowledged. First, the cross-sectional, single-center design precludes causal inference and limits external generalizability; moreover, because the study specifically enrolled patients with coexisting T2DM and hypertension, the findings may not be applicable to individuals with either condition alone or to the general population. Second, liver biopsy was not performed; however, as FIB-4 is intended for noninvasive risk stratification, this approach reflects real-world clinical practice and current guideline recommendations. Third, residual confounding from unmeasured factors, such as dietary patterns, physical activity, genetic susceptibility, detailed pharmacotherapy, and socioeconomic status, cannot be fully excluded despite multivariable adjustment. In addition, this single-center study was conducted in a Chinese population, with all participants of Chinese ethnicity, which may limit the applicability of the findings to other ethnic groups or healthcare settings. Fourth, because age is a component of FIB-4, potential confounding by age-related renal decline warrants attention. Nevertheless, our models adjusted for age as a continuous variable, and subgroup analyses showed consistent associations across age groups (p value for interaction>0.05), suggesting that the observed relationship is not driven by age alone. However, the association was statistically significant only among participants aged ≥65 years, indicating that the discriminatory performance of FIB-4 may be attenuated in younger populations and warrants further investigation. Fifth, information on specific subclasses of antidiabetic medications (eg, SGLT2 inhibitors, glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP)-1 receptor agonists) and antihypertensive medications (eg, angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors/angiotensin receptor blockers (ACEi/ARB)) was not available. Although overall use of oral antidiabetic drugs, insulin, and antihypertensive medications was adjusted for in multivariable analyses, residual confounding related to differential use of renoprotective therapies cannot be excluded. Future prospective studies are needed to validate whether incorporating FIB-4 into the KDIGO risk stratification framework improves prognostic discrimination and reclassification, and to determine whether targeted interventions in patients with elevated FIB-4 translate into improved renal and cardiovascular outcomes. Strengths of our study include the comprehensive evaluation of vascular comorbidities, application of the updated KDIGO 2024 framework, and validation of results through extensive sensitivity analyses. Conclusion In patients with T2DM and hypertension, elevated FIB-4 was independently associated with KDIGO high/very high risk and CKD, and identifies individuals with greater vascular comorbidity burden even within KDIGO low-risk. Importantly, this association persisted among patients achieving metabolic targets, suggesting that FIB-4 captures residual renal and vascular risk beyond conventional factors. As a low-cost, noninvasive index derived from routine laboratory tests, FIB-4 may provide complementary information to KDIGO risk categories, thereby facilitating more precise identification of patients who could benefit from intensified monitoring and early nephroprotective interventions. Further longitudinal/prospective studies are now warranted to determine whether integrating FIB-4 into the KDIGO framework improves risk stratification and clinical outcomes. chunks.content: Introduction Diabetes mellitus is a real global health problem. The estimated global population of adults with diabetes was 588.7 million in 2024, and the International Diabetes Federation (IDF) in the 11th edition of its Diabetes Atlas has projected that by the year 2050, about 852.5 million adults aged 20–79 years around the world will be living with diabetes mellitus. Among IDF regions, the African (AFR) and Middle East and North Africa (MENA) regions are projected to experience the largest relative increases in the number of people with diabetes. Morocco is one of the countries of the IDF MENA region and accounted for 9.7% of diabetes in adults in 2021. The increase in the prevalence of diabetes has been paralleled by an increase in the occurrence of its chronic complications, such as diabetic kidney disease (DKD). In 2011, it was estimated that diabetes was one of the main causes of chronic kidney disease (CKD) in Morocco. Diabetic kidney disease is the leading cause of CKD as well as end-stage renal disease (ESRD) and contributes considerably to the additional healthcare costs of the management of people with diabetes. Therefore, early diagnosis and treatment of DKD are critical to prevent kidney disease progression and other complications of diabetes. The detection of a positive albuminuria identifies the early stages of DKD, but screening relies on a dual assessment of urinary albumin (using a spot urinary albumin-to-creatinine ratio [UACR]) and estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR). For most people, DKD is asymptomatic and is often diagnosed through routine screening. Annual DKD screening is recommended by both the American Diabetes Association (ADA) and Kidney Disease Improving Global Outcomes (KDIGO) guidelines, , and should start at diagnosis of type 2 diabetes and 5 years after diagnosis of type 1 diabetes. , Based on these recommendations, DKD is diagnosed in the case of persistently positive albuminuria (≥ 30 mg/g) and/or persistently reduced eGFR (˂ 60 mL/min/1.73 m 2 ) for more than 3 months. , As most patients with diabetes are managed in primary care, primary care providers play an important role in the early detection of DKD. The role of primary practitioners is firstly, to make a timely diagnosis of DKD through early screening of patients with diabetes and secondly, to delay the progression of DKD through efficacious glycaemic and blood pressure control, Renin-Angiotensin system (RAAS) blockade and SGLT2 inhibition in addition to health promotion and comorbidities management. However, despite international guidelines for screening and managing DKD, early detection and treatment of DKD in primary care settings is not performed optimally in routine clinical settings. , A gap between ideal and actual care may be because of multiple factors, including a lack of knowledge about the disease itself, the fear of frightening patients with the announcement of CKD diagnosis, high workload or unfamiliarity with current guidelines. , Therefore, it is important to enhance the effectiveness of the management of patients with diabetes and the prevention of the development of complications. As primary care is usually the first point of contact for most patients with early-stage CKD, assessing the degree of adherence by the primary healthcare physicians to current guidelines that promote early detection, prevention and treatment of DKD is recommended. Objective of the study This study aimed to evaluate primary healthcare physicians’ knowledge regarding screening, referral and management guidelines of DKD in patients with diabetes. Research methodology and design Study design A cross-sectional study was conducted between May 2024 and June 2024, and all general practitioners working at primary care centres of the region of Marrakesh were included. Population, sample and sampling All primary healthcare practitioners working in the private and public sectors in the region of Marrakesh were contacted by phone and were informed about the study. Physicians who refused to participate in the survey were excluded. Data collection Participants were asked to complete a self-administered questionnaire. The questionnaire contained 16 items and was designed to assess practitioners’ knowledge of screening, diagnosis and management of DKD. The questions were constructed by consulting relevant ADA and KDIGO guidelines on DKD. This test included single-choice questions and consisted of two sections: section 1 (demographics of the physicians, length of professional experience and training in diabetes management), section 2 (knowledge level of guidelines about DKD screening, referral and treatment) ( ). A panel of experts, including six consultants in nephrology, reviewed the questionnaire and completed an online content validation form. The questionnaire’s reliability was assessed using the computation of Cronbach’s alpha coefficient. A reliability index of 0.88 was obtained. An online form of the questionnaire was created using Google Forms and was sent to the participants via email or work-related WhatsApp groups. level of guidelines about DKD screening, referral and treatment) ( ). A panel of experts, including six consultants in nephrology, reviewed the questionnaire and completed an online content validation form. The questionnaire’s reliability was assessed using the computation of Cronbach’s alpha coefficient. A reliability index of 0.88 was obtained. An online form of the questionnaire was created using Google Forms and was sent to the participants via email or work-related WhatsApp groups. The practitioners who agreed to participate and completed the questionnaire were recruited into the study. Each item of the questionnaire was assigned a score of 1 if the response was correct, and a total score was provided by adding all responses. The median value of the total scores of all participants’ responses to the questionnaire was utilised as a cut-off point to classify each physician as having low or high knowledge concerning DKD management, screening and referral. Statistical analysis Data were analysed using Statistical Package for Social Sciences (SPSS Inc, Chicago, US) (26.0). Participants’ demographic and professional characteristics were summarised for categorical variables as frequency with percentage, and for continuous variables as means ± standard deviation (s.d.) or median (minimum [min] – maximum [max]). In bivariate analysis, qualitative variables were compared using the Chi-square test or Fisher’s exact test when the expected frequencies were less than 5. In multivariate analysis, to identify factors associated with physicians’ knowledge of DKD guideline practice, a logistic regression model was used, and the results were expressed as odds ratios (OR). A p -value of ˂ 0.05 was statistically significant. Ethical considerations Ethical clearance to conduct this study was obtained from the Ethics Review Committee of Faculty of Medicine and Pharmacy of Marrakesh (No. 5/2025). The objectives of the study were explained to the participants, and voluntary informed verbal consent was obtained from all participants. All information collected from the participants was kept confidential and was carried out in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki. Results Response rate Of the 295 primary healthcare providers practising in the region of Marrakesh, 100 physicians agreed to participate in the survey, yielding a response rate of 33.9%. Demographic findings The demographic characteristics of the 100 primary physicians who agreed to participate are shown in . The mean age of the study population was 45.57 (s.d. ± 10.75 years) with 60% being female ( n = 60). The majority of the participants had less than 10 years of experience (57%), and 81% of them reported following more than 10 patients with diabetes per month. Forty-eight participants (48%) received training in diabetes management. Knowledge of screening, referral and management of diabetic kidney disease The median score of correct answers was 8 (2–13), and 61% of participants had a score higher than 8. The first part of the assessment was about diagnostic criteria of DKD, the timing of first screening and the frequency of screening. Within the project sample, 64% of the participants reported that the diagnosis of DKD was made in the case of a positive albuminuria with or without a reduced glomerular filtration rate (GFR), and that the usual start of screening of DKD should be performed at the time of diagnosis in the case of type 2 diabetes (77%) and 5 years after diagnosis in the case of type 1 diabetes (47%). Regarding the method used to screen for DKD, 34% of the participants chose the UACR, and 77% of them indicated that a positive UACR was defined by a result of 30 mg/g. Only 48% of the participants considered that a positive urine albuminuria screening should be repeated within 3–6 months of the first screen, and that the annual screening should include albuminuria (97% of the participants) and GFR (51% of the participants) ( ). The second part of the evaluation concerned the management of DKD. When the physicians were asked about the first-line anti-hypertensive drugs in the case of DKD, 70% of the participants reported that they prescribed angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) or angiotensin receptor blocker (ARB), and 61% indicated that the recommended target of arterial pressure was < 130/80 mmHg. Upon asking the physicians about HbA 1c recommended target, 48% reported that glycated haemoglobin should be < 7% ( ). Considering the use of metformin, 62% of the participants knew that metformin was contraindicated in patients with CKD and GFR < 30 mL/min per 1.73 m 2 , and 33% of the participants reported that SGLT2 inhibitors were recommended in patients with type 2 diabetes, CKD and GFR ≥ 20 mL/min per 1.73 m 2 . Regarding the timing of referral to a nephrologist, 46% of the participants answered that this referral should be at the time when GFR was < 30 mL/min per 1.73 m 2 on two consecutive visits or if there was a rapid decline of GFR ( ). In bivariate

metformin, 62% of the participants knew that metformin was contraindicated in patients with CKD and GFR < 30 mL/min per 1.73 m 2 , and 33% of the participants reported that SGLT2 inhibitors were recommended in patients with type 2 diabetes, CKD and GFR ≥ 20 mL/min per 1.73 m 2 . Regarding the timing of referral to a nephrologist, 46% of the participants answered that this referral should be at the time when GFR was < 30 mL/min per 1.73 m 2 on two consecutive visits or if there was a rapid decline of GFR ( ). In bivariate analysis, higher levels were found among practitioners over age 50 years and who reported attending training in diabetes management ( p ˂ 0.001) ( ). In multivariate analysis, only training in diabetes management was significantly associated with primary health practitioners’ knowledge (OR: 5.635, 95% confidence interval [CI]: 2.238–14.19, p ˂ 0.001) ( ). Discussion This study evaluated the knowledge level of Moroccan primary healthcare providers in the region of Marrakesh about DKD screening, management and referral guidelines, and determined its associated factors. Our study population was young, with 67% of participants under 50 years of age, the majority were female, and 57% had less than 10 years of experience. Similarly, in a study conducted in Saudi Arabia evaluating clinical practices of primary care providers in DKD, the mean age of the participants was 35 years with a mean experience length of 7 years, but the proportion of male physicians was higher than female physicians (59%). Regarding screening for DKD, our findings have indeed revealed that more than half of the participants correctly identified that a positive albuminuria and reduced GFR were key indicators of DKD. Compared to our results, an online survey of the proficiency of primary healthcare physicians in managing diabetes-related CKD showed that 52.4% of the participants were uncertain regarding their knowledge of the criteria for the diagnosis of DKD. Most of our participants reported that the ideal timing for first screening of DKD was at the time of diagnosis of type 2 diabetes, and that, essentially, albuminuria (97%) and, to a lesser extent, the GFR (51%) should be annually screened. However, our participants presented insufficient knowledge of the optimal timing for screening in patients with type 1 diabetes and the ideal test to use for screening for albuminuria. In a cross-sectional survey conducted among 160 Canadian physicians, including 60 general practitioners, the timing of CKD screening with patients in relation to type 2 diabetes diagnosis occurred for most physicians at diagnosis of type 2 diabetes (58.1%), using eGFR (100%) and UACR (96.8%). In the Saudi study, good knowledge was reported in terms of annual screening (77.4%), timely start of screening of DKD in patients with type 1 (52.1%) and type 2 (75.6%) diabetes and the use of UACR as a screening tool for DKD (85.5%). In our study, good scores were also reported about first-line recommended medications, but low scores were noted about the use of novel treatment (SGLT2i) and the timing of referral to a nephrologist. In a study of adult primary care patients with DKD, 80.3% had a care gap in SGLT2i prescription, and 42% had a care gap in RAASi prescription. These care gaps for SGLT2i and RAASi were especially observed in patients with DKD with well-controlled diabetes and blood pressure, suggesting failure to recognise DKD as an independent indication for these medications. On the contrary, the Saudi study showed high rates of prescription of ACE inhibitors (82.1%) and empagliflozin (73.9%) in addition to a good knowledge of indications of referral to a nephrologist (80.8%). In this Saudi study, higher levels of adherence to the guidelines were associated with the physicians’ education level, access to clinical guidelines and receipt of relevant training. Overall, the majority of our participants (61%) showed high levels of adherence to DKD guidelines, but our results also reflected varying degrees of knowledge across different aspects of DKD management. Our findings also revealed that higher levels of adherence to the guidelines were observed among physicians who received training in diabetes management. This training can be facilitated by setting up primary care kidney disease management programmes. Therefore, a multifactorial approach is necessary based on collaborative efforts to optimise the knowledge level of primary care providers in dealing with DKD. This lack of DKD knowledge among primary care providers may be one of the causes of delay in CKD identification and treatment, and may be because of many factors, such as the complexity and continuous evolution of the guidelines and the absence of communication between primary healthcare and nephrologists. The strengths of this study were that it provided an in-depth analysis of the knowledge level about DKD in Moroccan primary healthcare providers. However, there were some limitations. This study was limited by the

based on collaborative efforts to optimise the knowledge level of primary care providers in dealing with DKD. This lack of DKD knowledge among primary care providers may be one of the causes of delay in CKD identification and treatment, and may be because of many factors, such as the complexity and continuous evolution of the guidelines and the absence of communication between primary healthcare and nephrologists. The strengths of this study were that it provided an in-depth analysis of the knowledge level about DKD in Moroccan primary healthcare providers. However, there were some limitations. This study was limited by the small number of participants, its cross-sectional nature, and its reliance on self-reported data rather than a real-time evaluation of practices at primary care centres. Despite these limitations, we were able to identify shortcomings in the management of patients with DKD by general practitioners, which is relevant to running a comprehensive healthcare programme centred around DKD. The results of our study demonstrated the importance of continuous education and can guide the development of national programmes of training of primary healthcare providers in DKD in order to improve guideline compliance. Conclusion This study highlighted unmet needs for care and management of DKD patients at the primary care level. It is well-known that in order to ensure the success of any renal healthcare intervention, it is imperative to effectively involve general practitioners using a well-structured approach. Such an approach will need proper training and the implementation of effective primary care disease programmes.

chunks.content: More than 50% of cases with steroid-sensitive NS are frequently-relapsing and/or steroid-dependent. , Rituximab, a chimeric anti-CD20 monoclonal antibody, is an important therapy for FRSDNS. , , , Its efficacy in sustaining remission may be partly attributed to recent findings implicating an extrafollicular B-cell response during active disease and the presence of potential circulating antinephrin autoantibodies in ≤80% to 90% children with steroid-dependent NS. , , However, the causality of these autoantibodies is yet to be definitively established. Rituximab depletes B cells and B-cell subsets and thus may reduce potentially disease-causing autoantibodies that correlate with disease activity. , It also restores T-cell immune homeostasis through crosstalk between T and B cells. Existing efficacy and safety data from clinical trials, however, are largely derived from older children with FRSDNS, with a median age at rituximab administration ranging from 6.9 to 13.5 years. Published data on the youngest patients are not available. Our previous work showed that relapse risk reduced by 8% with each year increase in age at rituximab treatment. A cut-off age of < 10 years was recently identified to predict patients with less favorable response to rituximab. Younger patients are also more susceptible to complications, notably hypogammaglobulinemia and neutropenia. , , , Consequently, current recommendations do not advise to prescribe rituximab in young children aged < 7 years because of limited evidence. , , Nonetheless, it is well known that the youngest patients are the most challenging population to treat and often have a more complicated disease course. , They suffer from repeated relapses, resulting in frequent hospitalizations and significant steroid-related side effects. At the recent Kidney Disease: Improving Global Outcomes Controversies Conference on Therapies Targeting B Cell in Immune-Mediated Kidney Diseases, it was determined that the optimal therapeutic approach for young children who do not respond to oral immunosuppression remains a significant clinical gap. In view of these knowledge gaps, the present study aimed to examine the efficacy and safety of rituximab therapy through a multinational study to determine its role in young children aged < 6 years with FRSDNS. Methods We conducted a multinational, multicenter, retrospective cohort study between March 1, 2020, and December 31, 2023. In this study, we used 2 previously reported international pediatric cohorts with FRSDNS, which involved 16 tertiary pediatric nephrology centers from 10 countries in Asia, Europe, and North America. , We included young children with frequently-relapsing, steroid-dependent and/or multidrug-dependent NS who received their first course of rituximab before the age of 6 years between 2005 and 2022. We used standard terminologies for NS, frequently-relapsing, steroid dependent, primary and secondary steroid resistance, remission, and relapse. Multidrug dependence was defined as the requirement of ≥ 2 immunosuppressants (corticosteroids, mycophenolate mofetil, and/or calcineurin inhibitor) to maintain remission. , All patients were in complete remission at the time of their first rituximab administration, and rituximab was given with the aim of sustaining disease remission. The minimum observation period was 12 months following the first rituximab administration, unless a relapse occurred earlier. Subjects with a history of steroid resistance could be included if they attained remission after calcineurin inhibitor therapy and subsequently became steroid responsive, with a clinical course of FRSDNS that required rituximab therapy. , Patients who received repeated rituximab at fixed intervals (e.g., every 6 months), regardless of clinical response and B-cell population, were excluded. Further exclusion criteria were multidrug-resistant NS, in which rituximab was used to induce remission, and secondary NS (e.g., congenital or infantile NS, genetic podocytopathy, C3 glomerulopathy, membranous nephropathy, lupus nephritis, and IgA nephropathy). The study was divided into 2 parts. In the primary analysis, we examined the efficacy and safety of rituximab in these young children. In a secondary analysis, we further matched and compared these young patients with older children and young adults who received their first rituximab between the ages of 6 and 21 years. This matched analysis was performed to address potential confounders, enabling better understanding of age-related differences in treatment and immunological responses to rituximab. Rituximab was prescribed according to local policy, at 1 to 4 weekly infusions of 375 mg/m 2 or 1 to 2 biweekly infusions of 750 mg/m 2 . Dosing regimens were grouped according to the total dose per treatment course: low dose (375 mg/m 2 ), medium dose (750 mg/m 2 ), or high dose (1500 mg/m 2 ). Infusions that were prescribed > 4 weeks apart were considered as 2 distinct courses. The duration of concurrent immunosuppression was defined as the use of any agent, including corticosteroids, mycophenolate mofetil, and/or calcineurin inhibitors. Maintenance immunosuppression was defined as the use of concurrent immunosuppression after rituximab for ≥6 months or until relapse if that occurred within 6 months post-rituximab. Rituximab regimens and monitoring practices followed the local policies of participating centers. We collected fully anonymized data on baseline demographics, kidney histology,

The duration of concurrent immunosuppression was defined as the use of any agent, including corticosteroids, mycophenolate mofetil, and/or calcineurin inhibitors. Maintenance immunosuppression was defined as the use of concurrent immunosuppression after rituximab for ≥6 months or until relapse if that occurred within 6 months post-rituximab. Rituximab regimens and monitoring practices followed the local policies of participating centers. We collected fully anonymized data on baseline demographics, kidney histology, previous treatments, rituximab dosing regimens, immunosuppression use, relapse, kidney outcomes, adverse events, and total B-cell counts. This study was conducted in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki and the Declaration of Istanbul. Ethical approval was obtained from the Central Institutional Review Board of the Hong Kong Children’s Hospital as the lead study site (REC-2020-004). Participating centers obtained ethics approval in compliance to local policies where required, because some centers did not mandate such review for retrospective studies. Primary and Secondary Outcomes In the main analysis, the primary outcome was relapse-free survival, defined as time to relapse after rituximab administration. Children were censored at the time of additional rituximab administration or at the last follow-up, whichever occurred earlier. Secondary outcomes were B-cell depletion and repopulation, long-term remission (relapse-free for ≥ 2 years), rituximab resistance (relapse within first 3 months post-rituximab), the development of chronic kidney disease (estimated glomerular filtration rate < 60 ml/min per 1.73 m 2 ) and/or kidney failure, and rituximab-associated adverse events. B-cell depletion and repletion were defined as CD19+ B-cell levels < and ≥ 1% of the total lymphocyte population, respectively. Adverse events included death, severe infusion reactions, infections, hypogammaglobulinemia, neutropenia, neoplasia, and complications arising from cardiovascular, respiratory, and neurological systems. Agranulocytosis and neutropenia were defined as an absolute neutrophil count < 0.5 × 10 9 /l and < 1.5 × 10 9 /l. Hypogammaglobulinemia was defined as an IgG level that was below the reference range for age at each individual laboratory. In the secondary analysis, we evaluated the relapse-free survival, B-cell depletion duration, and adverse events between younger and older patients. Statistical Analyses Descriptive data were expressed as mean (SD), median (IQR), and number (percentage), as appropriate. Between-group differences were analyzed using the Chi-square or Fisher exact tests for categorical parameters and t tests or the Mann–Whitney U tests for continuous parameters. In the primary analysis of children aged < 6 years, the Kaplan-Meier method with log-rank test was used to compare relapse-free survival after the first rituximab administration. We determined the relationship between relapse and all potential risk factors in these young children using a multivariate Cox regression model. These factors included rituximab dosing, duration of concurrent immunosuppression, age at NS diagnosis, age at rituximab treatment, sex, ethnicity, disease severity, history of steroid resistance, and previous use of immunosuppression. Multicollinearity in the model was assessed using the variance inflation factor. For missing data, no imputation was used. Statistical analyses were performed using R version 4.1.1 (R Foundation for Statistical Computing, Vienna, Austria) with “survival,” “survminer,” “coxme,” “lme4,” and “performance” packages. Statistical significance was set at P < 0.05. In the secondary study, we conducted 1:1 propensity score–based nearest-neighbor matching without replacement using the “MatchIt” package in R version 4.5.2. The propensity score was estimated using logistic regression with age group as the exposure variable and the following baseline covariates: sex, ethnicity (Caucasians/Asians/others), rituximab dosing (low dose: 375 mg/m 2 ; medium dose: 750 mg/m 2 ; high dose: 1125–1500 mg/m 2 ), number of immunosuppressive agents immediately before rituximab (1, 2, or 3), interval between NS diagnosis and first rituximab (continuous), and history of steroid resistance (yes/no). Exact matching (caliper = 0) was enforced for all categorical covariates, and the interval between NS diagnosis and first rituximab was matched within an absolute caliper of 2 years. Calipers were specified on the original measurement scale (i.e., nonstandardized). A 1:1 matching ratio was applied. Covariate balance after matching was evaluated using standardized mean differences, and the matched cohort was used for subsequent outcome analyses. Relapse-free survival between younger and older patients at the time of first rituximab administration was compared using the Kaplan-Meier method with the log-rank test. Results Patient Population We included 101 young children (70 boys) who received their first course of rituximab before the age of 6 years ( ). They presented with NS at a median age of 2.3 years (IQR: 1.9–3.2). Majority of the patients were Europeans (42%), Southeast Asians (35%), and South Asians (12%). Among the patients, 74% and 22% were multidrug-dependent and steroid-dependent, respectively. Calcineurin inhibitors and mycophenolate mofetil were used in 86% and 25% patients, respectively. A history of steroid resistance was reported in 31% of patients (primary, 13%; secondary, 18%); however, all had achieved complete remission with calcineurin inhibitors. Among the 58% patients who underwent kidney biopsy, the prevalent histological diagnosis was minimal change disease (76%). Patients received their first course of rituximab at a median age of 4.5 years (IQR: 3.6–5.4). Low-, median-, and high-dose regimens were given in 54%, 25%, and 21% of patients, respectively. Concurrent immunosuppression was given to 61 children (60%). Baseline demographics and treatment regimens are summarized in and . Nineteen (19%), 40 (40%), 20 (20%), 8 (8%), 6 (6%), 5 (5%), and 3 (3%) children received a total of 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, and 7 rituximab courses, respectively ( ). A total of 273 courses of rituximab were evaluated during the observation period, with 168 and 105 courses administered before 6 and after 6 years of age, respectively. The median observation period after the first rituximab administration was 4.6 years (IQR, 3.2–6.6). Primary Outcome: Relapse-Free Survival Eight-six children (85%) relapsed after their first rituximab administration. Kaplan-Meier survival analysis showed that the median relapse-free survival of the cohort was 8.8 months (95% CI: 7.5–11.0) ( ). Relapse-free survival did not differ between children aged < 4 years and those aged from 4 to 6 years ( ). A history of steroid resistance was not associated with relapse ( A and B). Nine children (9%) relapsed within 3 months post-rituximab and were considered resistant to rituximab. Long-term remission > 2 years was achieved in 11 patients (11%), and total B cells repopulated in all of them. Five of these patients eventually relapsed. The number of relapses significantly reduced from 3 (IQR: 2–4) to 1 (IQR: 0–1) within 1-year before and after rituximab therapy ( P < 0.0001). Multivariable analysis demonstrated that each additional month of concurrent immunosuppression use (adjusted hazard ratio: 0.92; 95% CI: 0.89–0.96; P < 0.001) reduced relapse risk by 8%. Older age at first rituximab administration showed a trend toward a lower relapse risk (adjusted hazard ratio: 0.76; 95% CI: 0.57–1.03; P = 0.07). Although statistically insignificant, children receiving high-dose rituximab regimen (1125–1500 mg/m 2 ) appeared to experience a lower relapse risk than those who received low- and medium-dose regimens ( ). Sex, ethnicity, age at NS diagnosis, disease severity, history of steroid resistance, and number of previous immunosuppressive drugs did not affect relapse risk. summarizes the multivariable analysis of predictive factors for response. Total B-cell Depletion and Repopulation B cells were monitored within 1 month after the first rituximab administration in 70 patients, and B-cell depletion was observed in 99% of subjects ( n = 69/70). Total B cells were subsequently monitored in 58 children and repopulated at a median of 5.3 months (IQR: 4.3–6.8). Among these patients, 93% relapsed after B-cell repopulation, which had been documented a median of 2.2 months (IQR: 0.85–4.6) earlier; however, 22% of children did not relapse after B-cell repopulation. Subsequent Courses of Rituximab A second course of rituximab was administered to85 subjects (84%). The most frequent indication for redosing was NS relapse ( n = 77), followed by total B-cell repopulation ( n = 8). The rates of relapse, time to relapse, long-term remission, rituximab resistance, and duration of B-cell depletion after each rituximab course are summarized in . Importantly, 34% and 12% children attained long-term remission (≥ 2 years) following the second and third rituximab course, respectively. Between 5% and 13% of patients had rituximab resistance (relapse-free period < 3 months) during each cycle of treatment. Nine patients had very low IgG levels (< 200 mg/dl), and 4 patients required regular i.v. Ig replacement. Twenty episodes (66%) recovered over a median of 3.0 months (IQR: 1.3–6.9). Nine patients (9%) developed neutropenia, of whom 6 had agranulocytosis. The median absolute neutrophil count was 0.08 × 10 9 /l (IQR: 0.06–0.70). The neutropenic episodes lasted for a median of 20 (IQR: 5–49) days. Patients with agranulocytosis were treated with granulocyte-colony stimulating factor ( n = 3), systemic antibiotics ( n = 3), and acyclovir ( n = 1) with good recovery of the neutrophil count. Eight infectious episodes were reported in 7 patients (febrile neutropenia, n = 3; herpes simplex, n = 1; pneumocystis pneumonia, n = 1; community-acquired pneumonia, n = 1; viral gastroenteritis, n = 1; acute otitis media). Most of them had concurrent hypogammaglobulinemia ( n = 1) and/or neutropenia ( n = 5). We did not find any associated factor among these young patients with or without neutropenia, agranulocytosis, and infection. Of note, 2 patients were receiving mycophenolate mofetil as maintenance immunosuppression, whereas another patient with agranulocytosis was receiving cotrimoxazole as prophylaxis against pneumocystis. Details of side effects reported during the first and subsequent courses of rituximab are presented in . Hypogammaglobulinemia ( n = 85/173, 49%) remained the most common adverse event across all courses of rituximab evaluated in our cohort, followed by infections ( n = 19/273, 7%) and neutropenia ( n = 18/267, 7%) ( ). The rates of hypogammaglobulinemia were higher among courses of rituximab administered before the age of 6 years (54% vs. 43%, P = 0.02). A total of 42 children developed hypogammaglobulinemia before the age of 6 years. The first occurrence was observed after the first, second, and third courses of rituximab in 30, 10, and 2 patients, respectively. Twenty-nine children received further courses of rituximab therapy, and hypogammaglobulinemia recurred in 20 children (68%). Among the 18 children who received additional administrations after the age of 6 years, 13 developed hypogammaglobulinemia (72%). The rates of neutropenia (9% vs. 4%) and infection (8% vs. 5%) were also higher, although these differences did not reach statistical significance. Chronic Kidney Disease and Kidney Failure All 101 patients remained steroid sensitive during the observation period. Normal kidney function was reported in all children at the last follow-up, except 1 who had chronic kidney disease stage 2. The patient had multidrug-dependent NS since the age of 19 months and was treated with a calcineurin inhibitor for disease control. Rituximab was administered at 5.6 years of age, and the calcineurin inhibitor was continued as maintenance for more than 4 years at the last follow-up. Although a kidney biopsy was not performed, the impaired kidney function could be attributable to long-term calcineurin inhibitor–associated nephrotoxicity. No patients required kidney replacement therapy. Secondary Matched Analysis With Children Receiving First Rituximab at an Older Age We matched 70 young children with 70 older children who received their first rituximab ≥ 6 years of age). Rituximab was first administered at a median age of 4.7 (IQR: 3.9–5.4) years and 9.8 (IQR: 7.3–14.6) years in the younger and older groups, respectively. The difference in interval between NS diagnosis and first rituximab was significant yet modest in magnitude between the 2 groups (young: 2.1 ± 1.2 years vs. older: 2.7 ± 1.3 years). Baseline characteristics, including sex, ethnicity, disease severity, history of steroid resistance, number of immunosuppressive drugs immediately before rituximab, rituximab regimens, and maintenance immunosuppression, were comparable between groups ( ). Median relapse-free survival did not differ statistically, although young children demonstrated a trend toward earlier relapse ( ; 8.3 months, 95% CI: 6.7–10.6 vs. 11.3 months, 95% CI: 8.3–14.4; log-rank test P = 0.14). Time to B-cell repletion was similar between groups (young: 5.5, IQR: 3.7–6.4 months; vs. older: 5.6, IQR: 3.7–7.1 months). The side effects observed during the first course of rituximab were compared between the matched young and older patients. Young children had significantly higher rates of hypogammaglobulinemia (63% vs. 35%; P = 0.01) and tended to develop more complications, including neutropenia (13% vs. 7%; P = 0.27), agranulocytosis (7.5% vs. 2.9%), and infection (8.6% vs. 4.3%) ( ). Discussion Our multiethnic cohort provides long-term efficacy and safety data on rituximab in young children

The side effects observed during the first course of rituximab were compared between the matched young and older patients. Young children had significantly higher rates of hypogammaglobulinemia (63% vs. 35%; P = 0.01) and tended to develop more complications, including neutropenia (13% vs. 7%; P = 0.27), agranulocytosis (7.5% vs. 2.9%), and infection (8.6% vs. 4.3%) ( ). Discussion Our multiethnic cohort provides long-term efficacy and safety data on rituximab in young children aged < 6 years. Our data demonstrate that rituximab sustains remission even in young children with a complicated disease course. Hypogammaglobulinemia is prevalent in ≤57% of patients. Concomitant infection is uncommon but could be underreported. Although our findings suggest that rituximab can be used as a third-line or even second-line agent for complicated FRSDNS in young children, the therapy appears to be less effective and associated with more complications compared with those receiving the drug at an older age. Our cohort represented the most severe and complicated group of young children with FRSDNS. As expected, most of the patients were multidrug dependent, and the rest were steroid-dependent, with frequent relapses prior to rituximab administration. One-third of the children had a previous history of steroid resistance but regained steroid responsiveness following the use of calcineurin inhibitors, which has been associated with poorer treatment response to rituximab. , Up to 86% subjects with FRSDNS continued to relapse despite calcineurin inhibitor therapy, a potent steroid-sparing agent. This suggests that most pediatric nephrologists reserve rituximab as a last resort for FRSDNS in young children. Our data showed that the median relapse-free period in these young children was a median of 8.8 months after rituximab treatment. Although this efficacy is not as pronounced as that observed in older children, it is remarkable given that our cohort had a challenging disease course and had failed multiple steroid-sparing agents. To our best knowledge, there are no available data for comparison, because previous studies have enrolled mostly older children and did not perform specific subgroup analyses for young children. Furthermore, reported treatment outcomes of rituximab have been highly variable because of heterogeneity in patient populations and the prescription of rituximab and immunosuppression. We therefore matched our young patient cohort with older children of similar clinical and treatment characteristics to enable fair comparison and minimize potential confounders. Although the intervals from NS onset to first rituximab between groups were statistically different, a 6-month difference in rituximab initiation would be unlikely to affect overall clinical response or side effect profiles. Although statistically insignificant, older children demonstrated a trend toward a longer relapse-free period than younger children. This may be partly explained by the fact that memory B-cell levels, a more established biomarker for response than other B-cell subsets, were higher at baseline and reconstitute earlier in children aged < 10 years compared with those aged > 10 years receiving rituximab. Another potential explanation is that the natural course of FRSDNS tends to improve with age, especially around the time of puberty. In contrast, the duration of total B-cell depletion was not different between the 2 groups. Furthermore, among the young patients, each additional year of age at first rituximab administration showed a trend toward lower relapse risk. In concordance with our previous findings, , our data showed that maintenance immunosuppression was an effective measure to extend NS remission in young children. Each additional month of concurrent immunosuppression use reduced relapse risk by 8%. Although our study was not designed to evaluate the choice of maintenance therapy, mycophenolate mofetil appeared to be the preferred option, being the only immunosuppressive agent used over 6 months. In this context, a recent randomized trial showed that maintenance mycophenolate mofetil could reduce relapse risk by 80%; however, the effect disappeared after drug discontinuation. Our study did not evaluate the rituximab drug levels and anti-rituximab antibodies because these tests are unavailable in most clinical settings. Current evidence, however, suggests that these parameters correlate poorly with relapse and does not support regular monitoring. Our previous work described a progressive improvement in relapse-free period after repeated courses of rituximab, suggesting a potential disease-modifying effect. Similar findings were observed in the current cohort. After each cycle of rituximab therapy, 10% to 30% of children achieved sustained and prolonged remission over 2 years. Although this may, in part, be related to outgrowing the disease, many children in our cohort were prepubertal at the time of rituximab retreatment, a stage at which the disease typically remains active until puberty is reached. This result can be impactful if repeated rituximab treatments can ameliorate the overall clinical course. One possible postulation is that early rituximab use prevents the formation of long-lived plasma cell.

After each cycle of rituximab therapy, 10% to 30% of children achieved sustained and prolonged remission over 2 years. Although this may, in part, be related to outgrowing the disease, many children in our cohort were prepubertal at the time of rituximab retreatment, a stage at which the disease typically remains active until puberty is reached. This result can be impactful if repeated rituximab treatments can ameliorate the overall clinical course. One possible postulation is that early rituximab use prevents the formation of long-lived plasma cell. Further clinical and translational data are warranted to confirm this hypothesis. Rituximab appears to be generally safe, but its use is not without risk. , , , , Rare yet fatal adverse events such as viral hepatitis reactivation, lung injury, and multifocal leukoencephalopathy have been reported. , , Hypogammaglobulinemia, neutropenia, and agranulocytosis are the most prevalent adverse events and the incidences were reported to be 14% to 58%, 4% to 8% and 2% to 5%, respectively. , Our data reported more adverse events among young children than the general pediatric population. There were significantly higher rates of hypogammaglobulinemia in younger children, than in the matched older patient cohort. Although the difference in other adverse events was not significant between groups because of relatively small sample size and event numbers, this signal should be taken seriously into any treatment consideration. Interestingly, the observed adverse events were lower when rituximab was given to the same group of children after they turned 6 years or older. This concurs with previous findings that younger age at rituximab increased the risk of developing hypogammaglobulinemia and neutropenia. , IgG, IgA, and IgM levels and absolute neutrophil count should be regularly monitored, because all except one of our infective complications occurred in the presence of hypogammaglobulinemia and agranulocytosis. Furthermore, our data found that low IgG levels before rituximab was associated with hypogammaglobulinemia after rituximab therapy. The role of i.v. Ig substitution for asymptomatic numerical hypogammaglobulinemia, however, remains controversial. , The risk of developing complications remains a major and valid concern when prescribing rituximab to these young children. Another important consideration, as illustrated from our data, is that most children eventually relapse and require repeated courses of rituximab for disease control. In the short- to medium-term, there are concerns pertaining to vaccine competency and long-term immunological impairment. , , Future research is required to better understand the long-term impact, such as hematologic malignancy, of repeated rituximab treatments during an active stage of immunity development and maturation. , For these reasons, we recommend to use rituximab in young children with FRSDNS only after other second-line treatment options have been exhausted or resulted in side effects. Second generation anti-CD20, obinutuzumab, is effective in rituximab-resistant FRSDNS, even among children who relapse during complete depletion of circulating B cell. , Until further data become available, its use in young children should be exercised with great caution, only after balancing the risk and benefits. Obinutuzumab has, due to its mode of action, clear potentials of being more effective but also having more profound side effects than the first generation of anti-CD20 monoclonal antibodies. Despite a unique multiethnic patient cohort, our study had the limitations of a retrospective study, including selection and reporting bias. We tried to minimize them by stringent inclusion criteria and adequate observation. Second, there were variable practices between centers, including rituximab regimen, immunosuppression use, and redose indications. These might confound treatment responses and influence the reported rates of adverse events. In particular, hypogammaglobulinemia might have been underreported because of variable practices on IgG-level monitoring. Infection is an important complication after intensive immunosuppression and may be underreported. Finally, histology was not included as an adjusted factor in the regression model because kidney biopsy is not routinely indicated in FRSDNS ; available evidence however fails to substantiate its role as predictor. , , In conclusion, rituximab appears to have reasonable efficacy in young children with complicated FRSDNS. Maintenance immunosuppression may serve as a plausible option to prevent relapse and extend remission. Compared with older children, young children may experience a shorter relapse-free period and high rates of adverse events. Rituximab should therefore be considered only after exhausting other treatment options, until prospective trials provide more robust evidence to support its earlier use. Future trials should identify the prognostic values of specific B-cell subsets, examine the role of scheduled redosing, and compare the efficacy and safety of rituximab against novel therapeutics such as obinutuzumab and chimeric antigen receptor–based therapy.
