Notably, protocols for both CREDENCE and DAPA-CKD specified continuation of study drug when eGFR fell below initiation thresholds. Therefore, it is reasonable to continue therapy if the eGFR falls below the initiation thresholds unless the patient is not tolerating treatment or KRT is initiated ( ). Hypovolemia and hypoglycemia may occur with SGLT2i, but absolute risks are low, especially at low eGFR. Therefore, adjustment of background therapies is generally not required when initiating an SGLT2i, but it may be prudent in some patients, and follow-up to reassess volume status and glycemia is important ( ). Euglycemic ketoacidosis with minimal to no elevation in blood glucose may occur in patients taking SGLT2i. Patients with T2D requiring insulin are at particular risk. To mitigate risk, it is important to maintain at least low-dose insulin and consider pausing SGLT2i treatment during periods of acute illness or stressors. Blood or urine ketone monitoring may be used for ketosis detection. Patients with signs, symptoms, or biochemical evidence of ketoacidosis should discontinue SGLT2i therapy and seek immediate medical attention. Genital mycotic infections are a known complication of SGLT2i. A meta-analysis of clinical trials reported that genital mycotic infections occurred in 6% of participants assigned to an SGLT2i, compared with 1% of those assigned to placebo ( ). The risk is higher for women than men. Daily hygienic measures may lessen this risk, and most genital mycotic infections are easily treated, but severe cases of Fournier gangrene have been reported. Additional research is needed to determine the role of SGLT2i in improving kidney outcomes in patients with T1D, among whom diabetic ketoacidosis is more common, and posttransplant, in which case immunosuppression may modify infection risks ( ). Consensus Statement An SGLT2i with proven kidney or cardiovascular benefit is recommended for patients with T2D, CKD, and eGFR ≥20 mL/min/1.73 m 2 . Once initiated, the SGLT2i can be continued at lower levels of eGFR. Use of Additional Glucose-Lowering Agents For patients with T2D and CKD requiring additional glucose-lowering agents, selection should be made in consideration of patient- and medication-specific considerations ( ). Addition of a long-acting GLP-1 receptor agonist is preferred as per KDIGO for patients not achieving individualized glycemic targets despite use of metformin and/or SGLT2i therapy or for individuals unable to take these medications ( ). Similarly, the ADA gives strong support to use of GLP-1 receptor agonists in patients with T2D and CKD or ASCVD in consideration of their primary cardiovascular and secondary kidney benefits in large cardiovascular outcomes trials ( ). Notably, GLP-1 receptor agonists retain glycemic efficacy and safety even in advanced CKD stages. GLP-1 Receptor Agonists GLP-1 receptor agonists reduce albuminuria and slow eGFR decline, as evidenced by secondary outcomes assessed in the cardiovascular outcomes trials and a clinical trial for glycemic efficacy and safety in patients with T2D and eGFR 15–59 mL/min/1.73 m 2 ( ). In cardiovascular outcomes trials, GLP-1 receptor agonists reduced risk of major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE) in patients with T2D ( – ). Notably, the MACE risk reduction with liraglutide was significantly greater for those with eGFR <60 mL/min/1.73 m 2 than for those with eGFR ≥60 mL/min/1.73 m 2 ( ). Although most participants in the cardiovascular outcomes trials of GLP-1 receptor agonists had established cardiovascular disease, the MACE reduction was similar between those with and without previous cardiovascular or kidney disease ( ). Although there has not been a completed kidney disease outcome trial for GLP-1 receptor agonists, the cardiovascular outcomes trials have included participants with eGFR as low as 15 mL/min/1.73 m 2 . The GLP-1 receptor agonists with favorable CKD outcomes include lixisenatide, exenatide (once weekly), liraglutide, semaglutide, albiglutide, dulaglutide, and efpeglenatide ( , , , – ). In a meta-analysis of eight cardiovascular outcomes trials, GLP-1 receptor agonists significantly reduced risk for a composite kidney disease outcome (macroalbuminuria, eGFR decline, progression to kidney failure, or death from kidney disease) compared with placebo, largely driven by reduction in albuminuria ( ). In a glycemic efficacy and safety trial in patients with moderate-to-severe CKD (CKD stages G3 and G4), dulaglutide was compared with insulin glargine as basal therapy ( , ). Dulaglutide produced similar glycemic control but resulted in significantly slower GFR decline. There is an ongoing clinical trial for a GLP-1 receptor agonist in T2D and CKD to evaluate whether semaglutide will prevent ≥50% eGFR decline, kidney failure, or death due to kidney or cardiovascular causes (clinical trial reg. no. NCT03819153 , ClinicalTrials.gov ). Nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea are the most common side effects of GLP-1 receptor agonists. These symptoms occur in 15–20% of patients with moderate-to-severe CKD (CKD stages G3 and G4) but

There is an ongoing clinical trial for a GLP-1 receptor agonist in T2D and CKD to evaluate whether semaglutide will prevent ≥50% eGFR decline, kidney failure, or death due to kidney or cardiovascular causes (clinical trial reg. no. NCT03819153 , ClinicalTrials.gov ). Nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea are the most common side effects of GLP-1 receptor agonists. These symptoms occur in 15–20% of patients with moderate-to-severe CKD (CKD stages G3 and G4) but usually are tolerable with dose titration and abate over several weeks to months ( ). Injection site reactions are rare (<1%), and semaglutide is now available in an oral formulation. Heart rate typically increases by ∼5 bpm but has not been associated with higher BP or other adverse events. GLP-1 receptor agonist treatment is not recommended in patients at risk for thyroid C-cell tumors (e.g., multiple endocrine neoplasia), pancreatic cancer, or pancreatitis based on theoretical risks from preclinical models ( ). GLP-1 receptor agonists that have shown cardiovascular and CKD benefits (liraglutide, semaglutide, albiglutide [not currently available], and dulaglutide) are preferred agents. GLP-1 receptor agonists do not cause hypoglycemia per se but, when used with insulin or insulin secretagogues, doses of these drugs may be reduced to avoid hypoglycemia. However, in moderate-to-severe CKD (CKD stages G3 and G4), rates of hypoglycemia are reduced by one-half even with concurrent insulin therapy ( ). Consensus Statement GLP-1 receptor agonist with proven cardiovascular benefit is recommended for patients with T2D and CKD who do not meet their individualized glycemic target with metformin and/or an SGLT2i or who are unable to use these drugs. Glycemic Management in Advanced CKD (eGFR <30 mL/min/1.73 m<sup>2</sup> With or Without KRT) Glycemic management is particularly challenging for patients with eGFR <30 mL/min/1.73 m 2 , including those treated with dialysis, because of restrictions on drug use ( ) and lack of high-quality RCTs in this population. For T1D, insulin remains the only approved therapy. Doses are titrated to achieve individualized glycemic goals but may need to be decreased in comparison with earlier stages of CKD due to reduced insulin clearance and other changes in metabolism with advanced CKD ( ). In T2D, advanced CKD is a risk factor for hypoglycemia ( , ) and, when possible, drugs that control glycemia without increasing risk of hypoglycemia are preferred. Metformin is contraindicated with eGFR<30 mL/min/1.73 m 2 and with dialysis treatment. SGLT2i can be initiated with eGFR 20–29 mL/min/1.73 m 2 and continued at lower eGFR if previously initiated and well tolerated. However, SGLT2i have minimal effects on glycemia in this range of eGFR and are of use mainly for kidney and cardiovascular benefits not mediated through glycemia. GLP-1 receptor agonists have been studied with eGFR as low as 15 mL/min/1.73 m 2 and retain glucose-lowering potency across the range of eGFR and among dialysis patients. GLP-1 receptor agonists reduced ASCVD events and albuminuria in large RCTs and, thus, are theoretically appealing for people with T2D and CKD but have not been prospectively tested for cardiovascular efficacy or safety in this population. However, findings of a meta-analysis of the cardiovascular outcomes trials showed that ASCVD risk was reduced at least as much among individuals with eGFR <60 mL/min/1.73 m 2 compared with those with higher eGFR ( ). GLP-1 receptor agonists induce weight loss and can cause nausea and vomiting, so caution is warranted among patients with or at risk for malnutrition. Notably, in people with T2D and advanced CKD who have obesity exceeding BMI limits required for kidney transplant listing, GLP-1 receptor agonists can be used to aid with weight loss that may facilitate qualification for transplant. Selected dipeptidyl peptidase 4 inhibitors can be used with eGFR <30 mL/min/1.73 m 2 and in dialysis ( ) and provide a safe and effective option for treatment of patients who are not treated with GLP-1 receptor agonists. Thiazolidinediones improve insulin sensitivity, a common abnormality in advanced CKD, and retain antihyperglycemic effects in this population. Fluid retention and HF are concerns with low eGFR and require careful monitoring. Insulin and short-acting sulfonylureas are often necessary to control glucose when medications with less propensity to cause hypoglycemia are contraindicated, not tolerated, unavailable, or insufficient. Glycemic Management for Patients With a Kidney Transplant Patients with a kidney transplant have been excluded from most clinical trials of glucose-lowering therapy. Therefore, data must be extrapolated from general populations with diabetes, with consideration of differences in diabetes pathophysiology (i.e., posttransplant diabetes) and unique aspects of treatment (such as immunosuppressive medications). High-quality trial data are needed for this population. For T2D and posttransplant diabetes, it is reasonable to treat kidney transplant recipients with metformin according to eGFR, as

are often necessary to control glucose when medications with less propensity to cause hypoglycemia are contraindicated, not tolerated, unavailable, or insufficient. Glycemic Management for Patients With a Kidney Transplant Patients with a kidney transplant have been excluded from most clinical trials of glucose-lowering therapy. Therefore, data must be extrapolated from general populations with diabetes, with consideration of differences in diabetes pathophysiology (i.e., posttransplant diabetes) and unique aspects of treatment (such as immunosuppressive medications). High-quality trial data are needed for this population. For T2D and posttransplant diabetes, it is reasonable to treat kidney transplant recipients with metformin according to eGFR, as for the broader population with T2D, because risks of metformin are related to kidney function ( – ). SGLT2i are promising drugs for kidney transplant recipients because they reduce intraglomerular pressure, which may be elevated in single functional kidneys, and may improve graft outcomes through this and other mechanisms. However, these benefits have not been confirmed in clinical trials, and there is a theoretical concern that infection risks (i.e., genital mycotic infections, urinary tract infections, Fournier gangrene) may be increased due to immunosuppression. Therefore, more data are needed prior to making recommendations for or against treatment with SGLT2i for kidney transplant recipients. Kidney transplantation and its treatments do not substantially modify the known risks and benefits of other glucose-lowering medications, other than restrictions associated with eGFR. Renin-Angiotensin-Aldosterone System Inhibition ACE Inhibitors and ARBs RAS inhibition with ACEi or ARBs has been standard of care in patients with T1D and T2D and CKD for decades. ACEi or ARBs are the preferred first-line agent for BP treatment among patients with diabetes, hypertension, and ACR ≥300 mg/g because of their proven benefits for prevention of CKD progression. In the setting of lower levels of albuminuria (30–299 mg/g), ACEi or ARB therapy has been demonstrated to reduce progression to more advanced albuminuria (≥300 mg/g) and cardiovascular events but not progression to kidney failure. Therefore, both KDIGO and the ADA recommend an ACEi or ARB for treatment of hypertension among people with T1D or T2D who have hypertension and ACR ≥30 mg/g ( , ). Rarely, patients with albuminuria have normal BP, and in this situation, evidence for treatment with RAS inhibition is less strong. Although short-term studies demonstrated added benefit of the combination of ACEi and ARBs in albuminuria reduction, long-term studies showed no benefit and more adverse events, particularly hyperkalemia and AKI, and thus avoidance of this combination is recommended. ns-MRAs The steroidal mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist spironolactone is effective for management of resistant hypertension and treatment of primary hyperaldosteronism, in the setting of normal eGFR. Additionally, spironolactone reduces mortality in patients with HF with reduced ejection fraction. However, spironolactone causes hyperkalemia, particularly with reduced kidney function (i.e., eGFR <45 mL/min/1.73 m 2 ). There are no long-term kidney outcome studies with spironolactone, and only one study in heart failure with reduced ejection fraction with a mean follow-up of 2 years that showed benefit. A novel class of ns-MRAs, including esaxerenone and finerenone, has recently been investigated among people with T2D and CKD, added to RAS inhibition. Esaxerenone lowered BP and albuminuria with limited changes in potassium, but long-term studies with clinical end points are lacking ( ). Finerenone was investigated in two complementary phase 3 studies of patients with T2D, kidney disease (defined primarily as ACR ≥30 mg/g), and potassium <4.8 mmol/L and is the only ns-MRA approved in the world for slowing CKD progression and reducing cardiovascular events. In Finerenone in Reducing Kidney Failure and Disease Progression in Diabetic Kidney Disease (FIDELIO-DKD), both the primary kidney end point of progression of kidney disease (40% decline in eGFR or kidney failure) and the prespecified secondary composite cardiovascular end point (MACE or hospitalization for HF) were reduced with finerenone compared with placebo. Serum potassium was monitored regularly, and 2.6% of participants stopped treatment because of hyperkalemia with finerenone compared with 0.9% on placebo ( ). In Finerenone in Reducing Cardiovascular Mortality and Morbidity in Diabetic Kidney Disease (FIGARO-DKD), the primary composite cardiovascular end point (MACE or hospitalization for HF) was reduced with finerenone compared with placebo, with estimates of effect for kidney outcomes and hyperkalemia similar to those seen in FIDELIO-DKD ( ). Findings from the FIDELITY (Finerenone in Chronic Kidney Disease and Type 2 Diabetes: Combined FIDELIO-DKD and FIGARO-DKD Trial Programme Analysis) individual patient, prespecified combined analysis of both trials (13,191 total participants) demonstrated significant reductions of 18% for the composite cardiovascular outcome; 23% for a composite outcome of doubling of creatinine, kidney failure, or renal death; and 20% for dialysis initiation with a 22% reduction in HF hospitalizations ( ). While <10% of participants were treated with an SGLT2i or a GLP-1 receptor agonist, results of subgroup analyses suggested that benefits of finerenone were similar with and without concomitant SGLT2i or GLP-1

from the FIDELITY (Finerenone in Chronic Kidney Disease and Type 2 Diabetes: Combined FIDELIO-DKD and FIGARO-DKD Trial Programme Analysis) individual patient, prespecified combined analysis of both trials (13,191 total participants) demonstrated significant reductions of 18% for the composite cardiovascular outcome; 23% for a composite outcome of doubling of creatinine, kidney failure, or renal death; and 20% for dialysis initiation with a 22% reduction in HF hospitalizations ( ). While <10% of participants were treated with an SGLT2i or a GLP-1 receptor agonist, results of subgroup analyses suggested that benefits of finerenone were similar with and without concomitant SGLT2i or GLP-1 receptor agonist treatment. Moreover, the risk of hyperkalemia was significantly reduced by the presence of an SGLT2i ( ). In summary, FIDELIO-DKD and FIGARO-DKD demonstrated cardiovascular and kidney benefits for finerenone among people with T2D who were treated with standard of care (including an RAS inhibitor at maximally tolerated doses and good control of glycemia and BP) who were at high residual risk, based largely on albuminuria (ACR ≥30 mg/g). These effects appear to be additive, based on preclinical studies, to those of SGLT2i and GLP-1 receptor agonists, though further clinical research on these combinations is needed. Therefore, it is reasonable to add finerenone to the treatment regimen of patients with T2D who have any level of persistent albuminuria despite current standard of care treatment with glucose-lowering and antihypertensive medications ( ). Finerenone can be initiated with eGFR ≥25 mL/min/1.73 m 2 (as per trial eligibility) and serum potassium 4.8 mmol/L (per trial eligibility criteria) or ≤5.0 mmol/L (as per U.S. Food and Drug Administration label). As per trial protocols, finerenone should be started at a dose of 20 mg daily for eGFR >60 mL/min/1.73 m 2 and 10 mg for eGFR 25–60 mL/min/1.73 m 2 and uptitrated to 20 mg daily if possible. Potassium should be followed 4 weeks after dose change and regularly during treatment. With potassium <4.8 mmol/L, dose can be uptitrated to 20 mg and continued with potassium ≤5.5 mmol/L. If potassium increases to >5.5 mmol/L, finerenone should be withheld and can be restarted at 10 mg daily when potassium is ≤5.0 mmol/L. Finerenone can be continued with eGFR <25 mL/min/1.73 m 2 as long as potassium is acceptable and the drug is otherwise tolerated. Consensus Statement An ns-MRA with proven kidney and cardiovascular benefit is recommended for patients with T2D, eGFR ≥25 mL/min/1.73 m 2 , normal serum potassium concentration, and albuminuria (ACR ≥30 mg/g) despite maximum tolerated dose of RAS inhibitor. Conclusions The 2022 ADA Standards of Care and KDIGO 2022 guideline are aligned on issues of CKD screening and diagnosis, glycemia monitoring, lifestyle therapies, treatment goals, and pharmacologic management ( , ). Both recommend comprehensive care in which pharmacotherapy that is proven to improve clinical kidney and cardiovascular outcomes is layered upon a foundation of healthy lifestyle approaches. This consensus approach to management is based on high-quality evidence. Randomized clinical trial data are most abundant for drug therapies, and other professional societies have also made similar recommendations for use of these agents. Implementation of proven therapies is paramount to improving health outcomes. There is a critical need for patients with diabetes and CKD to be treated in accord with the most up-to-date recommendations. The ADA and KDIGO, individually and now in combination, offer clear guidance on applying and prioritizing interventions. High cost, limited workforce, and other resource constraints in health care systems will limit implementation of some recommendations among individuals and populations, and efforts to improve accessibility are essential to maximizing benefit and minimizing disparities. Investigation remains active in the fields of diabetes, CKD, and cardiovascular disease, and additional data on existing and novel approaches are anticipated. Clinical practice guidelines will continue to evolve. When possible, consensus approaches to diagnosis and management will help interpret new data in context and translate discoveries to improved outcomes for patients.

documents.title: KDIGO 2021 Clinical Practice Guideline for Management of Blood Pressure in CKD

chunks.content: Introduction Chronic kidney disease (CKD) is a global public health challenge, affecting approximately 10% of the adult population worldwide and contributing significantly to morbidity, mortality, and healthcare costs [ ]. Estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR), a key marker of kidney function, is widely used to assess CKD severity and progression [ ]. Declines in eGFR are associated with adverse outcomes, including cardiovascular disease, end-stage kidney disease, and premature death [ , ]. Cardiometabolic risk factors (CMRFs), including obesity, dyslipidemia, hypertension, and hyperglycemia, are well-established contributors to both CKD development and progression [ ]. These risk factors often cluster together, amplifying their adverse effects on kidney function through mechanisms such as systemic inflammation, oxidative stress, and endothelial dysfunction [ ]. In clinical practice, cardiometabolic abnormalities rarely occur in isolation; instead, they tend to cluster and interact through shared pathophysiological pathways-including hemodynamic overload, insulin resistance, chronic inflammation, and dyslipidemia-to affect renal structure and function [ , ]. Therefore, a cumulative cardiometabolic burden approach may better reflect real-world risk than modeling single factors separately. In cardiovascular epidemiology, cardiometabolic multimorbidity and risk-factor clustering have been associated with substantially higher risks of major adverse events than any single component alone, supporting the biological and clinical relevance of assessing aggregated risk burden in cardiorenal research. Investigating this cumulative burden is particularly relevant given the rising prevalence of metabolic syndrome and its components globally [ ]. The relationship between CMRFs and eGFR may also vary across populations due to differences in genetic predisposition, lifestyle, and healthcare access [ ]. For example, studies have shown that Asian populations, including Chinese individuals, may develop metabolic complications at lower body mass indices compared to Western populations [ ]. Similarly, disparities in socioeconomic status, education, and healthcare systems between countries may influence the prevalence and impact of CMRFs on kidney function [ ]. However, few studies have directly compared the association between incremental CMRFs and eGFR across diverse populations. In addition, Recent Kidney Disease: Improving Global Outcomes (KDIGO) guidelines emphasize the importance of accurate eGFR estimation, preferentially using equations that incorporate both creatinine and cystatin C and moving toward race-free formulations to reduce inequities in CKD assessment [ ]. We utilized data from two nationally representative cross-sectional studies: the China Health and Retirement Longitudinal Study (CHARLS) and the Health and Retirement Study (HRS), by incorporating a comprehensive assessment of eGFR scr-cysc using the Chronic Kidney Disease Epidemiology Collaboration (CKD-EPI) equation, which combines serum creatinine and cystatin C for improved accuracy across diverse populations [ , ]. This study aimed to quantify the association between the number of CMRFs and eGFR scr-cysc categories (normal, mildly decreased, and moderately/severely decreased). We hypothesize that the cumulative burden of CMRFs is associated with a graded increase in the risk of eGFR scr-cysc decline, independent of traditional confounders. We further hypothesize that the strength of this association may differ between Chinese and American populations due to differences in the prevalence and impact of CMRFs. Methods This study followed Strengthening the Reporting of Observational Studies in Epidemiology reporting guidelines [ ]. Study design and population This study utilized two nationally representative surveys: CHARLS wave 3 and HRS wave 13. Both studies were designed to assess the health, social, and economic conditions of middle-aged and older adults in China [ ] and the United States, respectively [ ]. The study protocols were approved by National Institute on Aging and the Social Security Administration (HRS: HUM0061128), the Ethical Review Committee of Perking University (CHARLS: IRB00001052-11015), and the detailed ethical approval could be found on respective origin surveys. Meanwhile, written informed consent was also obtained from any participant. For this analysis, we included individuals with age >45 years, complete data on eGFR scr-cysc , CMRFs, and relevant covariates. The final analytic sample consisted of 9,373 participants from HRS and 10,043 participants from CHARLS ( ). Outcome variable: estimated glomerular filtration rate The primary outcome, eGFR scr-cysc , was calculated using the CKD-EPI equation, which integrates serum creatinine and cystatin C to improve accuracy across populations [ ]. In both CHARLS and HRS, serum creatinine was measured using assays traceable to isotope dilution mass spectrometry reference standards, and cystatin C was calibrated against international reference materials, in line with recommendations for CKD‑EPI equations. Laboratory measurements were not formally cross‑standardized between CHARLS and HRS, which we acknowledge as a potential source of between-cohort variability in absolute eGFR values. Detailed formulas are listed in Table S1 . Consistent with recent recommendations to avoid race-based adjustments in eGFR estimation [ ], we did not apply the Black race coefficient when calculating eGFR in HRS participants, and race was not included as a multiplier in the final analytic models. eGFR scr-cysc was categorized into three categories according to the guideline: normal (≥90 mL/min/1.73m 2 ), mildly decreased (60–89 mL/min/1.73m 2 ), and moderately/severely decreased (<60

CKD‑EPI equations. Laboratory measurements were not formally cross‑standardized between CHARLS and HRS, which we acknowledge as a potential source of between-cohort variability in absolute eGFR values. Detailed formulas are listed in Table S1 . Consistent with recent recommendations to avoid race-based adjustments in eGFR estimation [ ], we did not apply the Black race coefficient when calculating eGFR in HRS participants, and race was not included as a multiplier in the final analytic models. eGFR scr-cysc was categorized into three categories according to the guideline: normal (≥90 mL/min/1.73m 2 ), mildly decreased (60–89 mL/min/1.73m 2 ), and moderately/severely decreased (<60 mL/min/1.73m 2 ) [ ]. Exposure variable: cardiometabolic risk factors CMRFs were defined based on the National Cholesterol Education Program Adult Treatment Panel III (NCEP-ATP III) criteria [ ]. Five CMRFs were included: Overweight or abdominal obesity: waist circumference >102 cm in men or >88 cm in women, or body mass index (BMI) ≥24 kg/m 2 for Chinese, BMI ≥25 kg/m 2 for American, reflecting Asian-specific and international BMI criteria recommended by regional and WHO-aligned guidelines [ ]. Elevated triglycerides: ≥150 mg/dl or use of lipid-lowering medications. Low high-density lipoprotein cholesterol: <40 mg/dl in men or <50 mg/dl in women, or use of lipid-lowering medications. Hypertension: systolic blood pressure ≥130 mmHg, diastolic blood pressure ≥85 mmHg, or use of antihypertensive medications. Elevated fasting glucose: fasting plasma glucose ≥100 mg/dl or HbA1c ≥ 5.7% or use of antidiabetic medications. Medication use was incorporated into the definitions of dyslipidemia and hyperglycemia/diabetes to capture treated cardiometabolic risk and to reduce misclassification of participants whose laboratory values may fall below diagnostic thresholds due to pharmacologic control, which is consistent with clinical risk stratification when summarizing cumulative cardiometabolic burden. Anthropometric and laboratory measurements were obtained following standardized CHARLS and HRS protocols. Waist circumference was measured at the midpoint between the lower margin of the last palpable rib and the top of the iliac crest using a flexible tape with participants standing. Triglycerides and HDL‑C were assayed from fasting venous blood samples using enzymatic methods in centralized laboratories in each study. Blood pressure was measured in the sitting position after at least 5 min of rest, using automated sphygmomanometers, and the mean of three measurements was used. Fasting plasma glucose and HbA1c were measured from venous blood using hexokinase‑based and high‑performance liquid chromatography methods, respectively, according to CHARLS and HRS laboratory manuals. Including medication use in the definitions of dyslipidemia and diabetes allowed us to capture participants with treated but persistent cardiometabolic risk, which is clinically relevant for assessing cumulative burden on kidney function. The number of CMRFs was summed for each participant, resulting in a score ranging from 0 to 5. Covariates We included the following covariates in the analysis, selected based on their potential confounding effects on the relationship between CMRFs and eGFR scr-cysc , including sociodemographic factors: age, sex, marital status (married vs. others), and education (less than middle school education, high school and vocational training, higher education), lifestyle behaviors: smoking (current smoker, former smoker, never smoker) and alcohol consumption (current drinker, former drinker, never drinker), cardiovascular disease: self-reported history of any cardiovascular condition, including myocardial infarction, stroke, or heart failure, biochemical markers: total cholesterol, low-density lipoprotein cholesterol, blood urea nitrogen, C-reactive protein, and hemoglobin, and country: a binary variable indicating study population (China vs. United States). Missing data We assessed missingness in key variables (eGFR biomarkers, cardiometabolic components, and covariates). The primary analyses used a complete-case approach by excluding participants with missing data in exposure, outcome, or prespecified covariates, yielding the final analytic sample reported in . We acknowledge that complete-case analysis may introduce selection bias if missingness is related to both cardiometabolic risk and kidney function; this limitation is discussed. Statistical analysis All analyses were performed using Stata 17.0 (StataCorp, College Station, TX, USA) and R 4.2.1 (R Foundation for Statistical Computing, Vienna, Austria). All descriptive statistics and regression models treated observations as independent and unweighted; we did not incorporate survey weights, strata, or clustering variables from CHARLS or HRS. A two-sided P -value <0.05 was considered statistically significant. Descriptive statistics were used to summarize participant characteristics by cohort. Continuous variables were presented as means with standard deviations, while categorical variables were presented as frequencies and percentages. Differences between groups were assessed using Welch Two Sample T-test for continuous variables and Pearson’s Chi-squared test for categorical variables. To examine the association between CMRFs and eGFR scr-cysc , multinomial logistic regression models were used, with eGFR scr-cysc categories as the dependent variable and the normal eGFR scr-cysc group (≥90 mL/min/1.73m 2 ) as the reference. The primary independent variable was the number of CMRFs (0–5), and the results were expressed as relative risk ratios (RRRs) with 95% confidence intervals (95% CIs). The primary independent variable was the number of CMRFs (0–5), and the results were expressed as relative risk ratios (RRRs) with 95% confidence intervals (95% CIs). Three models were constructed: Model 1 was a crude model, Model 2 adjusted for age and sex, and Model 3 further adjusted for socioeconomic factors, lifestyle factors, cardiovascular disease, biochemical markers, and country. Moreover, we conducted interaction analyses by including an interaction term for CMRFs and country in multivariable multinomial logistic regression models to assess whether the association differed between Chinese and American populations. Marginal effects were calculated to estimate the predicted probabilities of eGFR scr-cysc categories across different levels of CMRFs. We conducted several sensitivity analyses to test the robustness of our findings: 1) repeating the analysis using alternative eGFR equations (e.g., CKD-EPI creatinine-only equation or cystatin C-only equation). 2) Excluding participants with self-reported CVD ( n = 4,966) to minimize reverse causation. 3) Considering eGFR scr-cysc as a continuous variable and using multiple linear regression analysis to assess the association between CMRFs and eGFR scr-cysc . 4) Excluding eGFR scr-cysc lower than 15 mL/min/1.73m 2 ( n = 76). 5) Stratifying the analysis by country to explore potential heterogeneity between the CHARLS and HRS populations. Results Characteristics of included participants A total of 19,416 participants were included, with 10,043 from CHARLS and 9,373 from HRS ( ). The mean age was significantly higher in HRS (68.9 ± 10.0 years) compared to CHARLS (61.7 ± 9.2 years, p < 0.001). The proportion of females was greater in HRS (59.3%) than in CHARLS (53.0%, p < 0.001). CHARLS participants had higher rates of current smoking (27.8% vs. 11.2%, p < 0.001) and drinking (34.7% vs. 13.1%, p < 0.001), while HRS participants had higher rates of overweight (91.5% vs. 49.9%, p < 0.001). CHARLS participants having lower serum urea (15.6 ± 4.8 vs. 17.8 ± 7.2 mg/dl, p < 0.001), cystatin C (0.9 ± 0.2 vs. 1.2 ± 0.5 mg/l, p < 0.001), and CRP (2.8 ± 5.9 vs. 4.9 ± 11.1 mg/l, p < 0.001). Mean eGFR scr-cysc was higher in CHARLS (91.7 ± 18.1 mL/min/1.73m 2 ) than in HRS (70.4 ± 21.0 mL/min/1.73m 2 , p < 0.001), with moderate/severe eGFR scr-cysc decline (<60 mL/min/1.73m 2 ) more prevalent in HRS (29.8%) than CHARLS (5.7%, p < 0.001). The age- and sex-standardized prevalence of lower eGFR was 6.3% in CHARLS, while 28.5% in HRS. Association between CMRFs and eGFR<sub>scr-cysc</sub> Multinomial logistic regression demonstrated a significant association between the number of CMRFs and eGFR scr-cysc decline ( Table S2 and ). When treated as a continuous variable, each additional CMRF was associated with a statistically higher likelihood of being mild eGFR scr-cysc decline (RRR = 1.141, 95% CI: 1.108–1.175, p < 0.001) and moderate/severe eGFR scr-cysc decline (RRR = 1.433, 95% CI: 1.364–1.505, p < 0.001) in the fully adjusted model. When CMRFs were categorized, participants with five CMRFs had the highest risk of eGFR scr-cysc decline. Compared to those with non-CMRFs, the RRRs for mild eGFR scr-cysc decline were 1.357 (95% CI: 1.102–1.671, p = 0.004) for single CMRF and 2.278 (95% CI: 1.817–2.857, p < 0.001) for five CMRFs. For moderate/severe eGFR scr-cysc decline, the RRRs ranged from 1.377 (95% CI: 0.826–2.293, p = 0.220) for single CMRF to 6.178 (95% CI: 3.718–10.268, p < 0.001) for five CMRFs ( Table S2 and ). In addition, we estimated absolute risk differences. Compared with participants with 0 CMRFs, those with 5 CMRFs had an absolute increase of 4.9 percentage points (from 40.5% to 45.5%; 95% CI: 0.6–9.2) in the probability of mildly decreased eGFR scr‑cysc and an increase of 8.9 percentage points (from 12.0% to 20.9%; 95% CI: 5.8–12.0) in the probability of moderately/severely decreased eGFR scr‑cysc . Further analysis showed that the interaction term between CMRF and country was statistically significant for both mild eGFR scr-cysc decline (RRR for interaction = 0.908; P for interaction =0.002) and moderate/severe eGFR scr-cysc decline (RRR for interaction = 0.873; P for interaction =0.009). Predictive margins showed that mild eGFR scr-cysc decline was more prevalent in the American population compared to the Chinese population (52.87% vs. 39.86%, p < 0.001), while moderate/severe eGFR scr-cysc decline was also higher in Americans (21.93% vs. 10.64%, p < 0.001) ( Table S3 and ). Age and sex differences in eGFR<sub>scr-cysc</sub> decline Although the interaction between cumulative CMRFs and age was not statistically significant ( P for interaction of mild decline = 0.663 ; P for interaction of moderately/severely decline = 0.819), the main effect of age observed (all p < 0.001) highlights its independent role as a key determinant of lower eGFR. As shown in , the marginal effects of age illustrate a clear trend where the probability of eGFR deterioration increases progressively with advancing age. For the normal eGFR scr-cysc category, the probability decreased steadily from 94.97% (95% CI: 94.22%–95.73%) at age 30 to 9.01% (95% CI: 8.23%–9.79%) at age 80. Conversely, the probability of mild eGFR scr-cysc decline increased with age, from 4.18% (95% CI: 3.48%–4.88%) at age 30 to 60.74% (95% CI: 59.42%–62.06%) at age 80. Similarly, the probability of moderate/severe eGFR scr-cysc decline rose from 0.85% (95% CI: 0.72%–0.98%) at age 30 to 30.25% (95% CI: 29.07%–31.43%) at age 80 ( Table S4 ). For sex, males had a higher probability of being in the normal eGFR scr-cysc category compared to females (41.1% vs. 37.7%, p < 0.001) ( Table S5 and ). Conversely, females had a higher probability of being in the mildly decreased eGFR scr-cysc category compared to males (44.4% vs. 42.8%, p < 0.001). For the moderately/severely decreased eGFR scr-cysc category, females also had a higher probability than males (17.9% vs. 16.1%, p < 0.001). The interaction between CMRFs and sex was statistically significant only for the moderately/severely eGFR scr-cysc decline group ( P for interaction = 0.001). Sensitivity analyses Five sensitivity analyses confirmed the robustness of the findings. First, using serum creatinine-based eGFR, the association between CMRFs and lower eGFR weakened in fully adjusted models (e.g. RRR for <60 vs. ≥90 mL/min/1.73m 2 =1.365, 95% CI: 0.835–2.230, p = 0.214) ( Table S6 ); with cystatin C-based eGFR, the associations remained significant (e.g. RRR for single CMRF increase = 1.184, 95% CI: 1.150–1.219, p < 0.001) ( Table S7 ). Second, treating eGFR scr-cysc as a continuous variable, each additional CMRF was associated with a β of −1.418 (95% CI: −1.576 to −1.260, p < 0.001) ( Table S8 ). Third, excluding participants with cardiovascular disease, the associations persisted (e.g. RRR for [60, 90) vs. ≥90 mL/min/1.73m 2 =1.258, 95% CI: 1.013–1.562, p = 0.038) ( Table S9 ). Fourth, excluding participants with eGFR scr-cysc below 15 mL/min/1.73 m 2 , the significance of the association remained ( Table S10 ). Five, subgroup analyses by country yielded broadly similar associations. In CHARLS, each additional CMRF was associated with an RRR of 1.182 (95% CI: 1.138, 1.226) for mildly decreased eGFR and 1.492 (95% CI: 1.375, 1.62) for moderately/severely decreased eGFR; corresponding estimates in HRS were 1.072 (95% CI: 1.019, 1.127) and 1.332 (95% CI: 1.244, 1.428), respectively ( Tables S11–S12 ). Discussion This study explored the association between incremental CMRFs and eGFR scr-cysc using data from two nationally representative cross-sectional surveys. By incorporating eGFR scr-cysc calculated using both serum creatinine and cystatin C, we provided a robust assessment of kidney function in middle-aged and older adults across two diverse populations. Our findings revealed a significant and graded association between the number of CMRFs and eGFR scr-cysc decline, with stronger associations observed in participants with multiple CMRFs. Our work intersects with broader research on metabolic syndrome and aging epidemiology, which has highlighted the clustering of cardiometabolic abnormalities and their disproportionate impact on older adults. Previous studies have also underscored global health inequities in the burden and management of both metabolic disorders and CKD, particularly between high- and middle-income countries [ ]. Participants with five CMRFs were associated with lower kidney function compared to those with no CMRFs. This graded relationship persisted across both CHARLS and HRS cohorts, suggesting that the impact of CMRFs on kidney function is consistent across diverse populations. Furthermore, the sensitivity analyses conducted in this study further solidify the reliability of the observed associations. association between the cumulative burden of CMRFs and eGFR scr-cysc decline. Participants with five CMRFs were associated with lower kidney function compared to those with no CMRFs. This graded relationship persisted across both CHARLS and HRS cohorts, suggesting that the impact of CMRFs on kidney function is consistent across diverse populations. Furthermore, the sensitivity analyses conducted in this study further solidify the reliability of the observed associations. By employing alternative eGFR equations and excluding participants with preexisting cardiovascular disease, we demonstrated that the graded relationship between cumulative CMRFs and eGFR scr-cysc categories is not driven by specific population characteristics or computational choices. These results reinforce the generalizability and clinical relevance of our findings. The association between CMRFs and eGFR scr-cysc decline was particularly pronounced in the HRS cohort, where the prevalence of moderate/severe lower eGFR was significantly higher (29.8%) compared to CHARLS (5.7%). This disparity may reflect differences in baseline characteristics, such as higher rates of overweight and obesity, elevated triglycerides, and low HDL-C in the HRS cohort. These differences may be attributed to variations in lifestyle, healthcare access, and genetic predisposition between the two populations [ ]. Despite these differences, the association between CMRFs and eGFR scr-cysc decline was consistent across both cohorts, underscoring the universal impact of cardiometabolic risk on kidney function. Our findings are consistent with prior research demonstrating the detrimental effects of CMRFs on kidney function. For example, a meta-analysis by Thomas et al. reported that metabolic syndrome components, including hypertension, hyperglycemia, and dyslipidemia, are independently associated with an increased risk of CKD [ , ]. Similarly, a study by Chen et al. found that the cumulative burden of metabolic syndrome components was associated with a higher risk of CKD in a Chinese population [ ]. Our study extends these findings by incorporating data from two distinct populations and using a more comprehensive eGFR scr-cysc equation, which improves accuracy across diverse populations. The interaction analysis between CMRF and country revealed a significant modification in the association with eGFR scr-cysc categories. Compared to Chinese participants, American participants demonstrated a lower likelihood of mild and moderate/severe eGFR scr-cysc decline for each additional CMRF. These disparities may be attributed to differences in baseline cardiovascular risk profiles, lifestyle factors such as diet and physical activity levels, and healthcare accessibility. American participants may have been attenuated from the effects of CMRF on kidney injury by chronic disease management strategies, superior healthcare access, and related behavioral interventions. In addition, different racial distributions (e.g. obesity-related metabolic advantage in whites) and environmental exposures may also contribute to this phenomenon. The weaker per-CMRF association observed in HRS compared with CHARLS, despite a higher overall prevalence of lower eGFR in the United States, may reflect several factors. First, American participants had substantially higher baseline levels of obesity and dyslipidemia, such that additional CMRFs may confer relatively smaller incremental risk once a high-risk profile is established. Second, greater access to cardiometabolic and renal care, including wider use of statins, renin-angiotensin system blockers, and SGLT-2 inhibitors, might attenuate the marginal impact of each additional risk factor on kidney function. Third, differences in body composition, genetic susceptibility, and environmental exposures across racial and ethnic groups represented in HRS versus CHARLS may modify the relationship between CMRFs and eGFR. Sex and age differences The significant interaction between sex and CMRFs observed for the moderate/severe lower eGFR category highlights distinct sex-specific pathways in the association between cardiometabolic risk and kidney function deterioration. The observed biologic sex differences in eGFR scr-cysc categories warrants discussion. Females had a higher probability of being in the mildly decreased eGFR scr-cysc category and the moderately/severely decreased eGFR scr-cysc category compared to males. This finding contrasts with some previous studies that have reported higher CKD prevalence in males [ ]. This finding suggests that females experience a greater impact of cumulative cardiometabolic risk factors on severe lower eGFR, which may be attributed to biological differences in hormonal regulation, metabolic processes, and cardiovascular risk [ ]. Conversely, age exhibited a consistent and strong main effect across all eGFR categories, but its interaction with CMRFs was not statistically significant, indicating that the influence of CMRFs on lower eGFR is largely independent of age. Marginal effect showed that the probability of moderate/severe eGFR scr-cysc decline increased steadily with age, particularly in participants with multiple CMRFs. This finding is consistent with the well-established relationship between aging and reduced kidney function, as well as the increasing prevalence of CMRFs with age [ , ]. These results underscore the necessity of integrating age- and sex-specific considerations into CKD prevention strategies, focusing on reducing CMRFs in female and tailoring interventions to the unique needs of older adults [ ]. This finding is consistent with the well-established relationship between aging and reduced kidney function, as well as the increasing prevalence of CMRFs with age [ , ]. These results underscore the necessity of integrating age- and sex-specific considerations into CKD prevention strategies, focusing on reducing CMRFs in female and tailoring interventions to the unique needs of older adults [ ]. Although we used race-free CKD‑EPI equations and did not apply the Black race coefficient, racial/ethnic heterogeneity within the U.S. cohort may still influence observed per-CMRF gradients through differences in baseline risk, access to care, treatment intensity, environmental exposures, and structural determinants of health. The distribution and clustering of cardiometabolic risks, as well as differential susceptibility to kidney injury, may vary across racial/ethnic groups, potentially modifying the incremental association between additional CMRFs and lower eGFR. Biological mechanisms Several biological mechanisms may explain the observed association between CMRFs and eGFR scr-cysc decline. First, hypertension and diabetes, two of the most prevalent CMRFs, are well-established risk factors for CKD. Hypertension contributes to glomerular hyperfiltration and subsequent nephron loss [ ], while diabetes induces oxidative stress, inflammation, and advanced glycation end-product accumulation, all of which accelerate kidney damage [ ]. Second, dyslipidemia, characterized by elevated triglycerides and low high-density lipoprotein cholesterol, may exacerbate kidney injury through lipid accumulation in renal cells, endothelial dysfunction, and inflammation [ , ]. Obesity, another key CMRF, is associated with increased renal hemodynamic stress, insulin resistance, and systemic inflammation, all of which contribute to CKD progression [ , ]. Finally, elevated fasting glucose, even in the absence of overt diabetes, has been linked to microvascular damage and impaired renal autoregulation, further supporting the role of hyperglycemia in reduced kidney function [ , ]. The cumulative effect of these mechanisms likely explains the strong and graded relationship between the number of CMRFs and eGFR scr-cysc decline observed in our study. Implications for aging and cardiometabolic health policies Our findings have several implications for aging and cardiometabolic health policies. First, the graded association between cumulative CMRFs and lower eGFR scr-cysc across midlife and older ages supports integrating routine screening for obesity, hypertension, dyslipidemia, and hyperglycemia into health assessments for aging populations. Second, differences in CMRF profiles and eGFR distributions between China and the United States underscore the need for tailored prevention strategies, such as earlier identification of metabolic abnormalities at lower BMI in China and more intensive lipid and blood pressure control among older adults in the United States. Third, aligning CKD prevention policies with broader aging and non-communicable disease frameworks may help optimize resource allocation and reduce cross-national inequities in kidney health. Clinical implications Our findings have several important clinical implications. First, they highlight the need for comprehensive risk assessment and management of CMRFs in middle-aged and older adults to prevent CKD. Early identification and treatment of CMRFs, such as obesity, dyslipidemia, hypertension, and hyperglycemia, can reduce the burden of CKD and its associated complications [ , ]. Second, the observed sex and age differences in the association between CMRFs and eGFR scr-cysc suggest that tailored interventions are needed to address the unique needs of different demographic groups. For example, older adults and women may benefit from targeted strategies to manage hypertension and diabetes, while younger individuals may require interventions to address obesity and smoking [ ]. Third, the consistent association between CMRFs and eGFR scr-cysc across two diverse populations underscores the global relevance of our findings. Public health initiatives aimed at reducing the prevalence of CMRFs, such as promoting healthy lifestyles and improving access to preventive care, are critical for addressing the growing burden of CKD worldwide [ , ]. Country-specific interactions suggest a critical need for tailored public health strategies. In the United States, where higher prevalence rates of obesity, dyslipidemia, and metabolic syndrome were observed, interventions should focus on lifestyle modifications and early detection of CMRFs. Conversely, in China, where population norms for body composition differ, emphasis should be placed on individualized risk metrics such as waist-to-hip ratio alongside body mass index. Limitations Several limitations should be noted. First, the cross-sectional design precludes causal inference and assessment of temporal relationships between cumulative CMRFs and eGFR decline. Second, some covariates (e.g. smoking and alcohol use) were self-reported and may be subject to recall bias. Third, we used a complete-case approach, which may introduce selection bias and limit generalizability if missingness is not random. Fourth, despite extensive adjustment, residual confounding remains possible, including unmeasured differences in healthcare systems and other contextual factors between China and the United States. Fifth, creatinine and cystatin C were assayed in different laboratories without cross-cohort calibration, which may affect absolute eGFR comparability across cohorts, although within-cohort associations are less likely to be biased. Third, we used a complete-case approach, which may introduce selection bias and limit generalizability if missingness is not random. Fourth, despite extensive adjustment, residual confounding remains possible, including unmeasured differences in healthcare systems and other contextual factors between China and the United States. Fifth, creatinine and cystatin C were assayed in different laboratories without cross-cohort calibration, which may affect absolute eGFR comparability across cohorts, although within-cohort associations are less likely to be biased. Sixth, analyses did not apply survey weights, so prevalence estimates may not be strictly nationally representative. Finally, we did not conduct race/ethnicity-stratified or effect-modification analyses in HRS, which may mask within-U.S. heterogeneity. Future directions Future research should prioritize longitudinal and interventional designs to clarify the temporal and potentially causal relationships between cumulative CMRFs and kidney function decline observed in this cross-national analysis. Prospective follow-up of CHARLS and HRS participants would allow assessment of how changes in cardiometabolic burden over time, rather than cross-sectional accumulation, translate into trajectories of eGFR decline and incident chronic kidney disease. In addition, future studies should integrate repeated measurements of serum creatinine and cystatin C with standardized cross-cohort calibration, incorporate albuminuria and novel biomarkers of inflammation and metabolic dysregulation, and apply causal inference methods to reduce residual confounding. Given the observed country- and sex-specific heterogeneity, comparative research examining healthcare access, treatment patterns such as antihypertensives, statins, and SGLT2 inhibitors, lifestyle factors, and genetic susceptibility is warranted to explain differential risk gradients. Finally, randomized or quasi-experimental trials targeting simultaneous reduction of multiple cardiometabolic risk factors are needed to determine whether lowering cumulative cardiometabolic burden can preserve kidney function and reduce cross-national inequities in chronic kidney disease among aging populations. Conclusion Our cross-national findings support integrating systematic cardiometabolic risk assessment and management into CKD prevention initiatives for middle-aged and older adults, particularly in rapidly aging societies. However, given the cross-sectional design, these results should be interpreted as hypothesis-generating, and longitudinal studies are required to determine whether reducing cumulative cardiometabolic burden leads to preservation of kidney function. chunks.content: More than 50% of cases with steroid-sensitive NS are frequently-relapsing and/or steroid-dependent. , Rituximab, a chimeric anti-CD20 monoclonal antibody, is an important therapy for FRSDNS. , , , Its efficacy in sustaining remission may be partly attributed to recent findings implicating an extrafollicular B-cell response during active disease and the presence of potential circulating antinephrin autoantibodies in ≤80% to 90% children with steroid-dependent NS. , , However, the causality of these autoantibodies is yet to be definitively established. Rituximab depletes B cells and B-cell subsets and thus may reduce potentially disease-causing autoantibodies that correlate with disease activity. , It also restores T-cell immune homeostasis through crosstalk between T and B cells. Existing efficacy and safety data from clinical trials, however, are largely derived from older children with FRSDNS, with a median age at rituximab administration ranging from 6.9 to 13.5 years. Published data on the youngest patients are not available. Our previous work showed that relapse risk reduced by 8% with each year increase in age at rituximab treatment. A cut-off age of < 10 years was recently identified to predict patients with less favorable response to rituximab. Younger patients are also more susceptible to complications, notably hypogammaglobulinemia and neutropenia. , , , Consequently, current recommendations do not advise to prescribe rituximab in young children aged < 7 years because of limited evidence. , , Nonetheless, it is well known that the youngest patients are the most challenging population to treat and often have a more complicated disease course. , They suffer from repeated relapses, resulting in frequent hospitalizations and significant steroid-related side effects. At the recent Kidney Disease: Improving Global Outcomes Controversies Conference on Therapies Targeting B Cell in Immune-Mediated Kidney Diseases, it was determined that the optimal therapeutic approach for young children who do not respond to oral immunosuppression remains a significant clinical gap. In view of these knowledge gaps, the present study aimed to examine the efficacy and safety of rituximab therapy through a multinational study to determine its role in young children aged < 6 years with FRSDNS. Methods We conducted a multinational, multicenter, retrospective cohort study between March 1, 2020, and December 31, 2023. In this study, we used 2 previously reported international pediatric cohorts with FRSDNS, which involved 16 tertiary pediatric nephrology centers from 10 countries in Asia, Europe, and North America. , We included young children with frequently-relapsing, steroid-dependent and/or multidrug-dependent NS who received their first course of rituximab before the age of 6 years between 2005 and 2022. We used standard terminologies for NS, frequently-relapsing, steroid dependent, primary and secondary steroid resistance, remission, and relapse. Multidrug dependence was defined as the requirement of ≥ 2 immunosuppressants (corticosteroids, mycophenolate mofetil, and/or calcineurin inhibitor) to maintain remission. , All patients were in complete remission at the time of their first rituximab administration, and rituximab was given with the aim of sustaining disease remission. The minimum observation period was 12 months following the first rituximab administration, unless a relapse occurred earlier. Subjects with a history of steroid resistance could be included if they attained remission after calcineurin inhibitor therapy and subsequently became steroid responsive, with a clinical course of FRSDNS that required rituximab therapy. , Patients who received repeated rituximab at fixed intervals (e.g., every 6 months), regardless of clinical response and B-cell population, were excluded. Further exclusion criteria were multidrug-resistant NS, in which rituximab was used to induce remission, and secondary NS (e.g., congenital or infantile NS, genetic podocytopathy, C3 glomerulopathy, membranous nephropathy, lupus nephritis, and IgA nephropathy). The study was divided into 2 parts. In the primary analysis, we examined the efficacy and safety of rituximab in these young children. In a secondary analysis, we further matched and compared these young patients with older children and young adults who received their first rituximab between the ages of 6 and 21 years. This matched analysis was performed to address potential confounders, enabling better understanding of age-related differences in treatment and immunological responses to rituximab. Rituximab was prescribed according to local policy, at 1 to 4 weekly infusions of 375 mg/m 2 or 1 to 2 biweekly infusions of 750 mg/m 2 . Dosing regimens were grouped according to the total dose per treatment course: low dose (375 mg/m 2 ), medium dose (750 mg/m 2 ), or high dose (1500 mg/m 2 ). Infusions that were prescribed > 4 weeks apart were considered as 2 distinct courses. The duration of concurrent immunosuppression was defined as the use of any agent, including corticosteroids, mycophenolate mofetil, and/or calcineurin inhibitors. Maintenance immunosuppression was defined as the use of concurrent immunosuppression after rituximab for ≥6 months or until relapse if that occurred within 6 months post-rituximab. Rituximab regimens and monitoring practices followed the local policies of participating centers. We collected fully anonymized data on baseline demographics, kidney histology,

The duration of concurrent immunosuppression was defined as the use of any agent, including corticosteroids, mycophenolate mofetil, and/or calcineurin inhibitors. Maintenance immunosuppression was defined as the use of concurrent immunosuppression after rituximab for ≥6 months or until relapse if that occurred within 6 months post-rituximab. Rituximab regimens and monitoring practices followed the local policies of participating centers. We collected fully anonymized data on baseline demographics, kidney histology, previous treatments, rituximab dosing regimens, immunosuppression use, relapse, kidney outcomes, adverse events, and total B-cell counts. This study was conducted in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki and the Declaration of Istanbul. Ethical approval was obtained from the Central Institutional Review Board of the Hong Kong Children’s Hospital as the lead study site (REC-2020-004). Participating centers obtained ethics approval in compliance to local policies where required, because some centers did not mandate such review for retrospective studies. Primary and Secondary Outcomes In the main analysis, the primary outcome was relapse-free survival, defined as time to relapse after rituximab administration. Children were censored at the time of additional rituximab administration or at the last follow-up, whichever occurred earlier. Secondary outcomes were B-cell depletion and repopulation, long-term remission (relapse-free for ≥ 2 years), rituximab resistance (relapse within first 3 months post-rituximab), the development of chronic kidney disease (estimated glomerular filtration rate < 60 ml/min per 1.73 m 2 ) and/or kidney failure, and rituximab-associated adverse events. B-cell depletion and repletion were defined as CD19+ B-cell levels < and ≥ 1% of the total lymphocyte population, respectively. Adverse events included death, severe infusion reactions, infections, hypogammaglobulinemia, neutropenia, neoplasia, and complications arising from cardiovascular, respiratory, and neurological systems. Agranulocytosis and neutropenia were defined as an absolute neutrophil count < 0.5 × 10 9 /l and < 1.5 × 10 9 /l. Hypogammaglobulinemia was defined as an IgG level that was below the reference range for age at each individual laboratory. In the secondary analysis, we evaluated the relapse-free survival, B-cell depletion duration, and adverse events between younger and older patients. Statistical Analyses Descriptive data were expressed as mean (SD), median (IQR), and number (percentage), as appropriate. Between-group differences were analyzed using the Chi-square or Fisher exact tests for categorical parameters and t tests or the Mann–Whitney U tests for continuous parameters. In the primary analysis of children aged < 6 years, the Kaplan-Meier method with log-rank test was used to compare relapse-free survival after the first rituximab administration. We determined the relationship between relapse and all potential risk factors in these young children using a multivariate Cox regression model. These factors included rituximab dosing, duration of concurrent immunosuppression, age at NS diagnosis, age at rituximab treatment, sex, ethnicity, disease severity, history of steroid resistance, and previous use of immunosuppression. Multicollinearity in the model was assessed using the variance inflation factor. For missing data, no imputation was used. Statistical analyses were performed using R version 4.1.1 (R Foundation for Statistical Computing, Vienna, Austria) with “survival,” “survminer,” “coxme,” “lme4,” and “performance” packages. Statistical significance was set at P < 0.05. In the secondary study, we conducted 1:1 propensity score–based nearest-neighbor matching without replacement using the “MatchIt” package in R version 4.5.2. The propensity score was estimated using logistic regression with age group as the exposure variable and the following baseline covariates: sex, ethnicity (Caucasians/Asians/others), rituximab dosing (low dose: 375 mg/m 2 ; medium dose: 750 mg/m 2 ; high dose: 1125–1500 mg/m 2 ), number of immunosuppressive agents immediately before rituximab (1, 2, or 3), interval between NS diagnosis and first rituximab (continuous), and history of steroid resistance (yes/no). Exact matching (caliper = 0) was enforced for all categorical covariates, and the interval between NS diagnosis and first rituximab was matched within an absolute caliper of 2 years. Calipers were specified on the original measurement scale (i.e., nonstandardized). A 1:1 matching ratio was applied. Covariate balance after matching was evaluated using standardized mean differences, and the matched cohort was used for subsequent outcome analyses. Relapse-free survival between younger and older patients at the time of first rituximab administration was compared using the Kaplan-Meier method with the log-rank test. Results Patient Population We included 101 young children (70 boys) who received their first course of rituximab before the age of 6 years ( ). They presented with NS at a median age of 2.3 years (IQR: 1.9–3.2). Majority of the patients were Europeans (42%), Southeast Asians (35%), and South Asians (12%). Among the patients, 74% and 22% were multidrug-dependent and steroid-dependent, respectively. Calcineurin inhibitors and mycophenolate mofetil were used in 86% and 25% patients, respectively. A history of steroid resistance was reported in 31% of patients (primary, 13%; secondary, 18%); however, all had achieved complete remission with calcineurin inhibitors. Among the 58% patients who underwent kidney biopsy, the prevalent histological diagnosis was minimal change disease (76%). Patients received their first course of rituximab at a median age of 4.5 years (IQR: 3.6–5.4). Low-, median-, and high-dose regimens were given in 54%, 25%, and 21% of patients, respectively. Concurrent immunosuppression was given to 61 children (60%). Baseline demographics and treatment regimens are summarized in and . Nineteen (19%), 40 (40%), 20 (20%), 8 (8%), 6 (6%), 5 (5%), and 3 (3%) children received a total of 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, and 7 rituximab courses, respectively ( ). A total of 273 courses of rituximab were evaluated during the observation period, with 168 and 105 courses administered before 6 and after 6 years of age, respectively. The median observation period after the first rituximab administration was 4.6 years (IQR, 3.2–6.6). Primary Outcome: Relapse-Free Survival Eight-six children (85%) relapsed after their first rituximab administration. Kaplan-Meier survival analysis showed that the median relapse-free survival of the cohort was 8.8 months (95% CI: 7.5–11.0) ( ). Relapse-free survival did not differ between children aged < 4 years and those aged from 4 to 6 years ( ). A history of steroid resistance was not associated with relapse ( A and B). Nine children (9%) relapsed within 3 months post-rituximab and were considered resistant to rituximab. Long-term remission > 2 years was achieved in 11 patients (11%), and total B cells repopulated in all of them. Five of these patients eventually relapsed. The number of relapses significantly reduced from 3 (IQR: 2–4) to 1 (IQR: 0–1) within 1-year before and after rituximab therapy ( P < 0.0001). Multivariable analysis demonstrated that each additional month of concurrent immunosuppression use (adjusted hazard ratio: 0.92; 95% CI: 0.89–0.96; P < 0.001) reduced relapse risk by 8%. Older age at first rituximab administration showed a trend toward a lower relapse risk (adjusted hazard ratio: 0.76; 95% CI: 0.57–1.03; P = 0.07). Although statistically insignificant, children receiving high-dose rituximab regimen (1125–1500 mg/m 2 ) appeared to experience a lower relapse risk than those who received low- and medium-dose regimens ( ). Sex, ethnicity, age at NS diagnosis, disease severity, history of steroid resistance, and number of previous immunosuppressive drugs did not affect relapse risk. summarizes the multivariable analysis of predictive factors for response. Total B-cell Depletion and Repopulation B cells were monitored within 1 month after the first rituximab administration in 70 patients, and B-cell depletion was observed in 99% of subjects ( n = 69/70). Total B cells were subsequently monitored in 58 children and repopulated at a median of 5.3 months (IQR: 4.3–6.8). Among these patients, 93% relapsed after B-cell repopulation, which had been documented a median of 2.2 months (IQR: 0.85–4.6) earlier; however, 22% of children did not relapse after B-cell repopulation. Subsequent Courses of Rituximab A second course of rituximab was administered to85 subjects (84%). The most frequent indication for redosing was NS relapse ( n = 77), followed by total B-cell repopulation ( n = 8). The rates of relapse, time to relapse, long-term remission, rituximab resistance, and duration of B-cell depletion after each rituximab course are summarized in . Importantly, 34% and 12% children attained long-term remission (≥ 2 years) following the second and third rituximab course, respectively. Between 5% and 13% of patients had rituximab resistance (relapse-free period < 3 months) during each cycle of treatment. Safety Profiles Hypogammaglobulinemia was the most frequently observed side effect after the first course of rituximab. Among the 53 patients whose IgG levels were monitored, 30 children (57%) had hypogammaglobulinemia documented, with a median lowest IgG value of 289 (100–380) mg/dl. Of these patients, 21 had preexisting hypogammaglobulinemia before their first rituximab exposure. Low IgG levels at baseline, compared with normal IgG levels, were associated with hypogammaglobulinemia post-rituximab (68% vs. 27%, P = 0.005). Other factors, including age at first rituximab administration (low IgG: 4.9 [IQR: 3.9–5.5] years vs. normal IgG: 4.5 [IQR: 3.9–5.4] years) and maintenance immunosuppression use (low IgG: 73% vs. normal IgG: 65%), were not significantly associated with the development of hypogammaglobulinemia. The neutropenic episodes lasted for a median of 20 (IQR: 5–49) days. Patients with agranulocytosis were treated with granulocyte-colony stimulating factor ( n = 3), systemic antibiotics ( n = 3), and acyclovir ( n = 1) with good recovery of the neutrophil count. Eight infectious episodes were reported in 7 patients (febrile neutropenia, n = 3; herpes simplex, n = 1; pneumocystis pneumonia, n = 1; community-acquired pneumonia, n = 1; viral gastroenteritis, n = 1; acute otitis media). Most of them had concurrent hypogammaglobulinemia ( n = 1) and/or neutropenia ( n = 5). We did not find any associated factor among these young patients with or without neutropenia, agranulocytosis, and infection. Of note, 2 patients were receiving mycophenolate mofetil as maintenance immunosuppression, whereas another patient with agranulocytosis was receiving cotrimoxazole as prophylaxis against pneumocystis. Details of side effects reported during the first and subsequent courses of rituximab are presented in . Hypogammaglobulinemia ( n = 85/173, 49%) remained the most common adverse event across all courses of rituximab evaluated in our cohort, followed by infections ( n = 19/273, 7%) and neutropenia ( n = 18/267, 7%) ( ). The rates of hypogammaglobulinemia were higher among courses of rituximab administered before the age of 6 years (54% vs. 43%, P = 0.02). A total of 42 children developed hypogammaglobulinemia before the age of 6 years. The first occurrence was observed after the first, second, and third courses of rituximab in 30, 10, and 2 patients, respectively. Twenty-nine children received further courses of rituximab therapy, and hypogammaglobulinemia recurred in 20 children (68%). Among the 18 children who received additional administrations after the age of 6 years, 13 developed hypogammaglobulinemia (72%). The rates of neutropenia (9% vs. 4%) and infection (8% vs. 5%) were also higher, although these differences did not reach statistical significance. Chronic Kidney Disease and Kidney Failure All 101 patients remained steroid sensitive during the observation period. Normal kidney function was reported in all children at the last follow-up, except 1 who had chronic kidney disease stage 2. The patient had multidrug-dependent NS since the age of 19 months and was treated with a calcineurin inhibitor for disease control. Rituximab was administered at 5.6 years of age, and the calcineurin inhibitor was continued as maintenance for more than 4 years at the last follow-up. Although a kidney biopsy was not performed, the impaired kidney function could be attributable to long-term calcineurin inhibitor–associated nephrotoxicity. No patients required kidney replacement therapy. Secondary Matched Analysis With Children Receiving First Rituximab at an Older Age We matched 70 young children with 70 older children who received their first rituximab ≥ 6 years of age). Rituximab was first administered at a median age of 4.7 (IQR: 3.9–5.4) years and 9.8 (IQR: 7.3–14.6) years in the younger and older groups, respectively. The difference in interval between NS diagnosis and first rituximab was significant yet modest in magnitude between the 2 groups (young: 2.1 ± 1.2 years vs. older: 2.7 ± 1.3 years). Baseline characteristics, including sex, ethnicity, disease severity, history of steroid resistance, number of immunosuppressive drugs immediately before rituximab, rituximab regimens, and maintenance immunosuppression, were comparable between groups ( ). Median relapse-free survival did not differ statistically, although young children demonstrated a trend toward earlier relapse ( ; 8.3 months, 95% CI: 6.7–10.6 vs. 11.3 months, 95% CI: 8.3–14.4; log-rank test P = 0.14). Time to B-cell repletion was similar between groups (young: 5.5, IQR: 3.7–6.4 months; vs. older: 5.6, IQR: 3.7–7.1 months). The side effects observed during the first course of rituximab were compared between the matched young and older patients. Young children had significantly higher rates of hypogammaglobulinemia (63% vs. 35%; P = 0.01) and tended to develop more complications, including neutropenia (13% vs. 7%; P = 0.27), agranulocytosis (7.5% vs. 2.9%), and infection (8.6% vs. 4.3%) ( ). Discussion Our multiethnic cohort provides long-term efficacy and safety data on rituximab in young children aged < 6 years. Our data demonstrate that rituximab sustains remission even in young children with a complicated disease course. Hypogammaglobulinemia is prevalent in ≤57% of patients. Concomitant infection is uncommon but could be underreported. Although our findings suggest that rituximab can be used as a third-line or even second-line agent for complicated FRSDNS in young children, the therapy appears to be less effective and associated with more complications compared with those receiving the drug at an older age. Our cohort represented the most severe and complicated group of young children with FRSDNS. As expected, most of the patients were multidrug dependent, and the rest were steroid-dependent, with frequent relapses prior to rituximab administration. One-third of the children had a previous history of steroid resistance but regained steroid responsiveness following the use of calcineurin inhibitors, which has been associated with poorer treatment response to rituximab. , Up to 86% subjects with FRSDNS continued to relapse despite calcineurin inhibitor therapy, a potent steroid-sparing agent. This suggests that most pediatric nephrologists reserve rituximab as a last resort for FRSDNS in young children. Our data showed that the median relapse-free period in these young children was a median of 8.8 months after rituximab treatment. Although this efficacy is not as pronounced as that observed in older children, it is remarkable given that our cohort had a challenging disease course and had failed multiple steroid-sparing agents. To our best knowledge, there are no available data for comparison, because previous studies have enrolled mostly older children and did not perform specific subgroup analyses for young children. Furthermore, reported treatment outcomes of rituximab have been highly variable because of heterogeneity in patient populations and the prescription of rituximab and immunosuppression. We therefore matched our young patient cohort with older children of similar clinical and treatment characteristics to enable fair comparison and minimize potential confounders. Although the intervals from NS onset to first rituximab between groups were statistically different, a 6-month difference in rituximab initiation would be unlikely to affect overall clinical response or side effect profiles. Although statistically insignificant, older children demonstrated a trend toward a longer relapse-free period than younger children. This may be partly explained by the fact that memory B-cell levels, a more established biomarker for response than other B-cell subsets, were higher at baseline and reconstitute earlier in children aged < 10 years compared with those aged > 10 years receiving rituximab. Another potential explanation is that the natural course of FRSDNS tends to improve with age, especially around the time of puberty. In contrast, the duration of total B-cell depletion was not different between the 2 groups. Furthermore, among the young patients, each additional year of age at first rituximab administration showed a trend toward lower relapse risk. In concordance with our previous findings, , our data showed that maintenance immunosuppression was an effective measure to extend NS remission in young children. Each additional month of concurrent immunosuppression use reduced relapse risk by 8%. Although our study was not designed to evaluate the choice of maintenance therapy, mycophenolate mofetil appeared to be the preferred option, being the only immunosuppressive agent used over 6 months. In this context, a recent randomized trial showed that maintenance mycophenolate mofetil could reduce relapse risk by 80%; however, the effect disappeared after drug discontinuation. Our study did not evaluate the rituximab drug levels and anti-rituximab antibodies because these tests are unavailable in most clinical settings. Current evidence, however, suggests that these parameters correlate poorly with relapse and does not support regular monitoring. Our previous work described a progressive improvement in relapse-free period after repeated courses of rituximab, suggesting a potential disease-modifying effect. Similar findings were observed in the current cohort. After each cycle of rituximab therapy, 10% to 30% of children achieved sustained and prolonged remission over 2 years. Although this may, in part, be related to outgrowing the disease, many children in our cohort were prepubertal at the time of rituximab retreatment, a stage at which the disease typically remains active until puberty is reached. This result can be impactful if repeated rituximab treatments can ameliorate the overall clinical course. One possible postulation is that early rituximab use prevents the formation of long-lived plasma cell.
