After each cycle of rituximab therapy, 10% to 30% of children achieved sustained and prolonged remission over 2 years. Although this may, in part, be related to outgrowing the disease, many children in our cohort were prepubertal at the time of rituximab retreatment, a stage at which the disease typically remains active until puberty is reached. This result can be impactful if repeated rituximab treatments can ameliorate the overall clinical course. One possible postulation is that early rituximab use prevents the formation of long-lived plasma cell. Further clinical and translational data are warranted to confirm this hypothesis. Rituximab appears to be generally safe, but its use is not without risk. , , , , Rare yet fatal adverse events such as viral hepatitis reactivation, lung injury, and multifocal leukoencephalopathy have been reported. , , Hypogammaglobulinemia, neutropenia, and agranulocytosis are the most prevalent adverse events and the incidences were reported to be 14% to 58%, 4% to 8% and 2% to 5%, respectively. , Our data reported more adverse events among young children than the general pediatric population. There were significantly higher rates of hypogammaglobulinemia in younger children, than in the matched older patient cohort. Although the difference in other adverse events was not significant between groups because of relatively small sample size and event numbers, this signal should be taken seriously into any treatment consideration. Interestingly, the observed adverse events were lower when rituximab was given to the same group of children after they turned 6 years or older. This concurs with previous findings that younger age at rituximab increased the risk of developing hypogammaglobulinemia and neutropenia. , IgG, IgA, and IgM levels and absolute neutrophil count should be regularly monitored, because all except one of our infective complications occurred in the presence of hypogammaglobulinemia and agranulocytosis. Furthermore, our data found that low IgG levels before rituximab was associated with hypogammaglobulinemia after rituximab therapy. The role of i.v. Ig substitution for asymptomatic numerical hypogammaglobulinemia, however, remains controversial. , The risk of developing complications remains a major and valid concern when prescribing rituximab to these young children. Another important consideration, as illustrated from our data, is that most children eventually relapse and require repeated courses of rituximab for disease control. In the short- to medium-term, there are concerns pertaining to vaccine competency and long-term immunological impairment. , , Future research is required to better understand the long-term impact, such as hematologic malignancy, of repeated rituximab treatments during an active stage of immunity development and maturation. , For these reasons, we recommend to use rituximab in young children with FRSDNS only after other second-line treatment options have been exhausted or resulted in side effects. Second generation anti-CD20, obinutuzumab, is effective in rituximab-resistant FRSDNS, even among children who relapse during complete depletion of circulating B cell. , Until further data become available, its use in young children should be exercised with great caution, only after balancing the risk and benefits. Obinutuzumab has, due to its mode of action, clear potentials of being more effective but also having more profound side effects than the first generation of anti-CD20 monoclonal antibodies. Despite a unique multiethnic patient cohort, our study had the limitations of a retrospective study, including selection and reporting bias. We tried to minimize them by stringent inclusion criteria and adequate observation. Second, there were variable practices between centers, including rituximab regimen, immunosuppression use, and redose indications. These might confound treatment responses and influence the reported rates of adverse events. In particular, hypogammaglobulinemia might have been underreported because of variable practices on IgG-level monitoring. Infection is an important complication after intensive immunosuppression and may be underreported. Finally, histology was not included as an adjusted factor in the regression model because kidney biopsy is not routinely indicated in FRSDNS ; available evidence however fails to substantiate its role as predictor. , , In conclusion, rituximab appears to have reasonable efficacy in young children with complicated FRSDNS. Maintenance immunosuppression may serve as a plausible option to prevent relapse and extend remission. Compared with older children, young children may experience a shorter relapse-free period and high rates of adverse events. Rituximab should therefore be considered only after exhausting other treatment options, until prospective trials provide more robust evidence to support its earlier use. Future trials should identify the prognostic values of specific B-cell subsets, examine the role of scheduled redosing, and compare the efficacy and safety of rituximab against novel therapeutics such as obinutuzumab and chimeric antigen receptor–based therapy. documents.title: KDIGO Diabetic Kidney Disease Specific Recommendations

chunks.content: Introduction Diabetes is a prevalent chronic disease with substantial adverse effects on the health of over half a billion people globally [ ]. It is characterised by considerable heterogeneity in aetiology, pathophysiology, clinical presentation and therapeutic response. Individuals may exhibit varying degrees and combinations of insulin resistance and beta cell dysfunction, along with individual differences in disease progression and complication development. Therefore, the management and treatment of diabetes require a personalised approach rather than a one-size-fits-all strategy. Previous studies have attempted to identify distinct subtypes of diabetes using genetic loci [ , ] or clinical variables [ , ], aiming to capture the disease heterogeneity more accurately. In a seminal study, Ahlqvist and colleagues classified adults with newly diagnosed diabetes into five subgroups using data-driven k -means and hierarchical clustering analyses based on six clinical variables: glutamate decarboxylase antibodies, age at diagnosis, BMI, HbA 1c , HOMA2-B and HOMA2-IR [ ]. These novel subgroups exhibited distinct characteristics and varied risks of progression and complications [ ]. Furthermore, the classification approach has been validated in diverse ethnic populations, including the Chinese population and others [ , ]. Interestingly, recent research suggested that models recognising the continuum of phenotypic heterogeneity in diabetes may provide a more detailed description of progression risks than categorised models such as clustering, thereby enhancing clinical utility [ ]. To address this issue, Nair and colleagues have employed data dimensionality reduction algorithms in the Scottish population [ ], generating tree-like graph structures with branches to visualise the heterogeneity of diabetes in terms of progression and phenotype. This approach has been validated in the German Diabetes Study (GDS) and the Ludwigshafen Risk and Cardiovascular Health (LURIC) cohort [ , ], enabling the differentiation of diabetic heterogeneity through a continuous representation of pathophysiology. However, as diabetes is driven by both genetic and environmental factors and their interactions, population-based studies have identified different characteristics between European and Chinese individuals [ , ]. No research has focused on the continuous heterogeneity of diabetes progression in other ethnic groups, especially cohorts from China, which has the highest number of people living with diabetes globally. Thus, we employed the data dimensionality reduction algorithms in a prospective Chinese cohort to visualise the heterogeneity of newly diagnosed diabetes, identify glycaemic phenotypes and explore the risks of progression to clinical outcomes. Our objective was to distinguish the phenotypic characteristics of diabetes in a Chinese population across the tree structure, highlighting similarities and differences compared with European populations. Methods Participants and study population The China Cardiometabolic Disease and Cancer Cohort (4C) study was a nationwide, multicentre, prospective, population-based study which was designed to examine the relationship between glycaemic parameters and clinical outcomes, including diabetes, CVD and mortality [ – ]. The 4C study design has been described in detail previously [ ]. A total of 193,846 adults aged 40 years or older were recruited from 20 communities located in different geographical regions across mainland China during 2011–2012. A comprehensive set of questionnaires, clinical measurements and laboratory examinations were carried out at the baseline visit. There was no restriction on ethnicity. The study protocol was approved by the Medical Ethics Committee of Ruijin Hospital affiliated to the Shanghai Jiao Tong University School of Medicine, Shanghai, China. All participants provided written informed consent. Data collection Trained study personnel collected the data on demographic characteristics, social–psychological information and lifestyle risk factors using a standard questionnaire. Education was self-reported and categorised into low educational attainment (primary school or less, middle school education) or high school education and above. Depression was assessed with the self-reported Patient Health Questionnaire 9 (PHQ-9), and a score of ≥10 represents moderate or severe depression [ ]. Current smoking was defined as smoking at least one cigarette per day for the past 6 months. Current drinking was defined as consuming alcohol at least once a week for the past 6 months. Physical activity was assessed using the International Physical Activity Questionnaire [ ], with physically active defined as ≥150 min/week of moderate-intensity exercise, 75 min/week of vigorous-intensity aerobic exercise or an equivalent combination of moderate- and vigorous-intensity aerobic activities [ ]. Diet score was calculated according to recommendations from the American Heart Association, with whole grain consumption replaced by bean consumption [ , ]. It was calculated as the sum of each of the following components: fruits and vegetables ≥4.5 cups/day (1 point); fish ≥198 g/week (1 point); sweets/sugar-sweetened beverages ≤1882.8 kJ/week (1 point); and soy protein ≥25 g/day (1 point). A diet score of <3 was classified as unhealthy diet. Sleep duration was self-reported with standardised questions and defined as the interval between evening bedtime and morning wake-up time. The total number of hours slept per 24 h period during the preceding week was recorded, with a mean sleep duration of <6 h or >8 h per

by bean consumption [ , ]. It was calculated as the sum of each of the following components: fruits and vegetables ≥4.5 cups/day (1 point); fish ≥198 g/week (1 point); sweets/sugar-sweetened beverages ≤1882.8 kJ/week (1 point); and soy protein ≥25 g/day (1 point). A diet score of <3 was classified as unhealthy diet. Sleep duration was self-reported with standardised questions and defined as the interval between evening bedtime and morning wake-up time. The total number of hours slept per 24 h period during the preceding week was recorded, with a mean sleep duration of <6 h or >8 h per night considered unhealthy [ ]. Body weight and height were measured according to standard protocols by trained study nurses. BMI was calculated as weight in kilograms divided by the square of height in meters. Blood pressure was measured in the seated position after a 5 min period of quiet rest using an automated electronic device (OMRON Model HEM-752 FUZZY, Dalian, China). The average of three recorded values was calculated for further analysis. All participants underwent an OGTT, and plasma glucose was obtained at zero and 2 h time points during the test. Serum alanine aminotransferase (ALT), creatinine, HDL-cholesterol (HDL-C), total cholesterol (TC) and triglycerides (TGs) were measured at the central laboratory using an auto-analyser (ARCHITECT ci16200 analyser, Abbott Laboratories, IL, USA). HbA 1c was determined using HPLC (VARIANT II System, Bio-Rad Laboratories, CA, USA). Definitions of diabetes According to the ADA guidelines, diabetes was defined as fasting plasma glucose (FPG) ≥7.0 mmol/l (126 mg/dl), 2 h postload glucose (2h-PG) ≥11.1 mmol/l (200 mg/dl), HbA 1c ≥48 mmol/mol (6.5%) or a self-reported previous diagnosis by healthcare professionals [ , ]. Follow-up and outcome assessment During 2014–2016, all participants were invited to attend an in-person follow-up visit. Trained staff queried medical history using the same standard questionnaire as was used at baseline. Anthropometric values and blood pressure were measured, OGTT performed and blood samples obtained by using the same protocols that were used during the baseline examination. If participants were hospitalised or had visited an emergency department, trained staff used a standard form to obtain data including medical history, physical examination findings, laboratory tests, treatments and diagnosis at discharge from the participants’ medical records. Data regarding insulin initiation and the occurrence of hypoglycaemia were ascertained via a structured questionnaire survey. Information on vital status and clinical outcomes was also collected from the local death and disease registries of the National Disease Surveillance Point System and the National Health Insurance System. Two members of the 4C Morbidity and Mortality Adjudication Committee independently adjudicated each clinical event. All members of the committee were unaware of the baseline risk factors of study participants. Major CVD events included the first nonfatal myocardial infarction, nonfatal stroke, hospitalisation for or treatment of heart failure that occurred during follow-up and cardiovascular death [ ]. The composite outcome of chronic kidney disease (CKD) included incident kidney failure requiring dialysis or replacement therapy, death due to renal causes, a decline in eGFR defined as eGFR <60 ml/min per 1.73 m 2 at follow-up or a certain drop in eGFR category (from eGFR ≥90 ml/min per 1.73 m 2 at baseline to eGFR of 60–89 ml/min per 1.73 m 2 at follow-up) accompanied by a 25% or greater reduction in eGFR from baseline [ , ]. Statistical analysis Baseline characteristics of the study participants were presented as mean ± SD or median (interquartile range) for continuous variables, and as number (percentage) for categorical variables. The discriminative dimensionality reduction with trees (DDRTree) analysis was conducted using the method proposed by Nair et al [ ]. Briefly, nine routinely available clinical variables were used to explore phenotypic heterogeneity in diabetes: HbA 1c , BMI, TC, HDL-C, TG, ALT, systolic blood pressure (SBP), diastolic blood pressure (DBP) and creatinine. Outliers that were more than 5 SDs from the mean were excluded. The nine variables were rank normalised before analysis. After the dataset was age- and gender-residualised using linear regression analysis, the DDRTree (‘Monocle’ R package) approach was used to perform data dimensionality reduction and establish a tree structure. We used linear regression to estimate the associations between the nine clinical variables used in DDRTree and the two DDRTree dimensions. We regressed each of the social determinants and lifestyle factors on the tree dimensions to assess the distribution pattern of individual characteristics across the tree. To obtain the individual probabilities for developing each diabetes-related outcome for each study participant, we used the Cox proportional hazards models (insulin initiation, CVD and CKD) or logistic regression models (hypoglycaemia), with diabetes outcomes as events of interest and the two DDRTree dimensions as independent variables. The dimensions 1 and 2, derived from the dimensionality reduction of the nine clustering variables, represent individuals’ positions in the reduced phenotypic space. These dimensions

the two DDRTree dimensions. We regressed each of the social determinants and lifestyle factors on the tree dimensions to assess the distribution pattern of individual characteristics across the tree. To obtain the individual probabilities for developing each diabetes-related outcome for each study participant, we used the Cox proportional hazards models (insulin initiation, CVD and CKD) or logistic regression models (hypoglycaemia), with diabetes outcomes as events of interest and the two DDRTree dimensions as independent variables. The dimensions 1 and 2, derived from the dimensionality reduction of the nine clustering variables, represent individuals’ positions in the reduced phenotypic space. These dimensions are continuous numerical variables without a predefined clinical scale, reflecting systematic changes in multiple metabolic traits. The effect estimates (HRs or ORs) were calculated per 1 U increase in each dimension. Global and local Moran’s I were calculated using a spatial autocorrelation method (‘sdep’ R package) [ ]. We further developed an easy-to-use online application by constructing a ‘mapping function’ that assigns individuals with diabetes to the 4C reference tree. This function uses nine routinely available clinical variables (HbA 1c , BMI, TC, HDL-C, TG, ALT, SBP, DBP and creatinine), while accounting for age and gender, to assign each individual a position in the 4C tree. The mapping function comprises two components: (1) two generalised additive models with smooth terms fitted with cubic regression splines to predict the two DDRTree dimensions using nine variables, age and gender as covariates; these models demonstrated excellent performance with adjusted R 2 values of 0.854 and 0.881, respectively (electronic supplementary material [ESM] Table ); and (2) a distance-estimating algorithm to calculate the Euclidean distance between points in the two-dimensional space. When all nine variables, as well as age and gender, are provided, the trained spline model predicts the two dimensions for the individual, determining a provisional position on the tree. In step 2, the distance-estimating algorithm calculates the distance between the individual’s provisional position and all positions in the 4C tree. The mapping function then reassigns the individual to the position on the reference tree with the shortest distance to the provisional point. This process identifies the individual among the 19,612 participants who most closely resembles the new individual being mapped. Finally, the predicted probabilities of diabetes progression outcomes for newly diagnosed participants were overlaid onto this tree. All statistical analyses were performed using R software (version 4.3.2, https://www.r-project.org/ ). This study is reported following the Strengthening the Reporting of Observational Studies in Epidemiology (STROBE) guidelines. Results Baseline characteristics of the study participants A total of 193,846 adults were recruited from the 4C study at baseline, and 170,240 (87.8%) participants attended an in-person follow-up visit. Of these, 24,307 participants were newly diagnosed with diabetes, including 23,793 participants who had screen-detected diabetes based on OGTT and HbA 1c tests, and 514 participants who had self-reported diabetes within 12 months and were drug-naive. Subsequently, the analysis excluded 2747 participants due to the presence of major diseases and 1948 participants due to missing data or outlier values for the nine clustering variables. Ultimately, the study included 19,612 participants with newly diagnosed diabetes (ESM Fig. ). The population consisted predominantly of individuals with type 2 diabetes. Baseline characteristics of the study participants are shown in Table . The mean age was 59.01 (SD 8.63) years, with men composing 36.8% of the cohort. There were 209 and 3233 participants receiving lipid-lowering medication and anti-hypertensive medication at baseline, respectively. Heterogeneity of diabetes-related phenotypes To visualise the phenotypic characteristics, data for each of the nine clinical variables used for the DDRTree models were overlaid on the tree, as shown in Fig. a–i. Magenta colour indicates high values, while light yellow represents low values. A high number of participants with extreme values is observed in the distal parts of the tree branches, and the intermediate values are in the proximal portions (ESM Fig. ). To quantitatively estimate the phenotypic distribution patterns, we conducted regression analyses of each clinical variable against the two dimensions of the tree and calculated the global Moran’s I statistics to assess the spatial autocorrelation (Fig. j, k). Given the differing units of the nine clinical phenotypes, standardised regression coefficients based on rank-normalised values were provided in Fig. j and ESM Table to enable direct comparison across variables. To enhance clinical interpretability and support translation into practice, corresponding coefficients based on original clinical measurement units are presented in ESM Table . A 1 U increase in dimension 1 corresponds on average to increases of 3.68 mmol/mol (0.34%) in HbA 1c , 2.71 kg/m 2 in BMI, 0.84 mmol/l in TC, 0.02 mmol/l in HDL-C, 0.93 mmol/l in TG, 9.23 U/l in ALT, 4.19 µmol/l in creatinine, 19.62 mmHg in SBP and 11.04 mmHg in DBP. A 1 U increase in dimension 2 corresponds on average to increases of 4.86

A 1 U increase in dimension 1 corresponds on average to increases of 3.68 mmol/mol (0.34%) in HbA 1c , 2.71 kg/m 2 in BMI, 0.84 mmol/l in TC, 0.02 mmol/l in HDL-C, 0.93 mmol/l in TG, 9.23 U/l in ALT, 4.19 µmol/l in creatinine, 19.62 mmHg in SBP and 11.04 mmHg in DBP. A 1 U increase in dimension 2 corresponds on average to increases of 4.86 mmol/mol (0.44%) in HbA 1c , 2.90 kg/m 2 in BMI, 0.58 mmol/l in TG, 1.23 U/l in ALT and 1.28 mmHg in DBP, as well as decreases of 1.44 mmol/l in TC, 0.58 mmol/l in HDL-C, 5.11 µmol/l in creatinine and 0.60 mmHg in SBP. These spatial gradients provide a clinically interpretable representation of the abstract tree dimensions. For instance, the upper-right branches of the tree contained participants who were hyperglycaemic and obese, with high TG and ALT levels, slightly elevated blood pressure and low HDL-C. The participants located in the bottom-right parts of the tree exhibited high blood pressure, creatinine, ALT and TC. According to Moran’s I values, HDL-C ( r =0.63), TC ( r =0.54) and DBP ( r =0.37) demonstrated the most pronounced distribution across the tree, followed by BMI ( r =0.36), SBP ( r =0.33) and TG ( r =0.25). ALT ( r =0.17), creatinine ( r =0.08) and HbA 1c ( r =0.06) showed weaker, though still structured, distributions. Local Moran’s I maps for the nine clinical variables are plotted in ESM Fig. , showing how strongly individuals within the tree are correlated with their neighbours. Heterogeneity of social determinants and lifestyle factors in diabetic individuals Figure a illustrates the relationships between the two dimensions and the social determinants and lifestyle factors in individuals with diabetes. Dimension 1 showed a positive association with low educational attainment, current drinking status and physical inactivity. Dimension 2 demonstrated a positive association with unhealthy diet, and a negative association with current drinking and unhealthy sleep duration. The variables that contributed to the heterogeneity, as determined by the highest spatial autocorrelation within the tree, were ranked in decreasing order of their impact: current drinking, less than high school education, unhealthy sleep duration, current smoking, physical inactivity, unhealthy diet and moderate or severe depression (Fig. b). Heterogeneity of diabetes-related outcomes During a mean follow-up of 3.8 years, 233 (1.21%) participants initiated insulin therapy, 495 (4.19%) experienced hypoglycaemia, 691 (4.19%) developed CVD and 740 (5.62%) developed CKD, respectively. Subsequently, we investigated how the aforementioned baseline phenotypic variation correlates with variations in the four diabetes-related outcomes (Fig. ). The probability of initiation of insulin was marginally increased along dimension 1 (HR 1.16 [95% CI 0.93, 1.44]) and statistically significantly increased along dimension 2 (HR 1.53 [95% CI 1.17, 2.01]), with the highest risk observed in the upper part of the tree (Fig. a), corresponding to participants with high baseline HbA 1c , obesity and TG, as well as low TC and HDL-C. Meanwhile, the probabilities for hypoglycaemia and CKD were positively correlated with both dimension 1 (hypoglycaemia: OR 1.27 [95% CI 1.09, 1.48]; CKD: HR 1.34 [95% CI 1.19, 1.52]) and dimension 2 (hypoglycaemia: OR 1.31 [95% CI 1.09, 1.59]; CKD: HR 1.36 [95% CI 1.17, 1.59]), positioning individuals in the top-right quadrant of the tree with increased risks of hypoglycaemia and CKD. These individuals typically exhibited hyperglycaemia, obesity, dyslipidaemia, elevated ALT and slightly increased blood pressure at baseline. The risk of CVD significantly increased along the horizontal dimension (dimension 1: HR 1.39 [95% CI 1.22, 1.57]) and remained stable along the vertical dimension (dimension 2: HR 0.99 [95% CI 0.85, 1.16]), indicating that the highest probability of CVD was localised in the right parts of the tree, characterised by hypertension and high creatinine, TC and ALT levels. In sensitivity analyses, after adjusting for baseline use of anti-hypertensive and lipid-lowering medications, the highest probability of CVD remained concentrated in the right region of the tree (ESM Fig. ). Consistent with the results from the 3.8 years of follow-up, the risk of CVD over a 10.1 year period reaffirmed these results (ESM Fig. ). The global Moran’s I statistic, a measure of spatial autocorrelation, for hypoglycaemia, CVD and CKD (Fig. i) showed strong and statistically significant spatial correlations across the tree ( p <0.001). Additionally, the local Moran’s I (ESM Fig. ) provided insights into the degree of spatial correlation between individuals and their immediate neighbours within the tree for each outcome. CVD over a 10.1 year period reaffirmed these results (ESM Fig. ). The global Moran’s I statistic, a measure of spatial autocorrelation, for hypoglycaemia, CVD and CKD (Fig. i) showed strong and statistically significant spatial correlations across the tree ( p <0.001). Additionally, the local Moran’s I (ESM Fig. ) provided insights into the degree of spatial correlation between individuals and their immediate neighbours within the tree for each outcome. Visualising individual risk in relation to phenotype To aid clinicians and their patients in visualising individual patient profiles and understanding the associated risks of disease complications, we developed an online tool ( https://www.rjh.com.cn/2018RJPortal/4c/diabetes-ddrtree/ ). This tool allows for the placement of individuals with diabetes on the tree structure, predicting their risks of initiation on insulin, hypoglycaemia, CVD and CKD. These predictions are derived using age, gender and the nine other continuous phenotypic measures used to define the tree. Discussion In the current study, we recognised the heterogeneity of diabetic characteristics as a continuum in a nationwide multicentre prospective cohort from China, and highlighted the risks of progression to complications. To our knowledge, this study is the first in a non-European cohort to explore the continuum of phenotypic heterogeneity in diabetes. Our findings showed similarities in the relationship between phenotypic heterogeneity and risks of complications across European and Chinese populations. However, there are noteworthy differences in individual metabolic indicators, such as the distribution of blood pressure and the association between blood pressure and the probabilities of diabetes-related outcomes. These disparities might be partially attributed to genetic and lifestyle factors. To enhance interpretability and facilitate clinical translation of the data-derived dimensions, we quantified their associations with individual clinical variables in original units, and mapped these associations onto the tree structure. This analysis revealed a continuous but heterogeneous distribution of type 2 diabetes phenotypes across the tree, allowing for intuitive interpretation of cardiometabolic risk gradients. Dimension 1 was positively associated with higher values of most clinical phenotypes, and was associated with increased risks of hypoglycaemia, CVD and CKD. Dimension 2 reflected a more complex pattern, positively associated with HbA 1c , BMI, TG, ALT and DBP, but negatively associated with TC, HDL-C and creatinine, and was linked to an increased risk of insulin initiation, hypoglycaemia and CKD. These gradients delineated distinct high-risk regions along the phenotype tree. Individuals at an elevated risk of initiation of insulin were mainly located in the upper region of the phenotype tree, characterised by high HbA 1c , adiposity and dyslipidaemia. The upper-right region, showing high levels of HbA 1c , BMI, TG and ALT and modestly elevated blood pressure, was associated with a greater risk of both hypoglycaemia and CKD, reflecting a phenotype with advanced metabolic disturbance and hepatic involvement. In contrast, individuals at a greater risk of CVD were predominantly found in the right region, characterised by elevated blood pressure and TC. Together, these findings highlight the value of the tree-based structure in identifying clinically meaningful phenotypes and supporting personalised risk stratification. Linking tree dimensions to interpretable clinical features enhances model transparency and supports the integration of data-driven phenotyping into clinical care. We compared in detail the Chinese and European populations for similarities and differences in intricate relationships between diabetes-related phenotypes and the risks of complications. Consistent with the findings from the European populations [ ], we observed that individuals with a greater risk of glycaemic deterioration requiring insulin initiation were more likely to have high HbA 1c , obesity and dyslipidaemia. Insulin effectively reduces plasma glucose concentrations, and the administration of exogenous insulin becomes necessary when beta cell function declines and endogenous insulin secretion is insufficient. These data support the ADA’s consensus-based recommendation that diabetic individuals with very high HbA 1c levels should receive insulin treatment [ ]. We observed that participants with elevated risk of CKD were characterised by high HbA 1c , high BMI, high TG, low HDL-C and moderate to high blood pressure. Similarly, the tree structure derived from the European populations demonstrated a predisposition in individuals with diabetes towards adiposity, dyslipidaemia and high HbA 1c ; however, no statistically significant correlation was observed between blood pressure and CKD [ ]. A community-based prospective cohort study reported that even blood pressure levels below the hypertension threshold were associated with an increased risk of incident CKD [ ]. Interestingly, a recent Mendelian randomisation study indicated that the causal relationships between hypertension and CKD risk vary across different ancestries, suggesting the need to consider ethnicity in the management of CKD risk factors [ ]. Further in-depth studies into the underlying pathophysiological mechanisms are required to elucidate the discrepancies between our findings and the results derived from the tree-like representation in European populations [ , ]. Moreover, our findings revealed that the risk of incident CVD was highest in individuals characterised by higher blood pressure,

below the hypertension threshold were associated with an increased risk of incident CKD [ ]. Interestingly, a recent Mendelian randomisation study indicated that the causal relationships between hypertension and CKD risk vary across different ancestries, suggesting the need to consider ethnicity in the management of CKD risk factors [ ]. Further in-depth studies into the underlying pathophysiological mechanisms are required to elucidate the discrepancies between our findings and the results derived from the tree-like representation in European populations [ , ]. Moreover, our findings revealed that the risk of incident CVD was highest in individuals characterised by higher blood pressure, ALT, creatinine and TC. The European-oriented tree structures showed similar associations between phenotypic characteristics and major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE), with the exception of blood pressure [ ]. Observational studies demonstrated that hypertension was the leading risk factor for CVD [ ]. A meta-analysis containing 123 randomised controlled trials of blood pressure-lowering treatment suggested broadly generalisable benefits of blood pressure reduction on CVD [ ]. The different patterns between our results and the European-oriented tree structures could be attributed to ethnicity or lifestyle factors. A particular emphasis was placed on assessing hypoglycaemic risk. Individuals with the highest risk of hypoglycaemia were located at the upper-right branches, corresponding to the distribution patterns of both insulin initiation and CKD. Insulin use was widely recognised as one of the main causes of hypoglycaemia, a common adverse event among individuals with diabetes receiving pharmacological therapy [ ]. Furthermore, a similar distribution of hypoglycaemia and CKD was observed across the tree. This could potentially be explained by impaired renal excretion function, which might lead to the accumulation of hypoglycaemic agents, and consequently result in pharmacological hypoglycaemia [ , ]. A comparison between the models developed in this study and those constructed using the k -means method in Chinese populations revealed consistent associations, such as the link between blood pressure and CVD, and between glycaemic management and kidney complications [ , ]. However, the models presented in this study, which are derived from continuous data, offer a more comprehensive assessment by capturing individual risks of complications, thereby providing advantages over categorical models based on k -means clustering. With regard to social determinants, lower educational attainment, current alcohol consumption and physical inactivity were associated with dimension 1, implying poorer phenotypic characteristics and a higher risk of CVD, hypoglycaemia and CKD. These findings align with the previous prospective cohort study [ ] and Mendelian randomisation study [ ], which demonstrated statistically significant associations between education attainment and adverse outcomes including diabetes, CKD aetiology and MACE, with the mediation of modifiable risk factors. Moreover, our findings revealed a statistically significant association between an unhealthy diet and dimension 2, indicating higher risks of insulin initiation, hypoglycaemia and CKD. Overall, social determinants and lifestyle factors showed statistically significant differences across the tree. Given that adherence to a healthy lifestyle is associated with improved glycaemic management and prevention of comorbidities [ ], a deeper understanding of diabetes heterogeneity will facilitate the development of more effective lifestyle control strategies. Our study presents several advantages. It characterises the continuum of phenotypic heterogeneity in diabetes within a prospective Chinese population, emphasising the similarities and differences between European and Chinese individuals. Compared with subgroups derived from k -means clustering analysis, the current study offers more comprehensive information and allows for individual risk assessments of complications. Furthermore, the web-based tool developed in this study enables allocation of individuals from China on the reference tree branches, providing valuable guidance for clinicians and patients in identifying those with worsening phenotypes and in assessing the risks for comorbidities, including the initiation of insulin therapy, hypoglycaemia, incident CVD and CKD. For European populations, the tree structure established by Nair et al, which has been well validated, may be appropriate to be chosen. However, new tree models might be needed to evaluate applicability in populations of other ethnic backgrounds. Nonetheless, several limitations need to be addressed. First, as the average follow-up duration of 3.8 years was relatively short, and the long-term follow-up data for insulin initiation, hypoglycaemia and CKD outcomes are currently unavailable, extended follow-up will be necessary to confirm the results. Second, our participants consisted exclusively of individuals aged 40 years or older, limiting the diversity necessary to fully encompass the spectrum of diabetes characteristics. Third, although the majority of newly diagnosed diabetes cases are likely to be type 2, it is plausible that some study participants may have had type 1 or other types of diabetes. Finally, our study did not investigate genetic variants associated with diabetes heterogeneity, and the tree was constructed based solely on routinely measured clinical phenotypes, without incorporating insights into the underlying pathogenesis of the disease. In conclusion, we visualise the heterogeneity of diabetes and complication risks as a continuum within the Chinese cohort. While there

Third, although the majority of newly diagnosed diabetes cases are likely to be type 2, it is plausible that some study participants may have had type 1 or other types of diabetes. Finally, our study did not investigate genetic variants associated with diabetes heterogeneity, and the tree was constructed based solely on routinely measured clinical phenotypes, without incorporating insights into the underlying pathogenesis of the disease. In conclusion, we visualise the heterogeneity of diabetes and complication risks as a continuum within the Chinese cohort. While there are shared characteristics between Chinese and European diabetic populations, notable differences in metabolic profiles also exist. These findings suggest that diabetes management might benefit from consideration of individual phenotypic characteristics. In the future, incorporating individual phenotypic variation into clinical practice holds the potential to enhance the precision and effectiveness of diabetes care.
