Pneumonia onset within the first six months was more common in patients receiving Tac (p= 0.012) and glucocorticosteroids (GCs) (p= 0.017), while patients receiving everolimus (EVE) had a lower incidence (p= 0.026). Bacterial infections occurred earlier, particularly, within the first month, six months, and 12 months, while MTC infections were observed in the first 12 months. Fungal infections, including Candida spp., yeast-like fungi, and P. jirovecii were identified after 12 months, although none of these differences were statistically significant. The thoracic CT findings are presented in . Multilobar infiltration was observed more frequently in KT patients (p= 0.018), while pleural effusion was more common in LT patients (p= 0.027). Pleural effusion was significantly more prevalent in patients exhibiting symptoms of dyspnea and hypoxemia (p= 0.003). ETA was the most common diagnostic method employed for patients with focal and multilobar infiltration (p= 0.006; p= 0.022, respectively), centrilobular nodules (p= 0.040), and diffuse ground-glass nodules (p= 0.021). Focal infiltration was associated with a higher prevalence of bacterial growth (p= 0.004), particularly gram-negative bacteria (p= 0.010). Among the evaluated patients, 146 (86.9%) required hospitalization, with 53 patients (36.3%) needing admission to an intensive care unit (ICU) during their hospitalization. ICU admissions were higher in patients with pneumonia during the firstand sixth months post-transplantation (p< 0.001; p= 0.002, respectively). Bacterial infections (p< 0.001), gram-negative bacteria (p< 0.001), Acinetobacter spp. (p< 0.001), and Klebsiella spp. (p= 0.002) were more common in ICU admissions. Focal infiltration (p= 0.001) and pleural effusion (p< 0.001) were also more prevalent among ICU admissions. Of the 168 patients, 135 (80.4%) were discharged with full recovery, one was lost to follow-up, and 32 (19%) died. Mortality was significantly higher among patients with pneumonia within the first six months post-transplant (p= 0.042). Non-surviving patients more frequently had bacterial infections (p= 0.019), especially gram-negative bacteria (p= 0.010), Acinetobacter spp. (p= 0.001), and Klebsiella spp. (p= 0.021). Additionally, ICU admissions were notably higher among patients who did not survive (p< 0.001). DISCUSSION This study provides a detailed analysis of post-transplant pulmonary infections in adult SOT recipients spanning approximately 10 years, offering key insights into the frequency, etiology, and clinical management of these infections. The median time to pneumonia development was significantly shorter in LT recipients. We found that both invasive and non-invasive diagnostic methods play important roles, emphasizing the need to optimize these processes for better clinical outcomes. Notably, 86.9% of patients required hospitalization, with 36.3% admitted to the ICU, primarily due to pneumonia within the first six months post-transplant. The presence of gram-negative bacteria, such as Acinetobacter spp. and Klebsiella spp., correlated with increased ICU admissions, highlighting the critical need for effective infection management strategies during the post-transplant period. In line with previous studies, male patients were predominant among those developing pneumonia post-transplantation ( ). Comparative studies in Italy and Spain have similarly reported a median age of 62 in SOT recipients with post-transplant pneumonia, likely reflecting the demographic composition of the older population in those regions ( ). This may be related to the large elderly population in those countries. In another Turkish cohort, a 24-year follow-up revealed pneumonia in 20% of SOT recipients, with a mean age of 37.6 years and a predominance of male patients (72%) ( ). Notably, prophylaxis guidelines emphasize P. jirovecii prophylaxis for 3-6 months following KT or LT in Europe ( , ). Similarly, pre-transplant LTBI prophylaxis is advised for SOT recipients ( ). In our centre, prophylaxes were provided to 28 (16.7%) SOT recipients for P. jirovecii and 15 (8.9%) for LTBI, with durations of six and nine months, respectively. Pulmonary CoNS ultations advised against LTBI prophylaxis in 17.8% of the cases due to a low perceived need, although retrospective review limited data from 67 patients. Neofytos et al. stated that the vast majority (2465, 86.7%) of SOT received primary P. jirovecii prophylaxis for a median duration of 176 days ( ). In England, Periselneris et al. have reported out of 912 KT recipients that 243 (26.6%) received isoniazid for LTBI; however, 42 (4.6%) patients who needed prophylaxis did not ( ). It is obvious that the number of recipients receiving LTBI will increase in our country, considering that the tuberculosis burden should be considered, and the processes are working according to the guidelines in our centre. Our study revealed that the frequency of pneumonia was 87% (92% in KT patients, 82% in LT patients), out of the total patients consulted to the department of pulmonary diseases for a preliminary diagnosis of pneumonia. Prior studies have reported pneumonia incidence rates of 8-23% following LT and 25-30% after KT ( , ). The reason for the high prevalence of pneumonia in our study is thought to be that

number of recipients receiving LTBI will increase in our country, considering that the tuberculosis burden should be considered, and the processes are working according to the guidelines in our centre. Our study revealed that the frequency of pneumonia was 87% (92% in KT patients, 82% in LT patients), out of the total patients consulted to the department of pulmonary diseases for a preliminary diagnosis of pneumonia. Prior studies have reported pneumonia incidence rates of 8-23% following LT and 25-30% after KT ( , ). The reason for the high prevalence of pneumonia in our study is thought to be that the study population consisted of patients who had already been consulted with pulmonary diseases with this preliminary diagnosis, that was, selected patients. Clinical manifestations of pneumonia in SOT recipients are diverse, influenced by immunosuppression and the wide array of potential pathogens ( ). While typical symptoms such as fever, cough, sputum production, dyspnea, and hypoxemia were common in our study, a small proportion of patients (7.1%) presented with atypical symptoms, consistent with other reports from Türkiye ( ). Duration and severity of symptoms can be important clinical clues. Acuteonset symptoms are often indicative of bacterial pneumonia, whereas a more gradual presentation may suggest fungal, mycobacterial, or P. jirovecii infections ( ). Chronic cough, persistent fever, or unexplained hypoxemia may be the only clinical signs of infection in these patients. Also, we found a statistically significant association between fever symptoms and the detection of Candida spp. and MTC. Diagnostic sampling played a critical role, with at least one airway sampling method used in 128 patients (76%) and two or more methods in 61 (36%). Microbiological diagnosis was achieved in 81 (63.3%) patients. These findings are comparable with previous reports, where etiological diagnoses were achieved in 60.7% of cases ( ). Chang et al. stated that non-invasive and invasive procedures led to a diagnosis of pneumonia in 31.5% (n= 29) and 45.6% (n= 42) of patients, respectively. FOB was used in 64 patients and had a diagnostic yield in 38 cases (59.3%) ( ). Microbiological agents were isolated in 18.4% of the patients by non-invasive methods (sputum, ETA), 15.5% by invasive methods (FOB), and 19.0% by both methods. Except that Acinetobacter spp. was more common in LT recipients and fungal culture growth was more prevalent in KT recipients, there was no significant difference between pathogens by transplant type. In recent years, the management of opportunistic pathogens has improved, leading to a relative increase in the prevalence of conventional bacterial pathogens within transplant populations. Kara et al. conducted a retrospective review of medical records for all KT recipients from January 2010 to December 2014, identifying pneumonia in 18 patients (13.4%) out of 134 KT recipients ( ). Bacterial infections were the most common cause of pneumonia (28%), followed by fungal infections (8%). Similarly, Hoyo et al. diagnosed pneumonia in 54 patients (8.8%) among 610 KT recipients, with bacterial infection accounting for the most frequent etiology (44%) ( ). Our study similarly identified bacterial pathogens as the leading cause of pneumonia in 68.4% of cases. Furthermore, gram-negative bacteria represented 90% and 69% of bacterial pneumonia cases in LT and KT patients, respectively ( , ). In the current trial, gram-negative bacterial pathogens were identified as the most common pathogens, accounting for 35.7% of cases. This relatively low rate may be attributed to the limited use of additional diagnostic methods. Also, fungal infections were identified as a critical complication, which was crucial after bacterial isolation. These findings highlight the importance of considering fungal infections to ensure timely diagnosis and treatment. A study conducted in Türkiye reported bacterial infections as the most prevalent cause of pneumonia in 55 patients (49.5%), consistent with our findings, especially involving Haemophilus influenzae, Stenotrophomonas maltophilia , and P. aeruginosa ( ). Notably, 50.4% of the patients (n= 56) in that study showed no positive microbiological growth. In our study, the most commonly identified pathogens were Pseudomonas spp., Acinetobacter spp., Klebsiella spp., H. influenzae , and S. maltophilia , respectively. MTC was detected in nine patients (5.3%) and Nocardia in one. During the first month post-transplantation, infections typically arise from surgical complications, donor-derived infections, pre-existing recipient infections, or nosocomial sources ( ). The risk of infection is higher among LT recipients compared to KT recipients ( ). In the current study, pneumonia was observed at a median of 33 months (8-120) posttransplantation, with most cases occurring after the sixth month. Similarly, in a study conducted by Giannella et al., the median time to pneumonia onset in 54 patients was 25 months (3-96), with most cases also after the sixth month ( ). Pneumonia onset was significantly earlier in LT patients compared to KT patients with most in LT patients occurring within the first 12 months post-transplantation. In the study by Fishman et

The risk of infection is higher among LT recipients compared to KT recipients ( ). In the current study, pneumonia was observed at a median of 33 months (8-120) posttransplantation, with most cases occurring after the sixth month. Similarly, in a study conducted by Giannella et al., the median time to pneumonia onset in 54 patients was 25 months (3-96), with most cases also after the sixth month ( ). Pneumonia onset was significantly earlier in LT patients compared to KT patients with most in LT patients occurring within the first 12 months post-transplantation. In the study by Fishman et al., more than 90% of the infections occurring within the first month posttransplantation were nosocomial, primarily involving bacterial or Candida infections at surgical sites, lungs, urinary tract, or vascular access devices ( ). After the first month, the infection profile in transplant recipients shifts, and sustained immunosuppression predisposes patients to opportunistic infections, including P. jirovecii , Aspergillus spp., endemic fungi, MTC, NTM, Listeria spp., and various parasites, barring significant epidemiological risks. We investigated the relationship between the observed pathogens and the timing of their occurrence post-transplantation; Acinetobacter spp. infections were more prevalent within the first month and up to 12 months post-transplantation. MTC infections were particularly common during the first 12 months, while fungal infections, including Candida spp., yeast-like fungi, Aspergillus spp., and P. jirovecii , were more frequently observed after 12 months, although none of these associations reached statistical significance. In patients with compatible symptoms and physical examination findings, consolidation on chest radiographs, when present, is often sufficient to diagnose pneumonia. Microbiological diagnosis is crucial in guiding pneumonia treatment in immunocompromised patients, enabling the selection of targeted and effective antibiotics while reducing the risks of ineffective empirical regimens or unnecessary broadspectrum antibiotics ( ). However, obtaining a definitive diagnosis is often challenging, emphasizing the importance of determining the most appropriate sampling method based on clinical presentation and underlying risk factors. In a study by Ranzani et al., a median of three diagnostic methods ( , , ) was applied to 200 hospital-acquired pneumonia patients in six ICUs in Barcelona, Spain ( ). At least one respiratory sampling method was utilized in 93% of the patients, and two or more methods were employed in 40%, with microbiological diagnosis achieved in 50%. Similarly, in our study, microbiological diagnosis was obtained in 63% of the patients using one to four diagnostic methods employed. According to the Pneumonia in Solid Organ Transplantation: Guidelines from the American Society of Transplantation Infectious Diseases Community of Practice, sputum culture for gram stain and bacterial culture is recommended in adults with sputum production, though evidence is weak and data quality is low ( ). Additionally, the 2016 American Thoracic Society and the Infectious Diseases Society of America guidelines for hospitalacquired pneumonia recommend non-invasive respiratory sampling ( ). In our study, regardless of transplantation type, gram-positive bacteria, gram-negative bacteria, Acinetobacter spp., Klebsiella spp., and Haemophilus spp. were more frequently identified by non-invasive methods. Among these, sputum cultures showed particularly higher growth rates for Gram-positive bacteria, S. pneumoniae , Klebsiella spp., and Haemophilus spp. while ETA cultures had significantly higher growth rates of gram-negative bacteria and Acinetobacter spp. In certain cases, more invasive diagnostic procedures are required to achieve an accurate diagnosis ( ). The decision to perform such procedures should be carefully tailored to the individual patient, with a thorough clinician-led risk-benefit analysis. Invasive methods are particularly valuable for diagnosing fungal infections ( , , ). Several studies highlight the utility of FOB in identifying bacterial pneumonia in SOT recipients. For instance, Ranzani et al., in a study of 200 patients with hospital-acquired pneumonia across six ICUs, observed significantly higher microbiological diagnosis rates in the invasive group (BL and BAL) compared to non-invasive methods (56% vs. 39%, p= 0.018) ( ). A study from Türkiye by Küpeli et al. utilized FOB to evaluate lung infiltrates in 61 LT and KT patients, yielding microorganism growth in 39.3% of cases with common isolates including MTC (10/24), Staphylococcus aureus (3/24), Klebsiella pneumoniae (2/24), Escherichia coli (2/24), and S. pneumoniae (1/24) ( ). Similarly, Eyüboğlu et al., in a cohort of 90 LT and KT patients (including one heart transplant), found bacterial growth in 32 patients (35.5%), with pathogens such as S. aureus (4/32), Moraxella catarrhalis (4/32), S. pneumoniae (2/32), and S. maltophilia (1/32) ( ). In our study, FOB yielded diagnostic results in 32.5% of cases, with Candida spp. more frequently detected via invasive methods. Notably, BL samples often revealed S. maltophilia , MTC, NTM, and Candida spp., while BAL samples, regardless of transplant type, commonly identified Pseudomonas spp., P. jirovecii , Aspergillus spp., and non- P. jirovecii fungi. BAL is recommended for patients with diffuse or focal pulmonary infiltrates who do not respond to empirical antibacterial therapy and for whom

growth in 32 patients (35.5%), with pathogens such as S. aureus (4/32), Moraxella catarrhalis (4/32), S. pneumoniae (2/32), and S. maltophilia (1/32) ( ). In our study, FOB yielded diagnostic results in 32.5% of cases, with Candida spp. more frequently detected via invasive methods. Notably, BL samples often revealed S. maltophilia , MTC, NTM, and Candida spp., while BAL samples, regardless of transplant type, commonly identified Pseudomonas spp., P. jirovecii , Aspergillus spp., and non- P. jirovecii fungi. BAL is recommended for patients with diffuse or focal pulmonary infiltrates who do not respond to empirical antibacterial therapy and for whom a diagnosis could not be established through non-invasive methods (strong recommendation, moderate quality evidence) ( ). Our findings indicate that ETA is the most frequently used diagnostic method for patients with focal infiltration, multilobar infiltration, centrilobular nodules, diffuse ground-glass opacities, and pleural effusion. The diagnostic specificity of quantitative cultures from ETA and BAL is comparable ( ). While both methods have the potential to yield a diagnosis, the decision to proceed with further invasive procedures in a SOT recipient with pneumonia must carefully weigh the procedural risks against the potential diagnostic and therapeutic benefits. CT imaging is the preferred modality for evaluating pneumonia in SOT recipients, as it often provides more accurate diagnostic information than chest X-rays, which may be insufficient for accurate assessment. Bacterial pneumonia, including Legionella, may present as focal consolidation on CT scans ( ). Additionally, CT can identify diffuse infiltrates associated with viral pneumonias or P. jirovecii . In a study involving 45 pneumonia cases, the most common CT findings included Consolidation (n= 37; 82%), groundglass opacification (n= 34; 76%), septal thickening (n= 33; 73%), pleural effusion (n= 33; 73%), as well as multiple (n= 25; 56%) or single (n= 2; 4%) nodules ( ). Furthermore, no significant differences were observed in the prevalence of these findings among bacterial, viral, and fungal pneumonias. In our study, thoracic CT findings included focal consolidation, diffuse ground-glass nodules, multilobar infiltration, centrilobular nodules, cavitation, and mass/metastatic nodules. Notably, focal infiltrates were more frequently associated with bacterial and gram-negative bacterial growth. A multicentre study conducted across 35 centres (18 in Italy and 17 in Spain) examined 54 SOT patients with pneumonia and reported that 11.1% required ICU admission ( ). Similarly, data from a transplant centre in Türkiye indicated that 51 out of 193 recipients (26.4%) who developed pneumonia post-transplant were managed in the ICU ( ). In our study, 36.3% of the evaluated patients required ICU admission at some point during their hospitalization. Among the 168 patients consulted, 32 (19%) died. Of the surviving patients, 52.6% were KT recipients, though this observation did not reach statistical significance. A recent retrospective study from our country further analysed 51 out of 193 post-transplant patients with pneumonia who required ICU care, documenting a mortality rate of 39.2%, with no significant mortality difference across transplant types ( ). Chang et al. also reported a 29.3% mortality rate among 92 patients with pneumonia, accounting for 27 deaths ( ). Our study has several limitations. Galactomannan testing could not be performed due to intermittent technical issues, and as a result, this data could not be included in our study. This limitation may have impacted the ability to assess the full spectrum of infections, potentially leading to an underestimation of fungal-related complications. Additionally, the prognosis for all referred patients remains unknown, and the retrospective design presented certain challenges. Incomplete data, particularly regarding PCR for P. jirovecii , and the lack of evaluation of appropriate treatment regimens and comorbidities limited our ability to establish a clear link between ICU admission and mortality outcomes. CONCLUSION Despite the limitations inherent to its retrospective nature, this study offers valuable insights to the existing literature, by analysing data collected over nineyear period of data from a transplant centre. Our findings highlight the high frequency of pneumonia among clinically suspected cases, with bacterial pathogens, particularly in the early post-transplant period, being predominant. This underscores the critical need for heightened attention to nosocomial agents, especially considering the inadequacy of prophylaxis against opportunistic infections both pre- and post-transplant. The diagnostic accuracy for both invasive and non-invasive methods was above average. Notably, ICU admission and mortality rates were lower than those typically reported for pneumonia in immunocompromised populations. Continuous monitoring of pneumonia epidemiology and its risk factors in SOT recipients remains essential for advancing preventive and therapeutic strategies.

chunks.content: Introduction Individuals with chronic kidney disease (CKD) have up to 4 − 17 times higher risk of fracture, with risk increasing as kidney function declines and dialysis duration lengthens. – Unlike other diseases that impact the skeleton, bone changes in CKD are highly heterogeneous and extend beyond osteoporosis. CKD primarily involves the cortical compartment, the dense, compact tissue forming the outer shell of long bones, where increased porosity, cortical thinning, and alterations in intracortical composition, including a reduction in bound water and changes in collagen crosslinking, – are observed. These changes weaken the bone, making it more prone to fracture. Although trabecular bone also undergoes structural changes in CKD, such as reduced trabecular number (fewer structural elements) and increased separation, these changes contribute less to overall bone strength compared to cortical deterioration. , While imaging outcomes such as the trabecular bone score (TBS) reflects trabecular structure and fracture risk, cortical metrics are more strongly linked to strength and fracture in CKD, and thus should be considered. , In clinical practice, circulating biomarkers such as parathyroid hormone (PTH) and vitamin D (VitD) levels are typically evaluated first as part of the fracture risk work-up before proceeding to imaging. While dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry (DXA) is the most used imaging modality for fracture risk assessment due to its accessibility and ease, it can underestimate fracture risk in individuals with CKD. , This is in part because DXA measures areal bone mineral density (aBMD) from two-dimensional projections and cannot assess bone quality or distinguish cortical from trabecular compartments. , More advanced modalities such as high-resolution peripheral quantitative computed tomography (HR-pQCT), with its nominal isotropic voxel size (60-80 μm) and low effective radiation dose (3–5 μSv depending on scanner generation), enable three-dimensional evaluation of bone microarchitecture and improved sensitivity for detecting cortical deficits, even permitting estimation of bone strength through finite element analysis (FEA). HR-pQCT has therefore been used to evaluate the effects of CKD on cortical and trabecular microstructure and estimated strength, – and more recently, time-lapse HR-pQCT has demonstrated feasibility for quantifying local bone formation and resorption in advanced CKD. Yet even with HR-pQCT, conventional cortical parameters such as cortical volumetric BMD (vBMD), cortical thickness, and porosity have shown inconsistent group differences in CKD populations. , , These discrepancies likely reflect the complex, heterogeneous nature of CKD-related bone disease, which involves not only microarchitectural (e.g., increased cortical porosity and trabecularization of the endosteal surface) but also matrix-level changes in mineral and collagen organization, collagen cross-linking, and bone water content, which collectively influence matrix heterogeneity and overall bone quality. Such compositional changes are not captured by standard HR-pQCT or DXA metrics, underscoring the need for complementary analytical approaches, such as radiomics, capable of quantifying cortical matrix heterogeneity from existing imaging data. While prior studies have applied texture analysis to 2D radiographs, such images lack the resolution and depth to capture microarchitectural complexity. , HR-pQCT offers high-resolution, 3D datasets that are well suited for radiomic extraction of cortical heterogeneity. Radiomics is a quantitative image-analysis approach that extracts a large number of first-order, texture, and higher-order statistical features from medical images to characterize tissue heterogeneity that is not apparent to visual inspection. Despite its potential to improve understanding of renal bone disease, applications of radiomics in CKD remain limited. Recent studies have explored radiomics using opportunistic clinical chest CT to evaluate bone changes in CKD, but these efforts in the vertebra have not addressed the subtle cortical microarchitectural alterations characteristic of renal disease. In our prior work, we demonstrated the feasibility of texture-based analysis, a subset of the broader radiomics framework, by extracting gray-level co-occurrence matrix (GLCM) features from HR-pQCT images of cortical bone. Using machine- and deep-learning classifiers, this pilot study achieved excellent discrimination between CKD and non-CKD groups (AUC > 0.9), providing proof of concept that texture features derived from HR-pQCT can detect CKD-related cortical alterations. Building on this foundation, the present study applies a comprehensive radiomics framework encompassing first-order, texture, and higher-order features to HR-pQCT cortical bone to identify key image-based markers that differentiate CKD from non-CKD bone. We hypothesized that radiomic analysis would reveal distinct cortical patterns reflecting microarchitectural and compositional differences beyond those captured by conventional HR-pQCT metrics. If successful, this approach, combined with machine learning, could establish non-invasive imaging biomarkers that enhance characterization of CKD-related cortical bone alterations and support future efforts toward improved fracture risk assessment. Results Participant characteristics CKD patients were in kidney failure requiring dialysis, indicating stage 5D (on hemodialysis) disease. Patients in the dialysis group had elevated PTH levels (467.2 ± 98.9 pg/mL), while inactive vitamin D levels were within normal range (28.0 ± 2.9 ng/mL) (Table ). Non-CKD and CKD did not differ in age, height, weight, or BMI (Table ). Sex-stratified analyses showed that cortical area (Ct.Ar) was significantly higher in males than females in both CKD and non-CKD groups, whereas cortical vBMD and porosity did not differ by sex (Table ). Therefore, sexes were pooled across sexes for subsequent group-level comparisons Table . DXA-derived aBMD and t-scores were analyzed to complement HR-pQCT findings. The mean femoral neck t-score was −0.72 ± 0.93 in non-CKD participants and −1.32 ± 1.09 in CKD participants ( P = 0.012), confirming lower bone density in the CKD group. CKD had lower whole-body BMD z-scores than non-CKD ( P = 0.03). Among conventional cortical outcomes measured from HR-pQCT, the only difference between groups was for cortical thickness which was 9.3% thinner in CKD ( P = 0.02) at the tibial diaphysis but not at the distal tibial site (Table ). Other cortical parameters including vBMD and porosity did not differ significantly between groups. When considering the addition of FEA analysis, CKD had 13.8% lower stiffness and 13.1% lower failure load compared to non-CKD ( P = 0.016, 0.019) at the distal site only. Shapiro-Wilks results indicated that data from all groups exhibited a normal distribution ( P > 0.05). Radiomic feature selection and top-ranked features A bin width of 0.2 yielded the best feature extraction results. From both the distal and diaphyseal tibia in CKD and non-CKD image stacks, 753 features were extracted across the proximal and distal subregions. After filtering using optimized thresholds for low variance (below 0.2) and highly inter-correlated features (above 0.8), 11 to 23 key features were selected per subregion per tibial site (Table ). Figure show the remaining features after this process. A full list of selected features, normalized and ranked by average, is provided in Figs. and . The top five features with the highest feature importance per subregion for CKD and non-CKD are presented below. Radiomic feature importance rankings were determined separately for CKD and non-CKD groups within each subregion (proximal and distal) of the distal and diaphyseal tibia. The top features for each group are described below and illustrated in Figs. , . For each feature, the parenthetical terms denote the feature class (e.g., first-order, GLCM), the filter type (e.g., Laplacian of Gaussian or wavelet), and, where applicable, the filter parameter (e.g., σ = 1–5), which specifies the level of image smoothing applied prior to feature extraction. Distal Tibia Proximal Subregion For CKD (Fig. ), the top five ranked features were Autocorrelation (GLCM, sigma = 5; a measure of how voxel intensities are correlated with their neighbors, reflecting texture regularity) and Maximum (first-order; the highest voxel intensity, reflecting regions of greater mineralization) derived from Log-filtered images (sigma = 1, 3, 4, and 5). For non-CKD (Fig. ), top five features included: Maximum (First order) from Log-filtered images (sigma = 3); Minimum (first-order; lowest voxel intensity, corresponding to less mineralized or low-density regions) from wavelet-transformed images (high-pass filter); Minimum (first-order) derived from Log-filtered images (sigma = 2); and Maximum (first-order) derived from Log-filtered images (sigma = 1 and 2). Distal Subregion For CKD (Fig. ), the top five ranked features were Strength (Neighboring Gray Tone Difference Matrix, NGTDM; quantifies the overall intensity strength of neighboring voxels, with higher values reflecting greater texture heterogeneity) and Range (first-order; the difference between maximum and minimum voxel intensities, reflecting intensity spread) both derived from Log-filtered images (sigma = 3). Additional top features included Gray Level Non-Uniformity (GLRLM; a measure of irregularity in gray-level distribution, with higher values indicating less uniform density) from the original images, as well as Range (First order, sigma=1) and Maximum (First order, sigma = 5) from Log-filtered images. For non-CKD (Fig. ), the top five features included Minimum (First order) from Log-filtered images sigma = 4 and sigma = 5; Range (First order) and Interquartile Range (First order; the difference between the 75th and 25th percentile voxel intensities, reflecting mid-range density variation) from Log-filtered images (sigma = 1); and Maximum (First order) derived from wavelet-transformed images (high-pass filter). Diaphyseal Tibia Proximal Subregion For CKD (Fig. ), the top five ranked features included Minimum (first-order) from wavelet-transformed images (low-pass filter); Gray Level Non-Uniformity (GLRLM) from Log-filtered images (sigma = 3, 4); and Dependence Non-Uniformity (GLDM; quantifies non-uniformity in voxel dependence, reflecting heterogeneity) from both original and wavelet-transformed images (low-pass filter). For non-CKD

Log-filtered images sigma = 4 and sigma = 5; Range (First order) and Interquartile Range (First order; the difference between the 75th and 25th percentile voxel intensities, reflecting mid-range density variation) from Log-filtered images (sigma = 1); and Maximum (First order) derived from wavelet-transformed images (high-pass filter). Diaphyseal Tibia Proximal Subregion For CKD (Fig. ), the top five ranked features included Minimum (first-order) from wavelet-transformed images (low-pass filter); Gray Level Non-Uniformity (GLRLM) from Log-filtered images (sigma = 3, 4); and Dependence Non-Uniformity (GLDM; quantifies non-uniformity in voxel dependence, reflecting heterogeneity) from both original and wavelet-transformed images (low-pass filter). For non-CKD (Fig. ), the top five features were Maximum (first-order) from Log-filtered images (sigma = 3); Variance (first-order; quantifies the spread of voxel intensities) from Log-filtered images (sigma = 4); Mesh Surface (2D shape-based; quantifies the surface area of the cortical mask) from the original images; and Minimum (first-order) from both wavelet-transformed images (high-pass filter) and Log-filtered images (sigma = 2). Distal Subregion The top five ranked features for CKD (Fig. ) were all from log filtered images and included Gray Level Non-Uniformity (GLDM, sigma = 1), Minimum (first-order, sigma = 2), Cluster Prominence (GLCM, sigma = 2; measures the peakedness of gray-level clusters), Long Run High Gray Level Emphasis (GLRLM, sigma = 4; captures long consecutive runs of high-intensity voxels, reflecting denser regions), and Maximum (first-order, sigma = 3). For non-CKD (Fig. ), the five top features were Variance (first-order) from Log-filtered images (sigma = 4); Cluster Shade (GLCM) from wavelet-transformed images (high-pass filter); Minimum (first-order) from Log-filtered images (sigma = 3); Complexity (NGTDM; measures the complexity of texture patterns) from Log-filtered images (sigma = 5); and Mesh Surface (2D shape-based) from the original images. In summary, when comparing across anatomical sites, CKD bone at the distal tibia was predominantly characterized by Autocorrelation and Strength, whereas diaphyseal CKD bone was defined by Minimum and Gray Level Non-Uniformity, indicating site-specific textural heterogeneity. In contrast, non-CKD bone showed greater consistency across sites, with Maximum, Minimum, and Variance features repeatedly emerging as top-ranked descriptors. Validation of Feature Independence and Correlation Analysis Heatmaps of all the top-ranked features showed minimal inter-correlation, confirming feature independence and robustness (Figs. S – ). The correlation coefficient distribution was centered near zero, with most values ranging between −0.75 and 0.75, further supporting low redundancy among extracted features (Figs. S and S ). To examine the relationship between radiomic texture and estimated mechanical properties from HR-pQCT, we correlated the two most discriminative features in CKD, Strength (NGTDM) and Minimum (first-order) with µFE outcomes. No significant correlations were observed between either feature and µFE stiffness or failure load (Tables , S ). Correlation coefficients were low in magnitude ( | r | < 0.30), with weak negative trends for Strength and weak positive trends for Minimum, consistent with the possibility that greater cortical textural heterogeneity is associated with reduced mechanical competence. Discriminating CKD vs. Non-CKD Using Top Radiomic Features For the proximal region of the distal tibia, where both CKD ( P = 0.600) and non-CKD ( P = 0.176) groups for the Strength feature met the assumption of normality, a t-test was applied and showed no significant difference between groups ( P < 0.434, Cohen’s d = 0.251 [95% CI (−0.373, 0.872)]. For all other subregions that did not satisfy normality ( P -values ranging from 0.002 to 0.045), the Mann-Whitney U test was used, revealing statistically and practically significant differences between CKD and non-CKD groups for both the Strength and Minimum features ( P < 0.001, Effect size r = from 0.813 to 0.856). As shown in Fig. , the features chosen for evaluation were selected based on their ability to capture key aspects of bone texture in CKD and non-CKD cortical bone. Radiomic maps in Fig. illustrate that Entropy, Strength, and Minimum highlight different aspects of cortical heterogeneity. Entropy, which quantifies textural complexity, showed higher values (red/yellow) in CKD bone, consistent with increased cortical disorganization. The NGTDM-Strength feature (Fig. ), the top-ranked feature for CKD cortical bone at the distal tibia (Fig. ), measures the intensity of local texture strength, particularly in irregular and complex regions. This feature was significantly higher in CKD compared to non-CKD at the distal subregion ( P < 0.001) but not the proximal subregion (normal distribution, P = 0.434, Cohen’s d = 0.251 [95% CI (−0.373, 0.872)] (Fig. ). For the diaphyseal stack, NGTDM-Strength was significantly higher in CKD vs. non-CKD in both subregions (both P < 0.001). The Minimum feature (Fig. ), a top radiomics feature in non-CKD cortical bone (Fig. ), reflects the ability to capture areas of low intensity associated with more homogeneous bone tissue. Non-CKD cases exhibited higher values for this feature compared to CKD in the distal stack (Fig. , proximal and distal subregions both P <

the distal subregion ( P < 0.001) but not the proximal subregion (normal distribution, P = 0.434, Cohen’s d = 0.251 [95% CI (−0.373, 0.872)] (Fig. ). For the diaphyseal stack, NGTDM-Strength was significantly higher in CKD vs. non-CKD in both subregions (both P < 0.001). The Minimum feature (Fig. ), a top radiomics feature in non-CKD cortical bone (Fig. ), reflects the ability to capture areas of low intensity associated with more homogeneous bone tissue. Non-CKD cases exhibited higher values for this feature compared to CKD in the distal stack (Fig. , proximal and distal subregions both P < 0.001) and diaphyseal stack (Fig. , proximal and distal subregions both P < 0.001). All subregions aside from the proximal subregion of the distal image stack did not satisfy normal distribution thus the Mann-Whitney U-test was used and effect sizes ranged from 0.813 to 0.856). Based on the matched conventional HR-pQCT parameters at the distal tibia (CKD stage 5D: Ct.Ar = 127.5 mm², Ct.vBMD = 884.4 mgHA/cm³, Ct.Po = 2.6%; non-CKD: Ct.Ar = 138.5 mm², Ct.vBMD = 906.4 mgHA/cm³, Ct.Po = 2.4%), representative cases were selected to illustrate that conventional cortical measures can appear comparable between CKD and non-CKD bone (Fig. ). Despite similar conventional measures, these radiomic differences capture textural alterations beyond what is reflected by cortical porosity and are not qualitatively apparent in the original HR-pQCT images. Discussion Our findings highlight distinct radiomic features of tibial cortical bone in individuals with CKD stage 5D, which were notably heterogeneous across subregions. Conventional HR-pQCT outcomes, such as vBMD, cortical thickness, and porosity, were limited in distinguishing between CKD and non-CKD, with only modest differences in stiffness and failure load from µFE. In contrast, top radiomic features demonstrated stronger discrimination with larger effect sizes, supporting future machine learning model development defining the radiomic bone phenotype in CKD. Radiomics revealed heterogeneous texture alterations in CKD bone. For example, in non-CKD bones, top features were primarily derived from first-order statistics, reflecting basic intensity distribution, while CKD features were derived from higher-order statistics, consistent with alterations in microarchitecture and organization. Specifically, the “first-order minimum” intensity, representing the lowest voxel intensity in a given region, was lower in CKD bone across all tibial subregions, suggesting less dense tissue, potentially due to porous or degraded bone. These findings align with Wang et al. who demonstrated lower maximum intensity in osteoporotic bones on dual-energy CT, linking this to increased resorption and reduced mineral content. Although the original HR-pQCT images showed no obvious visual differences between CKD and non-CKD samples, the radiomic map revealed higher cortical heterogeneity in CKD stage 5D. This aligns with expected pathophysiological changes such as increased porosity and disrupted intracortical organization. Such findings support the biological relevance of radiomic features in detecting early cortical deterioration that may be overlooked by conventional assessments. Notably, Ct.Po derived from conventional HR-pQCT analysis did not differ significantly between groups (Table ). However, the radiomics approach captured broader textural heterogeneity within the cortical compartment. This may reflect the combined influence of intracortical remodeling, subtle trabecularization at the endosteal surface, and spatial variations in mineral or matrix density that are not resolved by threshold-based porosity metrics. Because the cortical segmentation included small intracortical pores and transitional regions, the extracted features likely encode both porosity-related changes and other microarchitectural variations, which could explain why radiomics distinguished CKD from non-CKD bone even when Ct.Po did not. In CKD, top radiomics features, such as NGTDM strength, were derived from advanced statistical methods (GLCM, GLRLM, GLDM, NGTDM), capturing subtle textural variations. NGTDM strength, which measures contrast in relation to neighboring voxels, was higher in the distal subregion of the distal tibia and all diaphyseal subregions, suggesting more heterogeneous tissue in CKD bone, potentially linked to compromised bone quality. These findings expand upon earlier studies, such as those associating GLCM-based features with osteoporotic changes, further supporting the clinical relevance of subregional texture analysis in CKD bone. , Importantly, our feature selection focused on robust metrics with low variation, utilizing an automated deep-learning pipeline for cortex segmentation, enhancing reproducibility, and reducing manual segmentation error or need for manual correction. This is crucial for clinical and research applications, as previous studies have shown that radiomic features can vary based on imaging parameters, including exposure settings (kV, mAs), filter type, and imaging distance, underscoring the importance of robust feature selection in radiomics. Subregional analysis of tibial stacks further illustrates that key radiomic features varied within the same image stack. For example, Autocorrelation (GLCM) and Strength (NGTDM) characterized CKD bone in the distal tibia, while Maximum and Minimum (first-order) features were more prominent in non-CKD bone. At the diaphyseal tibia, CKD features included Minimum (first-order) and Gray Level Non-Uniformity (GLDM), whereas non-CKD bone was characterized by Maximum and Variance (first-order). Such site-specific patterns may reflect differences in cortical organization

Subregional analysis of tibial stacks further illustrates that key radiomic features varied within the same image stack. For example, Autocorrelation (GLCM) and Strength (NGTDM) characterized CKD bone in the distal tibia, while Maximum and Minimum (first-order) features were more prominent in non-CKD bone. At the diaphyseal tibia, CKD features included Minimum (first-order) and Gray Level Non-Uniformity (GLDM), whereas non-CKD bone was characterized by Maximum and Variance (first-order). Such site-specific patterns may reflect differences in cortical organization and loading environment between distal and diaphyseal regions, factors that could contribute to their differing fracture susceptibility. Radiomic signatures appeared more consistent at the diaphyseal site, which may relate to its thicker, more uniform cortex and reduced partial-volume effects relative to the distal tibia with its thinner cortices. This observation suggests that the diaphysis could provide a more stable region for radiomic evaluation, although validation in larger, multi-site studies is needed to confirm reproducibility. Correlation analysis showed that Strength and Minimum, while top radiomic features able to significantly distinguish CKD vs. non-CKD cortical bone, were not significantly correlated with µFE-derived stiffness or failure load. This may suggest that these radiomic features may be sensitive to compositional or matrix-level alterations that are not reflected in bulk mechanical estimates. This interpretation aligns with prior work showing that tissue compositional changes, such as altered mineralization, collagen cross-linking, or bound water loss, can degrade bone quality independently of apparent stiffness. – Importantly, stiffness and failure load were the only HR-pQCT outcomes that differed significantly between CKD and non-CKD at the distal tibia (Table ). However, these µFE-based estimates reflect only the apparent, pre-yield mechanical behavior and do not account for post-yield or failure characteristics such as toughness or energy dissipation. Future studies should therefore test whether top radiomic features correlate with post-yield properties, alongside compositional measures of collagen, mineral, and water content obtained from spectroscopy or magnetic resonance imaging to better define their biological basis. Such multimodal validation would further clarify whether radiomics can detect composition-related cortical deficits that are not captured by density- or stiffness-based measures in CKD. Our findings align with previous findings on altered bone in CKD, , but extend these insights by characterizing texture changes not evident through conventional analysis. This approach is consistent with broader radiomics applications, where it has successfully captured subtle tissue changes in tumors, lungs, brain tissue, and bone. For example, a recent study achieved 94% accuracy in classifying osteoporosis using radiomics from dual-energy CT spine images. To our knowledge, this study is the first to apply radiomics to HR-pQCT imaging for cortical bone analysis. Previous research has applied textural analysis to trabecular bone, originating from the trabecular bone score (TBS) in DXA, now an additional osteoporosis management tool. Similarly, the distinct radiomic features identified in CKD bone may serve as non-invasive biomarkers, addressing limitations of DXA in assessing CKD bone quality. – Limitations of our study include the single-institution sample design, which may introduce bias. Future studies should validate these findings in larger, multi-center, prospective cohorts across a broader range of CKD stages. Model development deliberately began with advanced disease stages to first confirm that radiomic features can reliably distinguish clearly established cortical abnormalities before extending application to earlier and more subtle disease stages. This stepwise approach was informed by our previous pilot study, in which advanced CKD at the tibial sites, particularly the diaphyseal region, demonstrated excellent classification performance (AUC = 0.99, F1 = 0.99 in test data; AUC = 0.94, F1 = 0.96 in independent validation. Therefore, future studies should include earlier CKD stages to validate the robustness of radiomic features and evaluate their potential utility in guiding preventive treatment strategies. HR-pQCT is currently limited to certain research centers; however, the radiomics pipeline developed in this study is modality-agnostic and could be adapted to emerging imaging platforms. In particular, photon-counting CT (PCCT), which is becoming increasingly available and offers spatial resolution approaching that of HR-pQCT, may provide a clinically scalable alternative for radiomics-based cortical bone assessment. Further exploration of the biological basis of these radiomic features, including their associations with mineral, collagen, and water content, could provide new insights into CKD-related bone pathology. Although prior studies have frequently reported higher cortical porosity in CKD compared with controls, our cohort did not demonstrate statistically significant group differences. This may reflect the limited sample size, the heterogeneity of CKD-related bone disease, and the relatively higher BMI in the CKD group, which could confer partial protective mechanical loading and attenuate porosity differences. Evidence from a recent twin study by Nissen et al. supports this interpretation, showing that individuals with higher body weight exhibit lower cortical porosity and greater cortical cross-sectional area due to increased mechanical loading.
