Results Patient Population We included 101 young children (70 boys) who received their first course of rituximab before the age of 6 years ( ). They presented with NS at a median age of 2.3 years (IQR: 1.9–3.2). Majority of the patients were Europeans (42%), Southeast Asians (35%), and South Asians (12%). Among the patients, 74% and 22% were multidrug-dependent and steroid-dependent, respectively. Calcineurin inhibitors and mycophenolate mofetil were used in 86% and 25% patients, respectively. A history of steroid resistance was reported in 31% of patients (primary, 13%; secondary, 18%); however, all had achieved complete remission with calcineurin inhibitors. Among the 58% patients who underwent kidney biopsy, the prevalent histological diagnosis was minimal change disease (76%). Patients received their first course of rituximab at a median age of 4.5 years (IQR: 3.6–5.4). Low-, median-, and high-dose regimens were given in 54%, 25%, and 21% of patients, respectively. Concurrent immunosuppression was given to 61 children (60%). Baseline demographics and treatment regimens are summarized in and . Nineteen (19%), 40 (40%), 20 (20%), 8 (8%), 6 (6%), 5 (5%), and 3 (3%) children received a total of 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, and 7 rituximab courses, respectively ( ). A total of 273 courses of rituximab were evaluated during the observation period, with 168 and 105 courses administered before 6 and after 6 years of age, respectively. The median observation period after the first rituximab administration was 4.6 years (IQR, 3.2–6.6). Primary Outcome: Relapse-Free Survival Eight-six children (85%) relapsed after their first rituximab administration. Kaplan-Meier survival analysis showed that the median relapse-free survival of the cohort was 8.8 months (95% CI: 7.5–11.0) ( ). Relapse-free survival did not differ between children aged < 4 years and those aged from 4 to 6 years ( ). A history of steroid resistance was not associated with relapse ( A and B). Nine children (9%) relapsed within 3 months post-rituximab and were considered resistant to rituximab. Long-term remission > 2 years was achieved in 11 patients (11%), and total B cells repopulated in all of them. Five of these patients eventually relapsed. The number of relapses significantly reduced from 3 (IQR: 2–4) to 1 (IQR: 0–1) within 1-year before and after rituximab therapy ( P < 0.0001). Multivariable analysis demonstrated that each additional month of concurrent immunosuppression use (adjusted hazard ratio: 0.92; 95% CI: 0.89–0.96; P < 0.001) reduced relapse risk by 8%. Older age at first rituximab administration showed a trend toward a lower relapse risk (adjusted hazard ratio: 0.76; 95% CI: 0.57–1.03; P = 0.07). Although statistically insignificant, children receiving high-dose rituximab regimen (1125–1500 mg/m 2 ) appeared to experience a lower relapse risk than those who received low- and medium-dose regimens ( ). Sex, ethnicity, age at NS diagnosis, disease severity, history of steroid resistance, and number of previous immunosuppressive drugs did not affect relapse risk. summarizes the multivariable analysis of predictive factors for response. Total B-cell Depletion and Repopulation B cells were monitored within 1 month after the first rituximab administration in 70 patients, and B-cell depletion was observed in 99% of subjects ( n = 69/70). Total B cells were subsequently monitored in 58 children and repopulated at a median of 5.3 months (IQR: 4.3–6.8). Among these patients, 93% relapsed after B-cell repopulation, which had been documented a median of 2.2 months (IQR: 0.85–4.6) earlier; however, 22% of children did not relapse after B-cell repopulation. Subsequent Courses of Rituximab A second course of rituximab was administered to85 subjects (84%). The most frequent indication for redosing was NS relapse ( n = 77), followed by total B-cell repopulation ( n = 8). The rates of relapse, time to relapse, long-term remission, rituximab resistance, and duration of B-cell depletion after each rituximab course are summarized in . Importantly, 34% and 12% children attained long-term remission (≥ 2 years) following the second and third rituximab course, respectively. Between 5% and 13% of patients had rituximab resistance (relapse-free period < 3 months) during each cycle of treatment. Among the 53 patients whose IgG levels were monitored, 30 children (57%) had hypogammaglobulinemia documented, with a median lowest IgG value of 289 (100–380) mg/dl. Of these patients, 21 had preexisting hypogammaglobulinemia before their first rituximab exposure. Low IgG levels at baseline, compared with normal IgG levels, were associated with hypogammaglobulinemia post-rituximab (68% vs. 27%, P = 0.005). Most of them had concurrent hypogammaglobulinemia ( n = 1) and/or neutropenia ( n = 5). We did not find any associated factor among these young patients with or without neutropenia, agranulocytosis, and infection. Of note, 2 patients were receiving mycophenolate mofetil as maintenance immunosuppression, whereas another patient with agranulocytosis was receiving cotrimoxazole as prophylaxis against pneumocystis. Details of side effects reported during the first and subsequent courses of rituximab are presented in . Hypogammaglobulinemia ( n = 85/173, 49%) remained the most common adverse event across all courses of rituximab evaluated in our cohort, followed by infections ( n = 19/273, 7%) and neutropenia ( n = 18/267, 7%) ( ). The rates of hypogammaglobulinemia were higher among courses of rituximab administered before the age of 6 years (54% vs. 43%, P = 0.02). A total of 42 children developed hypogammaglobulinemia before the age of 6 years. The first occurrence was observed after the first, second, and third courses of rituximab in 30, 10, and 2 patients, respectively. Twenty-nine children received further courses of rituximab therapy, and hypogammaglobulinemia recurred in 20 children (68%). Among the 18 children who received additional administrations after the age of 6 years, 13 developed hypogammaglobulinemia (72%). The rates of neutropenia (9% vs. 4%) and infection (8% vs. 5%) were also higher, although these differences did not reach statistical significance. Chronic Kidney Disease and Kidney Failure All 101 patients remained steroid sensitive during the observation period. Normal kidney function was reported in all children at the last follow-up, except 1 who had chronic kidney disease stage 2. The patient had multidrug-dependent NS since the age of 19 months and was treated with a calcineurin inhibitor for disease control. Rituximab was administered at 5.6 years of age, and the calcineurin inhibitor was continued as maintenance for more than 4 years at the last follow-up. Although a kidney biopsy was not performed, the impaired kidney function could be attributable to long-term calcineurin inhibitor–associated nephrotoxicity. No patients required kidney replacement therapy. Secondary Matched Analysis With Children Receiving First Rituximab at an Older Age We matched 70 young children with 70 older children who received their first rituximab ≥ 6 years of age). Rituximab was first administered at a median age of 4.7 (IQR: 3.9–5.4) years and 9.8 (IQR: 7.3–14.6) years in the younger and older groups, respectively. The difference in interval between NS diagnosis and first rituximab was significant yet modest in magnitude between the 2 groups (young: 2.1 ± 1.2 years vs. older: 2.7 ± 1.3 years). Baseline characteristics, including sex, ethnicity, disease severity, history of steroid resistance, number of immunosuppressive drugs immediately before rituximab, rituximab regimens, and maintenance immunosuppression, were comparable between groups ( ). Median relapse-free survival did not differ statistically, although young children demonstrated a trend toward earlier relapse ( ; 8.3 months, 95% CI: 6.7–10.6 vs. 11.3 months, 95% CI: 8.3–14.4; log-rank test P = 0.14). Time to B-cell repletion was similar between groups (young: 5.5, IQR: 3.7–6.4 months; vs. older: 5.6, IQR: 3.7–7.1 months). The side effects observed during the first course of rituximab were compared between the matched young and older patients. Discussion Our multiethnic cohort provides long-term efficacy and safety data on rituximab in young children aged < 6 years. Our data demonstrate that rituximab sustains remission even in young children with a complicated disease course. Hypogammaglobulinemia is prevalent in ≤57% of patients. Concomitant infection is uncommon but could be underreported. Although our findings suggest that rituximab can be used as a third-line or even second-line agent for complicated FRSDNS in young children, the therapy appears to be less effective and associated with more complications compared with those receiving the drug at an older age. Our cohort represented the most severe and complicated group of young children with FRSDNS. As expected, most of the patients were multidrug dependent, and the rest were steroid-dependent, with frequent relapses prior to rituximab administration. One-third of the children had a previous history of steroid resistance but regained steroid responsiveness following the use of calcineurin inhibitors, which has been associated with poorer treatment response to rituximab. , Up to 86% subjects with FRSDNS continued to relapse despite calcineurin inhibitor therapy, a potent steroid-sparing agent. This suggests that most pediatric nephrologists reserve rituximab as a last resort for FRSDNS in young children. Our data showed that the median relapse-free period in these young children was a median of 8.8 months after rituximab treatment. Although this efficacy is not as pronounced as that observed in older children, it is remarkable given that our cohort had a challenging disease course and had failed multiple steroid-sparing agents. To our best knowledge, there are no available data for comparison, because previous studies have enrolled mostly older children and did not perform specific subgroup analyses for young children. Furthermore, reported treatment outcomes of rituximab have been highly variable because of heterogeneity in patient populations and the prescription of rituximab and immunosuppression. We therefore matched our young patient cohort with older children of similar clinical and treatment characteristics to enable fair comparison and minimize potential confounders. Although the intervals from NS onset to first rituximab between groups were statistically different, a 6-month difference in rituximab initiation would be unlikely to affect overall clinical response or side effect profiles. Although statistically insignificant, older children demonstrated a trend toward a longer relapse-free period than younger children. This may be partly explained by the fact that memory B-cell levels, a more established biomarker for response than other B-cell subsets, were higher at baseline and reconstitute earlier in children aged < 10 years compared with those aged > 10 years receiving rituximab. Another potential explanation is that the natural course of FRSDNS tends to improve with age, especially around the time of puberty. In contrast, the duration of total B-cell depletion was not different between the 2 groups. Furthermore, among the young patients, each additional year of age at first rituximab administration showed a trend toward lower relapse risk. In concordance with our previous findings, , our data showed that maintenance immunosuppression was an effective measure to extend NS remission in young children. Each additional month of concurrent immunosuppression use reduced relapse risk by 8%. Although our study was not designed to evaluate the choice of maintenance therapy, mycophenolate mofetil appeared to be the preferred option, being the only immunosuppressive agent used over 6 months. In this context, a recent randomized trial showed that maintenance mycophenolate mofetil could reduce relapse risk by 80%; however, the effect disappeared after drug discontinuation. Our study did not evaluate the rituximab drug levels and anti-rituximab antibodies because these tests are unavailable in most clinical settings. Current evidence, however, suggests that these parameters correlate poorly with relapse and does not support regular monitoring. Our previous work described a progressive improvement in relapse-free period after repeated courses of rituximab, suggesting a potential disease-modifying effect. Similar findings were observed in the current cohort. After each cycle of rituximab therapy, 10% to 30% of children achieved sustained and prolonged remission over 2 years. Although this may, in part, be related to outgrowing the disease, many children in our cohort were prepubertal at the time of rituximab retreatment, a stage at which the disease typically remains active until puberty is reached. This result can be impactful if repeated rituximab treatments can ameliorate the overall clinical course. One possible postulation is that early rituximab use prevents the formation of long-lived plasma cell.

Although this may, in part, be related to outgrowing the disease, many children in our cohort were prepubertal at the time of rituximab retreatment, a stage at which the disease typically remains active until puberty is reached. This result can be impactful if repeated rituximab treatments can ameliorate the overall clinical course. One possible postulation is that early rituximab use prevents the formation of long-lived plasma cell. Further clinical and translational data are warranted to confirm this hypothesis. Rituximab appears to be generally safe, but its use is not without risk. , , , , Rare yet fatal adverse events such as viral hepatitis reactivation, lung injury, and multifocal leukoencephalopathy have been reported. , , Hypogammaglobulinemia, neutropenia, and agranulocytosis are the most prevalent adverse events and the incidences were reported to be 14% to 58%, 4% to 8% and 2% to 5%, respectively. , Our data reported more adverse events among young children than the general pediatric population. There were significantly higher rates of hypogammaglobulinemia in younger children, than in the matched older patient cohort. Although the difference in other adverse events was not significant between groups because of relatively small sample size and event numbers, this signal should be taken seriously into any treatment consideration. Interestingly, the observed adverse events were lower when rituximab was given to the same group of children after they turned 6 years or older. This concurs with previous findings that younger age at rituximab increased the risk of developing hypogammaglobulinemia and neutropenia. , IgG, IgA, and IgM levels and absolute neutrophil count should be regularly monitored, because all except one of our infective complications occurred in the presence of hypogammaglobulinemia and agranulocytosis. Furthermore, our data found that low IgG levels before rituximab was associated with hypogammaglobulinemia after rituximab therapy. The role of i.v. Ig substitution for asymptomatic numerical hypogammaglobulinemia, however, remains controversial. , The risk of developing complications remains a major and valid concern when prescribing rituximab to these young children. Another important consideration, as illustrated from our data, is that most children eventually relapse and require repeated courses of rituximab for disease control. In the short- to medium-term, there are concerns pertaining to vaccine competency and long-term immunological impairment. , , Future research is required to better understand the long-term impact, such as hematologic malignancy, of repeated rituximab treatments during an active stage of immunity development and maturation. , For these reasons, we recommend to use rituximab in young children with FRSDNS only after other second-line treatment options have been exhausted or resulted in side effects. Second generation anti-CD20, obinutuzumab, is effective in rituximab-resistant FRSDNS, even among children who relapse during complete depletion of circulating B cell. , Until further data become available, its use in young children should be exercised with great caution, only after balancing the risk and benefits. Obinutuzumab has, due to its mode of action, clear potentials of being more effective but also having more profound side effects than the first generation of anti-CD20 monoclonal antibodies. Despite a unique multiethnic patient cohort, our study had the limitations of a retrospective study, including selection and reporting bias. We tried to minimize them by stringent inclusion criteria and adequate observation. Second, there were variable practices between centers, including rituximab regimen, immunosuppression use, and redose indications. These might confound treatment responses and influence the reported rates of adverse events. In particular, hypogammaglobulinemia might have been underreported because of variable practices on IgG-level monitoring. Infection is an important complication after intensive immunosuppression and may be underreported. Finally, histology was not included as an adjusted factor in the regression model because kidney biopsy is not routinely indicated in FRSDNS ; available evidence however fails to substantiate its role as predictor. , , In conclusion, rituximab appears to have reasonable efficacy in young children with complicated FRSDNS. Maintenance immunosuppression may serve as a plausible option to prevent relapse and extend remission. Compared with older children, young children may experience a shorter relapse-free period and high rates of adverse events. Rituximab should therefore be considered only after exhausting other treatment options, until prospective trials provide more robust evidence to support its earlier use. Future trials should identify the prognostic values of specific B-cell subsets, examine the role of scheduled redosing, and compare the efficacy and safety of rituximab against novel therapeutics such as obinutuzumab and chimeric antigen receptor–based therapy. documents.title: KDIGO Cardiovascular Disease in CKD Controversies Conference

chunks.content: Chronic kidney disease (CKD), defined by persistent reduction in glomerular filtration rate (GFR) and/or the presence of other signs of kidney damage, is classified based on GFR and albuminuria categories. The risk for adverse outcomes, including mortality and kidney failure, increases with decreasing GFR and increasing albuminuria. Individuals with a GFR below 30 ml/min per 1.73 m 2 (i.e., CKD G4 or G5) are at particularly high risk across all albuminuria categories ( ). In addition, CKD-specific complications increase markedly at low levels of GFR, with cardiovascular disease (CVD) being a leading cause of morbidity and mortality. Of particular relevance is heart failure (HF), one of the most common CVD conditions for patients with CKD G4 or higher. Kidney replacement therapy (KRT; i.e., dialysis or transplantation) can mitigate the consequences of kidney failure and improve prognosis. However, there are large variations in incidence rates of KRT , and globally only approximately half of those with kidney failure receive KRT. Inequalities in access to KRT play an important role, but differences in practice patterns also exist. There is agreement that level of GFR alone should not be used as a trigger for KRT initiation, and that signs and symptoms associated with kidney failure should be considered. Nevertheless, defining the optimal time for KRT initiation remains a challenge. Importantly the first few months on dialysis have been identified as a very high-risk period, though it remains unknown to what extent adverse events are triggered by dialysis initiation. , Referral to nephrology services shortly before dialysis initiation has been associated with an increased risk of adverse outcomes as compared with earlier referral. , Thus, low GFR (<30 ml/min per 1.73 m 2 ) corresponding to CKD G4 or G5 (excluding patients on KRT and referred to subsequently as “CKD G4+”) reflects a critical state for patients. A better understanding of prognosis of patients with CKD G4+ may inform treatment strategies, including decision-making for initiation of KRT. Therefore, Kidney Disease: Improving Global Outcomes (KDIGO) collaborated with the CKD Prognosis Consortium (CKD-PC) to initiate a global meta-analysis of cohort studies (population-based cohorts, referred CKD cohorts, and research cohorts). The primary aim was to determine the prognosis of patients with advanced CKD with respect to initiation of KRT, CVD events, mortality, and relative timing of these events, with a second aim to determine variability of patient prognosis according to cohort, demographic, or health characteristics. The results from the global meta-analysis were presented to an international expert group at a KDIGO Controversies Conference in December 2016, and implications for patient management were discussed. Breakout groups focused on: (i) management of CKD G4+, (ii) diagnostic and therapeutic challenges of HF in CKD G4+, (iii) shared decision-making for KRT initiation, and (iv) optimization of clinical trials in CKD G4+ patients. To curtail the scope of the conference, specific aspects of children and patients with a failing transplant were not addressed. We present here a summary of the discussion and main conference conclusions with respect to management and future research in patients with CKD G4+. Detailed presentations of the meta-analysis are published in the companion papers. , Prognosis of patients with CKD G4+: novel insights from a global meta-analysis of cohort studies In preparation for the conference, we conducted a global meta-analysis with the goal of examining absolute and relative risks of outcomes in a large, diverse population of patients with CKD stage G4+. The meta-analysis of risk factors for KRT, CVD events, and death included 28 cohorts ( n = 185,024) using standard survival analysis and Cox regression. The risk prediction meta-analysis included 29 cohorts ( n = 264,296). The main findings included that established risk factors for CVD were highly relevant in CKD G4+ patients, but their relative importance differed by outcome ( ). Age and history of CVD were negatively related to risk of KRT but positively related to CVD and death risk. Current smoking was most strongly associated with death. Blood pressure was positively associated with KRT risk but showed a U-shaped association with CVD and mortality. Diabetes and male sex were risk factors for all outcomes but strongest for CVD and KRT, respectively. Black race was only positively related to KRT. Lower estimated GFR (eGFR) and higher albumin-to-creatinine ratio (ACR) were more strongly associated with KRT than other outcomes. Finally, time-varying CVD events and initiation of KRT were strongly associated with subsequent occurrence of death. The second meta-analysis focused on the development of a new risk calculator for CVD events, KRT and death, as diagramed in . The CKD G4+ risk calculator uses a pie chart format to show the probability of all outcomes in a given follow-up period (2 or 4 years) (online calculator: http://www.kdigo.org/equation/ ). Finally, time-varying CVD events and initiation of KRT were strongly associated with subsequent occurrence of death. The second meta-analysis focused on the development of a new risk calculator for CVD events, KRT and death, as diagramed in . The CKD G4+ risk calculator uses a pie chart format to show the probability of all outcomes in a given follow-up period (2 or 4 years) (online calculator: http://www.kdigo.org/equation/ ). For example, as illustrated in , at an eGFR of 25 ml/min per 1.73 m 2 and the covariates noted in the figure legend, the proportion of participants predicted to receive KRT within 4 years increases from 13% to 32% with increasing albuminuria, while the risk of death increases from 22% to 30%. In the overall population examined who had a median eGFR of 24 ml/min per 1.73 m 2 and ACR of 168 mg/g, over 50% of participants were predicted to be event free at 4 years. The predicted risk of remaining event free for 2 years varies from less than 20% to greater than 80%, illustrating the predictive power of measured patient characteristics. This CKD-PC global meta-analysis extends the established kidney failure risk equation (KFRE) for prediction of KRT , as well as confirms its value in CKD G4+. Together with the KFRE, the new CKD G4+ risk calculator provides easily accessible tools to physicians, patients, and policy makers that translate patient characteristics into powerful risk discrimination. It is still important to keep in mind that additional characteristics, often unmeasured, influence risk further, and hence part of individualization should include recognition of the limitations of quantitative risk estimates. Management of patients with CKD G4+ Risk-based assessment and management People with CKD G4+ are at risk for kidney failure, hospitalizations, CVD events, death, and often under-recognized outcomes such as disability, cognitive impairment, falls, and infection. The KFRE equation and the new CKD G4+ risk calculator provide useful tools in risk prediction, and their consistency is reassuring. Other similar models have also been published. , Further refinement including prediction of additional patient-relevant outcomes remains an important task for future research. Nevertheless, the available models appear sufficient to advocate for their implementation. Incorporating patient preferences and values There is growing recognition that patients want to be involved as equal partners in their care. Shared decision-making can lead to productive interactions between patients, family, carers, and health care providers, thus actively involving all partners in treatment decisions, providing sufficient education about treatment options and their attributes, utilizing strategies to elicit patients’ values, identifying patient preferences, and achieving agreement about the course of treatment. , Further work to develop and evaluate strategies and resources for shared decision-making within CKD care is required to achieve these goals. Models of care So far, data on the systematic implementation of models of care for people with CKD G4+ are relatively sparse, and the relationships between specific elements of CKD care and patient outcomes remain to be determined. Nevertheless a number of overarching considerations appear valid ( ), and specific stakeholder issues should be considered ( ). Moreover, key competencies can be outlined that appear critical for successful implementation of models of care ( ). The potential benefits of a multidisciplinary team approach have been described over 20 years ago. A recent systematic review (18 studies; 8853 patients) found that multidisciplinary care of patients with CKD was associated with lower risks of all-cause mortality, dialysis, and central venous catheter use for dialysis access. Although initially associations with improved outcomes have been limited to observational studies and had not been borne out in randomized trials, 2 recent trials have reported encouraging results. The ESCORT (Effectiveness of Integrated Care on Delaying Progression of Stage 3-4 Chronic Kidney Disease in Rural Communities of Thailand) study, a community-based, cluster randomized controlled trial, reported significant delay in progression of CKD associated with improvements in blood pressure and diabetes control and serum bicarbonate with the introduction of an integrated CKD care program. In addition to routine care, comprehensive medical care and education including advice on diet, exercise, and medication was provided as part of the intervention. In another cluster randomized controlled trial, Lalonde and colleagues introduced a training and communication network program for pharmacists as part of the multidisciplinary care of people with CKD in Quebec, Canada. In a cohort of patients already benefiting from multidisciplinary care, the introduction of the program improved the quality of medication use and reduced the number of drug-related problems by 15%. It seems intuitive that access to multidisciplinary care providers may be attractive to many patients; however, the impact on patient experience and the optimal design and involvement of team members still remains unclear. In a cohort of patients already benefiting from multidisciplinary care, the introduction of the program improved the quality of medication use and reduced the number of drug-related problems by 15%. It seems intuitive that access to multidisciplinary care providers may be attractive to many patients; however, the impact on patient experience and the optimal design and involvement of team members still remains unclear. We suggest that models of care should place patients at the center of a transparent and open structure that ensures optimal communication and use of available resources ( ). Additional research is needed to explore models that address context-specific care in low- and middle-income countries, multi-morbidity and integration of multidisciplinary care providers and other specialists around the patient; new technologies that can enhance communication between stakeholders; and strategies to bridge transitions of care between hospital and community, as well as between phases of CKD, dialysis, and transplant care. Uncertainties about targets and therapies There are important uncertainties in CKD G4+ management ( ). In general these include interventions that are either targeting the underlying kidney disease or aim at primary and secondary prevention of CVD complications. Frequently, evidence has been extrapolated from studies in other stages of CKD or younger age groups, or is based on observational studies. For example, although some trials of reninangiotensin-aldosterone system (RAAS) blockage have included patients with CKD G4+, uncertainty remains about generalizing its efficacy to CKD G4+ patients. Results of a trial designed to test the role of stopping treatment with RAAS blockade to stabilize kidney function in patients with progressive or late CKD G4+ are awaited. Current evidence and guideline recommendations for several important therapeutic areas are shown in . Given the high burden and altered metabolism of drugs in CKD G4+, exploration of drug interactions and adverse medication safety events should also be a priority. Research recommendations for management of patients with CKD G4+ are summarized in . Cardiovascular complications during CKD G4+: heart failure A focus of management during CKD G4+ is on preventing CVD, which remains one of the leading causes of morbidity and mortality. HF is of special relevance for CKD G4+ patients as it is one of the most common cardiovascular conditions, and yet there remain many diagnostic and therapeutic uncertainties in the management of HF during CKD G4+, particularly in patients approaching the transition to KRT. Definition, risk factors, and diagnosis of heart failure in CKD G4+ Patients with CKD have an elevated risk of HF , that increases with severity of CKD. Among patients receiving KRT, 40% have HF, with higher prevalence rates among patients on hemodialysis compared with peritoneal dialysis and kidney transplant recipients. The cumulative incidence of HF is also high among patients with CKD and those receiving KRT ( ). HF is defined as a syndrome of inadequate filling and/or pumping to meet systemic demands. There are 2 types of HF, with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF) and reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF), and defining HF subtypes has been an area of ongoing work by the ACCF/AHA and ESC ( ). HFpEF is more common in patients with CKD. Diagnosis of HF remains challenging in patients with CKD, particularly in CKD G4+, given the difficulty in distinguishing causes of volume overload. HF should be defined as the presence of HF symptoms and structural and/or functional abnormalities on cardiac imaging ( ). In observational studies, imaging data are frequently not available. In fact, in the CKD-PC analysis, HF definitions were not sufficiently harmonized across cohorts to allow a valid analysis of incidence rates and risk prediction. Moreover, despite the recognized importance of HF, it remains unknown whether screening for HF, either with imaging or cardiac biomarkers, leads to improved outcomes in patients with CKD G4+. Traditional as well as novel risk factors, including metabolic abnormalities, uremic toxins, and sympathetic over-activity, accelerate the development of HF in patients with CKD G4+ ( ). , Outcomes associated with heart failure in CKD G4+ HF is associated with poor outcomes in patients with CKD, including greater risk of death, particularly in patients who are older, have HFrEF ( ), , or have severely decreased GFR ( ). HF contributes significantly to morbidity among CKD patients, leading to frequent hospitalizations and re-hospitalizations. – HF is also associated with episodes of acute kidney injury and progression of CKD. , Among incident dialysis patients, volume overload compared with other dialysis indications is associated with the greatest risk of post-KRT mortality. Progression of clinical and subclinical heart failure after initiation of dialysis Only a few studies have evaluated longitudinal changes in subclinical HF, as assessed by echocardiograms, in patients with CKD G4+, and the results are not consistent. In the CRIC study, mean left ventricular mass index did not change after the initiation of KRT. However, there was a modest but statistically significant decline in left ventricular ejection fraction. The CASCADE study examined echocardiograms in patients with CKD G3+ and reported that left ventricular mass index and left atrial volume both increased within a year; however, the change in left ventricular ejection fraction was not statistically significant. In the IDEAL trial, serial echocardiograms performed 12 months apart showed no change in left ventricular mass index, left atrial diameter, diastolic dysfunction, or left ventricular ejection fraction after dialysis initiation. It should be noted, however, that in this study, over 40% initiated peritoneal dialysis (PD) versus hemodialysis (HD). In another study of 41 HF patients, left ventricular mass index decreased after initiation of HD. Vascular access and heart failure Vascular access preparation is a key component of management in CKD G4+ patients. There are numerous postulated changes in the cardiovascular system after creation of an arteriovenous fistula ( ). Small studies or case reports have suggested that arteriovenous fistula may lead to development of high-output HF. – Arteriovenous fistula creation has also been reported in small studies to worsen right ventricular hypertrophy and pulmonary hypertension , and found to be associated with significant right ventricular dilatation and remodeling and an increased risk for development of incident heart failure. On the other hand, other studies found a stabilization of kidney function after access creation. Larger prospective studies are needed to understand optimal access management in patients with CKD G4+ and HF. Management of heart failure in CKD G4+ Management of HF in patients with CKD, particularly CKD G4+, is complicated ( ). Almost all HF trials have excluded patients with advanced CKD, and few have been successful in improving outcomes in patients with HFpEF. Post hoc analyses have included some patients with moderate CKD, but suggest an attenuated effect of therapies such as β-blockers and implantable cardioverter defibrillators. – In addition, the presumed risk of hyperkalemia limits the use of RAAS inhibitors and mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists in CKD G4+. , Among patients receiving KRT with known HF, the proportion of patients with prescribed therapies such as RAAS inhibitors and β-blockers remains low. Further studies of HF therapies and cardiac devices specifically in CKD G4+ are needed, particularly for HFpEF, which remains the leading type of HF in patients with CKD G4+ ( and ). Although the rates of incident (i.e., de novo ) and recurrent heart failure are reported to be lower in PD versus HD patients, – in patients with established HF the mortality rate may be higher in PD versus HD patients. This likely reflects confounding by indication because frail HF patients are preferentially offered PD as it causes less acute hemodynamic stress. Prospective clinical trials comparing PD with HD are warranted. Shared decision-making for kidney failure therapy Predicting adverse outcomes after initiation of kidney replacement therapy Several registries , and cohort studies, provide population-based risks of mortality in patients initiating KRT. An important observation is that mortality rates are highest within the first 4 months of starting dialysis and decline in subsequent months. In the DOPPS cohort, such high early mortality was observed across countries, and differences between early and later mortality were more pronounced among patients aged ≥65 years compared with younger patients. Although dialysis withdrawal accounts for some of the early mortality, it does not provide the only explanation. CVD events are also much higher in the first weeks after KRT initiation. Studies have also demonstrated a high residual burden of symptoms and geriatric syndromes, such as dementia and disability, and utilization of health care among patients commencing dialysis, especially in those who are frail, have multiple chronic conditions, and start dialysis in the context of a prolonged hospitalization. – These outcomes are important to patients and sometimes more so than mortality. High early morbidity and mortality raises questions about the potential causes and risk mitigation strategies; in particular it raises concerns that for some patients, initiation of KRT may not be the optimal choice of therapy. and geriatric syndromes, such as dementia and disability, and utilization of health care among patients commencing dialysis, especially in those who are frail, have multiple chronic conditions, and start dialysis in the context of a prolonged hospitalization. – These outcomes are important to patients and sometimes more so than mortality. High early morbidity and mortality raises questions about the potential causes and risk mitigation strategies; in particular it raises concerns that for some patients, initiation of KRT may not be the optimal choice of therapy. Several prognostic tools have been developed to predict short-term mortality among patients who have initiated dialysis. – Nevertheless, it is difficult to predict with sufficient certainty which patients will do poorly on dialysis. By providing quantitative estimates of the risk of KRT initiation, CVD events, and mortality based on individual patient characteristics, the novel CKD-G4+ risk calculator may facilitate decision-making ( ). For patients not yet in kidney failure, it is also noteworthy to recognize that a substantial proportion of CKD G4+ patients survive without CVD events and KRT over 2- and 4-year observation periods. Optimal counseling for treatment modality decisions Counseling for KRT should be risk-based, iterative, and patient-centered. In addition, it should be tailored to the cultural setting, health literacy, and psychosocial and emotional needs while being mindful of the presence of cognitive impairment. Options available once kidney failure is expected include comprehensive conservative care without dialysis, in-center or home HD, PD, and transplantation. Circumstances may exist in which a specific modality of KRT may be contraindicated, but when options exist, a shared decision-making approach to the choice of KRT optimizes patient engagement and may potentially improve outcomes. Discussions should be revisited at regular intervals to ensure that important health or social circumstances have not changed. Two scenarios require special considerations: counseling for transplantation in older adults and counseling to forgo dialysis. It is accepted that, among patients placed on the waiting list, kidney transplantation improves life expectancy and quality of life compared with those remaining on dialysis across all age ranges. In and of itself, older age is not a contraindication to transplantation. Although only a proportion of patients will qualify for transplantation, transplantation should be considered in all patients who do not have obvious contraindications for KRT. Referral and evaluation for transplantation should be based on patient characteristics, preferences, and regional circumstances. Unwarranted regional variability in access to transplantation is well-documented, and transplant programs should establish transparent policies for accepting patients on the waiting list. General counseling about KRT should also include information about the option to forgo dialysis and receive conservative care. The Renal Physicians Association has published guidelines regarding circumstances in which forgoing dialysis may be appropriate ( ). Although the benefit of initiating KRT declines with increasing age, older age per se should not be considered as a contraindication for KRT; in fact, conference participants questioned the Renal Physicians Association recommendation to generally forgo dialysis in patients ≥75 years with poor prognosis and favored a more individualized approach, taking into account patient preferences and values along with prognosis. Uncertainties about initiation of kidney replacement therapies and research priorities A recent meta-analysis of cohort studies and trials has demonstrated that those who commence dialysis with a higher eGFR have a higher mortality. It is likely that this is due to reverse causality, with frailty and accumulated comorbidities, in particular HF, pushing the patient and clinician to initiate dialysis. Global differences exist in how planned KRT is initiated. These include a “PD first” approach, commencement with a functioning arteriovenous fistula and differences in site of fistula placement and “incremental” start to dialysis with either reduced blood flow rates, reduced hours, or limited PD exchanges. To which extent these factors influence outcomes is largely unclear. The indication for initiation of dialysis should be recorded routinely in registry data in addition to reporting elective versus unplanned start to dialysis. In the IDEAL study the majority of patients allocated to late start who started early had the indication for start identified as “uremia.” Hence, it would be useful to understand the spectrum of symptoms that prompted initiation of dialysis to provide greater clarity regarding the optimum commencement. Needs, opportunities, and challenges for clinical trials in patients with CKD G4+ Barriers for clinical trials in patients with CKD G4+ and strategies to overcome them There is an urgent need to increase the number and quality of completed clinical trials in patients with CKD, including people with CKD G4+ ( ). , A summary of selected barriers and proposed solutions is shown in and . For industry, the potential economic benefits of a successful clinical trial must be offset against the potential financial and nonfinancial risks. Slow recruitment, higher-than-average adverse event rates, a relatively small total patient population (i.e., prospective users), and several recent null clinical trials in CKD populations may all increase perceived risk. However, trials in populations with CKD G4+ also have key advantages, including the large potential economic benefits of preventing kidney failure and CVD events, a relatively captive and highly motivated patient population, and high event rates (reducing the required sample size or duration of follow-up). Investigator-initiated trials have different challenges: the nephrology community understands the clinical need and opportunities in the CKD G4+ population but often struggles to complete adequately powered studies. Environmental scans of ongoing trials suggest that certain topics (e.g., sodium bicarbonate treatment in CKD G4+) are being independently studied by multiple groups in different countries. One potential solution could be to link multiple existing national trial networks to increase statistical power, either by use of common protocols or by pooling results from similar but not identical protocols using meta-analysis. Choosing patient-relevant interventions and outcomes As for most medical disciplines, available trial evidence in CKD G4+ populations reflects the interests and priorities of clinicians and researchers rather than patients and families. Correcting this misalignment is critical for improving the utility of trial findings and potentially for facilitating trial conduct by increasing participant recruitment and retention. Existing processes for identifying patient-centered research priorities and patient-relevant outcomes (e.g., those identified using the James Lind Alliance methodology) will be helpful for achieving this aim. A list of such priorities for CKD G3a to G5 patients is already available , and could be used as the basis for people with CKD G4+ specifically. Initiation of KRT is clinically meaningful and, therefore, the obvious choice as an outcome in trials of therapies aimed at slowing the loss of kidney function. However, KRT initiation is determined by many factors such as local habits and guidelines, physicians’ and patients’ preferences, and patients’ well-being and comorbidities. Functional and symptomatic outcomes that are patient-oriented, both before and after the initiation of KRT, are important to address for safety as well as efficacy, and are relevant for the patient. A toolbox that includes validated symptomatic assessment will support trials with functional outcomes. Increasing and sustaining patient engagement in trials and other clinical research is critical, but no consensus was reached on how this goal should be achieved or approached. A key starting point could be to describe lessons learned from leading patient-centered initiatives (e.g., SONG-HD and NICE) and establish an organization responsible for patient engagement in CKD G4+ research specifically. Increasing the success of clinical trials in CKD G4+ by optimizing other aspects of trial design Besides outcomes, other aspects of clinical trial design could be optimized. Thus, the KFRE and the newly developed predictive instrument specific for CKD G4+ could be used in potential trial participants to inform power calculations or enrich recruitment of participants at higher-than-average risk. Alternative methods (e.g., pragmatic trials, stepped-wedge designs, or registry-based studies) could also be used to facilitate trial conduct. Pragmatic trials are well suited for patients with CKD G4+ because such trials can enroll socially disadvantaged populations (usually excluded from traditional randomized controlled trials), are directly applicable to patient care, allow assessment of a range of interventions, include patient-centered outcomes, and are cheaper than traditional randomized controlled trials. There are also some challenges, such as lack of experience, collection and ascertainment of outcomes, and informed consent procedure, which may pose challenges given the increasing use of electronic health records. Conclusions and perspectives Patients with CKD G4+ represent a high-risk population that requires specialized care and expertise that should ideally be coordinated by nephrologists. Despite their severely reduced level of GFR, the prognosis of patients with CKD G4+ is variable, with a substantial proportion of up to more than 50% surviving CVD event- and KRT-free for at least several years. The newly developed risk prediction tool specific for CKD G4+ may help to establish a comprehensive quantitative analysis of possible adverse outcomes, including CVD events, kidney failure and mortality, and thereby guide therapy. Such prognostic information can be factored into decisions for surveillance, CVD risk reduction, and eventual preparation for KRT. Another important finding of the meta-analysis is that traditional CVD risk factors appear to be relevant in CKD G4+, like in earlier stages of

with CKD G4+ is variable, with a substantial proportion of up to more than 50% surviving CVD event- and KRT-free for at least several years. The newly developed risk prediction tool specific for CKD G4+ may help to establish a comprehensive quantitative analysis of possible adverse outcomes, including CVD events, kidney failure and mortality, and thereby guide therapy. Such prognostic information can be factored into decisions for surveillance, CVD risk reduction, and eventual preparation for KRT. Another important finding of the meta-analysis is that traditional CVD risk factors appear to be relevant in CKD G4+, like in earlier stages of CKD and in the absence of CKD. Although such associations do not prove the efficacy of risk factor targeting, it appears rational to apply such strategies as long as no opposing evidence is available. Finally, there was general agreement that the complex comorbidities of people with CKD G4+, particularly those with functional impairment, older age, and limited life expectancy, mandate a patient-centric approach with joint decision-making both in routine practice as well as during the design of trials to optimize management and outcomes. chunks.content: KEY LEARNING POINTS What was known: Radical nephrectomy is associated with a substantial risk of postoperative chronic kidney disease (CKD), but systematic evaluation of the non-neoplastic renal parenchyma is not routinely performed. CKD and renal cell carcinoma share bidirectional links through shared risk factors, chronic inflammation, and treatment-related nephrotoxicity. Paraneoplastic nephropathies associated with renal tumors are considered rare and are likely underdiagnosed due to limited histological assessment. This study adds: Histological examination of non-neoplastic renal parenchyma at radical nephrectomy revealed a high prevalence of occult renal pathology, including chronic tubulointerstitial damage and previously undiagnosed glomerular diseases. Nearly one-quarter of patients had confirmed nephropathies, including paraneoplastic forms that resolved after tumor removal. Intraoperative renal histology directly informed nephrological risk stratification and postoperative management, avoiding additional kidney biopsies. Potential impact: Routine assessment of non-neoplastic renal tissue during radical nephrectomy may enable earlier identification of CKD risk and occult nephropathies. This approach can guide individualized nephrological follow-up, optimize oncological treatment decisions, and reduce unnecessary invasive procedures. Integration of nephrology into surgical oncology pathways could improve long-term renal outcomes in patients with kidney cancer. INTRODUCTION Chronic kidney disease (CKD) and renal cell carcinoma (RCC) are two critical clinical conditions that significantly impact global healthcare and the quality of life for millions of people [ ]. CKD is characterized by a progressive decline in kidney function due to the natural aging process of kidney. Accordantly, its prevalence is higher in older populations—and partly attributed to risk factors such as hypertension, diabetes, and primary nephropathies. RCC shares several risk factors with CKD, and in recent years, the bidirectional relationship between these two conditions has become increasingly evident [ ]. Chronic inflammation induced by uremia and oxidative stress (all hallmarks of CKD) are key contributors to RCC development [ , ]. On the other hand, the use of antineoplastic drugs, their associated toxicity, and the necessity for radical nephrectomies are factors that promote the progression of CKD in patients initially diagnosed with RCC [ ]. Patients with kidney cancer eligible for surgical treatment can undergo partial nephrectomy or radical nephrectomy, with an associated risk [independently of baseline estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR)] of developing chronic kidney disease of 20% and 33.7%, respectively. The risk increases to 36% in patients who had stage IV chronic kidney failure according to the Kidney Disease: Improving Global Outcomes (KDIGO) classification before surgery [ ]. Patients with renal neoplasms often do not receive a nephrological assessment before or immediately after undergoing radical nephrectomy. This increases the probability of a nephrological intervention only when the opportunity to prevent a decline in renal function has been lost. At that point, the nephrologist can only avoid progressive renal deterioration. This study identifies radical nephrectomy as a critical, yet often overlooked, opportunity to evaluate the condition of the non-neoplastic renal parenchyma through detailed histological evaluation. The study aims to achieve two main goals: first, to assess the quality of the non-neoplastic renal parenchyma in patients undergoing radical nephrectomy, to identify early signs of potential renal function decline, and to provide timely intervention for high-risk patients. Second, to determine the prevalence of undiagnosed nephropathies—whether paraneoplastic or unrelated—that could offer further insights into the bidirectional relationship between CKD and RCC. MATERIALS AND METHODS We conducted a prospective observational study including 30 consecutive adult patients diagnosed with renal or urothelial cancer who were scheduled for elective radical nephrectomy between March 2023 and December 2024. No patients were excluded based on preoperative evaluation. Samples of non-neoplastic renal parenchyma were collected during surgery. To ensure the tissue reflected baseline renal architecture and was free from tumor compression effects, samples were harvested at least 2 cm from the tumor margin. The histological analysis included optical microscopy and immunofluorescence. The renal function was assessed both before and after surgery through serum creatinine measurement and glomerular filtration rate (GFR) calculation using the CKD-EPI formula. Preoperative serum creatinine values were obtained from routine tests upon patient admission to the hospital, on the day of surgery. Subsequently, patients diagnosed with confirmed nephropathy, or those deemed at high risk for CKD progression based on histological findings and comorbidities, were enrolled in a structured nephrological follow-up program. The definition of paraneoplastic nephropathy was based on: (1) Occurrence of nephropathy in chronological coincidence (either before, as a paraneoplastic syndrome, or during the course or in rapid succession) with the oncological disease; (2) ‘Spontaneous’ remission after surgery; (3) In the absence of history or immunological or clinical signs suggestive of a primary form. Individual patient characteristics, key comorbidities, and corresponding histological findings of the non-neoplastic renal parenchyma are reported in Table . RESULTS Among the thirty adult patients who underwent nephrectomy, there are 19 men and 11 women, with a median age of 65.5 years (min 29–max 83). Individual patient characteristics, key comorbidities, and corresponding histological findings of the non-neoplastic renal parenchyma are reported in Table . Hypertension, diabetes, smoking, and a BMI > 25 are the most relevant comorbidities evaluated in this patient population, as they are well-established risk factors for a more rapid decline in renal function. They are distributed in our patient population as reported in Fig. . The different tumor types are reported in Table . An example of a non-neoplastic renal cortical tissue in a patient with right kidney neoplasm is shown in Fig. . Before radical nephrectomy, 33% of patients had an eGFR <60 ml/min. Conversely, in the postoperative period, 50% of patients who possessed a preserved preoperative eGFR (>60 ml/min) experienced a decline in renal function. The analysis of the non-neoplastic renal parenchyma revealed different histological findings (Table ): 7 out of 30 pts (24%) of were diagnosed with confirmed nephropathy (1 minimal change disease, 1 IgA nephropathy, 1 fibrillary glomerulonephritis, 2 membranous glomerulonephritis, 2 early diabetic glomerulosclerosis). Forty-one percent of patients were diagnosed with chronic tubulointerstitial damage and 38% of patients were diagnosed with mild arteriosclerotic vascular damage or advanced atherosclerotic damage. In light of the histological examination findings, the patient cohort was stratified into distinct treatment categories as follows: seven out of 30 diagnosed with confirmed nephropathy were initiated on targeted pharmacological therapy and enrolled in a structured nephrological follow-up program. Eight out of 30 were scheduled for nephrological follow-up at 6-month or annual intervals, due to their reduced postoperative eGFR associated with risk factors predisposing them to further renal function decline. The remaining 15 patients, who either maintained preserved renal function or exhibited a decline not linked to specific comorbidities or risk factors, were referred to their primary care physician for routine clinical monitoring. The seven patients with confirmed nephropathy were managed as follows: Minimal change disease and IgA nephropathy : these conditions spontaneously regressed following radical nephrectomy, with only supportive care required. Based on the clinical course, specifically the spontaneous remission following nephrectomy, these findings strongly suggest a paraneoplastic origin for the observed Minimal Change Disease and IgA nephropathy. Diabetic glomerulosclerosis : management included lifestyle modifications (cessation of smoking and dietary interventions, since both patients were smokers and had a BMI > 25), along with the administration of Sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 (SGLT2) inhibitors. Both patients were referred for continuous nephrology follow-up. Fibrillary glomerulonephritis : the patient was treated with Rituximab therapy. The patient was referred for nephrological follow-up due to significant renal function impairment caused by the nephropathy. Membranous glomerulonephritis with positive anti-PLA2R antibodies : this nephropathy was diagnosed in a patient with advanced metastatic neoplastic disease and multiple comorbidities. In collaboration with oncology specialists, it was decided to start supportive nephrological therapy while awaiting the patient’s transition to palliative care. Membranous glomerulonephritis with negative anti-PLA2R antibodies : this nephropathy was likely exacerbated by the administration of immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICI). Early interruption of ICI therapy was required due to the development of proteinuria and renal function deterioration. Glomerulonephritis was managed with observation and corticosteroid therapy, and the patient was directed to continuous nephrology follow-up. DISCUSSION The overall analysis of the data showed a significant prevalence of comorbidities in patients with renal cancer, with particular reference to hypertension, found in 77% of the subjects, and smoking, present in 63.3% of the patients. These results confirm the importance of these risk factors, as previously highlighted [ ], in the predisposition to the development of renal neoplasms. BMI > 25, present in 30% of the patients, and diabetes mellitus, found in 16.6% of the patients, were instead found to be less frequent risk factors within the cohort examined. Furthermore, the distribution of comorbidities was not uniform among the patients: 60% of the subjects had at least two concomitant risk factors, increasing the probability of an accelerated deterioration of renal function in the postoperative period. Another relevant parameter analyzed was renal function, assessed through the eGFR both in the preoperative and postoperative period. Before surgery, 33% of patients had an eGFR < 60 ml/min. This data, considering the median age of the cohort equal to 65.5 years, is consistent with previous literature reports, according to which 22% of candidates for nephrectomy present with an eGFR < 60 ml/min, a percentage that increases to 40% in patients over 70 years of age. In the postoperative period, 50% of patients who initially presented

increasing the probability of an accelerated deterioration of renal function in the postoperative period. Another relevant parameter analyzed was renal function, assessed through the eGFR both in the preoperative and postoperative period. Before surgery, 33% of patients had an eGFR < 60 ml/min. This data, considering the median age of the cohort equal to 65.5 years, is consistent with previous literature reports, according to which 22% of candidates for nephrectomy present with an eGFR < 60 ml/min, a percentage that increases to 40% in patients over 70 years of age. In the postoperative period, 50% of patients who initially presented with an eGFR greater than 60 ml/min showed a decline in renal function to eGFR values <60 ml/min. This percentage is higher than the expected rate, which is around 33.7% according to the literature [ ], probably due to the limited size of the cohort and the significant number of pre-existing comorbidities in the patients included in the study. Histological analysis of healthy renal parenchyma revealed that 41% of patients had chronic tubulointerstitial damage, indicating a significant prevalence of this condition within the population studied. The genesis of this tubulointerstitial damage is likely closely related to chronic inflammation. This may reflect a paraneoplastic microenvironment where the tumor induces systemic or local inflammation and potential thrombotic lesions. This data takes on particular significance as it suggests that, in patients undergoing partial nephrectomy, the portion of the residual kidney could also likely be involved in this pathological process, with potentially significant implications for long-term renal function. The most relevant finding for the objectives of this study is represented by the fact that 24% of patients (seven in total) had confirmed nephropathy. Among these patients, two cases of confirmed paraneoplastic nephropathies were observed, one IgA nephropathy and one minimal lesion disease, since both resolved spontaneously after surgical removal of the renal tumor. Considering the limited size of the sample analyzed, the finding of two paraneoplastic nephropathies represents a particularly relevant finding. Although recognized in oncology [ ], paraneoplastic nephropathies associated with renal tumors are infrequently documented, largely due to the lack of routine histological assessment of the non-neoplastic kidney [ ]. We can assert that there is a certain lack of knowledge regarding the specific prevalence of paraneoplastic nephropathies in patients with renal cancer, and these cases suggest that paraneoplastic nephropathies from renal tumor may be more common than expected. Membranous glomerulonephritis was found in two other patients, while fibrillary glomerulonephritis was observed in another case. These cases likely do not have a paraneoplastic origin, as no regression of the nephropathy was observed following surgery. In these circumstances, the evaluation of healthy renal parenchyma was essential to avoid repeated biopsies aimed at acquiring a definitive diagnosis. In particular, in one of the patients with membranous glomerulonephritis, the early initiation of treatment with ICI, before having histological results, led to a rapid worsening of renal function, making it necessary to interrupt the therapy. This example supports the importance of the evaluation of healthy renal parenchyma in the oncological management of the patient. CONCLUSIONS Although this analysis is based on a limited sample size, it highlights that chronic tubulointerstitial damage is the predominant alteration in the non-neoplastic renal parenchyma of patients undergoing radical nephrectomy. Furthermore, the percentage of confirmed nephropathies observed is significant, and their early identification allowed an optimization of the therapeutic management. The identification of two cases of paraneoplastic nephropathy holds particular significance, indicating a potentially higher incidence of such conditions in patients with renal cancer than what has been previously documented in the literature. In conclusion, evaluating the non-neoplastic renal parenchyma during radical nephrectomy is crucial. It allows for the early identification of undiagnosed nephropathies, estimates the functional reserve of the contralateral kidney, and helps avoid repeated biopsies in patients with a solitary kidney. Ultimately, this approach optimizes therapeutic choices and reduces exposure to nephrotoxic treatments in high-risk patients.

chunks.content: Introduction Chronic kidney disease (CKD) is a global health hazard and one of the primary causes of increased mortality rates worldwide [ ]. A significant cross-sectional study reported an 8.2% prevalence rate of CKD in Chinese adults during 2018–2019 [ ]. As renal function progressively deteriorates, CKD may advance to end-stage kidney disease (ESKD), necessitating renal replacement treatments (RRTs), thereby imposing significant burdens on patients and the healthcare system at large. Sodium-glucose transporter 2 inhibitors (SGLT2is) have recently gained significant attention as a new class of oral glucose-lowering drugs. Studies have found that SGLT2i may protect kidney through various mechanisms, such as restoring tubule-glomerular feedback, reducing renal fibrosis, anti-inflammatory, antioxidative stress, improving renal hypoxia, and reducing uremic toxicity [ – ]. Importantly, large-scale randomized controlled trials (RCTs) on SGLT2i have verified its capabilities in kidney protection and cardiovascular disease (CVD) risk reduction beyond glycemic control, such as CREDENCE [ ], DAPA-CKD [ ], EMPA-KIDNEY [ ]. Moreover, the 2022 Kidney Disease Improving Global Outcomes (KDIGO) guidelines have designated SGLT2i as the treatment of choice for individuals with type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) and CKD [ ]. SGLT2i plays a crucial role in managing the metabolism of DM patients by modulating lipid profiles [ ], decreasing uric acid (UA) levels [ ], reducing blood pressure [ ], and facilitating weight loss [ ]. The DONATE study reported significant reductions in glycated hemoglobin (HbA1c), body mass index (BMI), waist circumference, and both systolic blood pressure (SBP) and diastolic blood pressure (DBP) in T2DM patients [ ]. Furthermore, Anson et al. [ ] have confirmed similar improvements in HbA1c, weight, blood pressure, estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR), and lipid levels across type 1 DM (T1DM) patients treated with SGLT2i. These studies demonstrated that SGLT2i is an effective option for comprehensive metabolic management in diabetes. Although the benefit of SGLT2i on T2DM patients has been well studied, their impact on renal progression in CKD patients remains unclear in a real-world clinical practice setting. This study aims to analyze the effect of SGLT2i on renal, cardiovascular, and clinical outcomes in CKD patients based on the China Renal Data System (CRDS) databases in China. Methods Study Design, Participants, and Data Source This multicenter retrospective cohort study, following Strengthening the Reporting of Observational Studies in Epidemiology (STROBE) reporting standards, employed de-identified data from the CRDS [ , ]. Additional data details are provided in online supplementary Methods (for all online suppl. material, see https://doi.org/10.1159/000550222 ). This study included adults diagnosed with CKD and hospitalized, spanning January 1, 2002 – January 16, 2023. Stringent CKD identification was performed, including repeated laboratory measurements (eGFR <60 mL/min/1.73 m 2 , proteinuria ≥1+, urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio (UACR) ≥30 mg/g, or microalbuminuria ≥30 mg/L) and a definitive ICD-10 diagnosis, encompassing those admitted for CKD-related complications or as a comorbidity [ ]. Individuals with a history of T1DM, secondary or gestational DM, polycystic kidney disease (PKD), pancreatitis, cirrhosis, hepatitis, organ transplants, or malignant tumors were excluded from the study. Patients with ESKD, as identified by the ICD-10 code, or with an eGFR below 15 mL/min/1.73 m 2 for at least 4 weeks, who had started RRTs or received kidney transplant before the index date were also excluded. Both SGLT2i and glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1RAs) had similar clinical indications and temporal trends in use [ , ]. Additionally, patients who used GLP-1RA during the study were excluded due to their metabolism effects and CVD risk reduction [ ]. A breakdown of patient selection is summarized in a. Details of SGLT2i prescriptions were extracted from the CRDS database and verified using electronic medical records from respective academic centers. The study included users on the medication for over 90 days, with all participants followed for at least 3 months. For SGLT2i users, the index date was the date of their first prescription of SGLT2i. Nonusers, those without prescriptions for SGLT2i, had an index date randomly assigned to any medical admission. Outcomes The primary outcomes were the first occurrence of CKD progression, ESKD, or composite outcomes during follow-up. According to KDIGO guidelines, CKD progression was defined as a significant eGFR decrease, both a drop in category (≥90 [G1], 60–89 [G2], 45–59 [G3a], 30–44 [G3b], 15–29 [G4], <15 [G5] mL/min/1.73 m 2 ) and a 25% or more reduction from the baseline eGFR [ ]. Additionally, we analyzed cardiovascular events such as myocardial infarction (MI), heart failure (HF), stroke, and transient ischemic attack (TIA). A 3-month lag was implemented to evaluate the long-term efficacy of SGLT2i. The secondary outcomes were safety and clinical effects of SGLT2i. Safety outcomes encompassed adverse effects after SGLT2i initiation, including diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA), severe hypoglycemia, urinary tract infection (UTI), pyelonephritis, genital candidiasis, acute pancreatitis, gastrointestinal upset, etc. Clinical outcomes involved metabolic parameter changes, analyzed from 3 months to 3 years post-SGLT2i initiation.

Individuals with secondary outcomes cannot be reviewed and are retained in the subsequent analysis. The follow-up started on the index date and ended at the occurrence of any primary outcome or loss to follow-up. b illustrates the study’s analytical timeframe and the length of inclusion criteria. Covariates We collected demographic information (age, sex) and assessed comorbidities (based on ICD-10 codes) within 1 year before the index date. Drug utilization data included antidiabetic medications, anti-hypertension agents (angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors, angiotensin receptor blockers, renin-angiotensin system inhibitors (RASis), etc.), lipid-lowering drugs, UA-lowering medications, etc. Additional medications recorded were nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, glucocorticoids, immunosuppressants, and diuretics. The Anatomic Therapeutic Chemical codes for these drugs are provided in online supplementary Table S1. We extracted physical examination and laboratory measurements (within 3 months before the index date), including BMI, SBP, DBP, serum creatinine (Scr), eGFR, blood urea nitrogen (BUN), serum UA, total cholesterol (TC), triglycerides (TG), low-density lipoprotein cholesterol (LDL-C), HbA1c, hemoglobin, hematocrit, and urinary protein, etc. We calculated the eGFR using the CKD Epidemiology Collaboration equation [ ]. Statistical Analysis Categorical variables were presented as frequency (percentages) and analyzed using the Pearson χ 2 test, while continuous variables are shown as mean ± standard deviation and tested using an unpaired, 2-tailed t test or Wilcoxon test. We evaluated baseline characteristics using standardized mean differences (SMDs) to estimate their relative balance. Propensity score matching (PSM), implemented with R’s “MatchIt” package, aimed to minimize bias and control confounders, with a 1:2 matching ratio and a caliper set at 0.02. After matching, an SMD below 0.2 was regarded as balanced between the groups [ , ]. Time-to-event analyses for outcomes were performed using the Kaplan-Meier method and log-rank test to estimate cumulative incidences, alongside multivariate Cox proportional-hazards models to determine hazard ratios (HRs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs) and p values. The partly adjusted model (model 1) was adjusted for age, gender, baseline eGFR, and urinary protein, while the fully adjusted model (model 2) included additional adjustments for CKD duration, use of anti-hypertensive, other glucose-lowering, lipid-lowering, and UA-lowering agents. In sensitivity analyses, we additionally adjusted for the number of prior hospitalizations, SBP and serum sodium to address the residual imbalance of these covariates after PSM. Subgroup analyses for the renal outcomes considered age (<60 or ≥60 years), eGFR (<45 or ≥45 mL/min/1.73 m 2 ), urine protein (urine dipstick [positive: 1+–4+ or negative: − or ±]), RASi use, patients with T2DM, diabetes complications, hypertension, and coronary heart disease (CHD). We performed a time-based analysis on changes in metabolic parameters. Statistical analyses were conducted in situ on the CRDS platform using R version 4.3.1. All tests were two sided, with a p value <0.05 considered statistically significant. Results Baseline Characteristics of the Total Study Population We identified 155,053 CKD patients, including 1,829 treated with SGLT2i for over 3 months without any GLP-1RA prescription. Their baseline characteristics are detailed in . The follow-up duration averaged 907.23 ± 1,044.64 days. Patients averaged 56.96 ± 20.67 years old, with a CKD duration of 1.69 ± 2.86 years, and 54.5% were male. Patients had a mean eGFR, urinary protein, and HbA1c of 60.81 ± 43.53 mL/min/1.73 m 2 , 1+, and 9.1 ± 2.0%, respectively. In the whole CKD cohort, prevalent comorbidities included hypertension (56.31%), T2DM (34.89%), and CHD (26.78%). Medication use was widespread, with 55.0% of patients on anti-hypertensive agents (angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitor 18.0%, angiotensin receptor blockers 26.8%, and RASi 33.7%). Additionally, 35.4% received other glucose-lowering treatments, such as insulin (21.0%), metformin (8.6%), and dipeptidyl peptidase-4 inhibitors (DPP4i, 5.9%). Lipid-lowering drugs, primarily statins, were used by 30%, while 19.0%, 34.2%, and 36.8% were treated with UA-lowering drugs, diuretics, and nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, respectively. Glucocorticoids and immunosuppressants were prescribed to 24.0% and 5.7% of the cohort. SGLT2i users were generally older, more frequently male and had longer CKD durations compared to nonusers. They also presented with higher BMI, baseline eGFR, and HbA1c levels. Initially, SGLT2i users were more likely to have T2DM, diabetic complications, hypertension, hyperlipidemia, hyperuricemia, and CHD. After applying PSM, the core analysis included 1,477 SGLT2i users and 2,674 nonusers, summarized in .
